(p-267) Surah al-Ma'idah

Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Ḍaḥḥak said: it is Madani. Muqatil said: it was revealed during the day, and all of it is Madani. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: among it is what is Makki, [namely] ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾. He said: It has also been said: among it is what is Makki, [namely] ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾. The correct view is that His words ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ were revealed at ʿArafah, on the day of ʿArafah, and for this reason it is attributed to Makkah.

﴿O you who have believed, fulfill [your] contracts. Lawful for you are the quadrupeds of livestock, except for what is recited to you, [but] not permitting hunting while you are in the state of ihram. Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills.﴾

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿O you who have believed﴾: the scholars differed regarding who is addressed by this, on two views.

The first: they are the believers of our Ummah, and this is the view of the majority.

The second: they are the People of the Book; this was said by Ibn Jurayj. And "al-ʿUqud" (the contracts): the covenants; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Ḍaḥḥak, al-Suddi, and the community. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-ʿUqud" are the most binding of covenants.

The scholars differed regarding what is meant by "covenants" here, on five views. (p-268) The first: they are the covenants of Allah which He took from His servants concerning what He made lawful and unlawful; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid.

The second: they are all the covenants of the religion; this was said by al-Hasan.

The third: they are the covenants of the Jahiliyyah, which is the alliance that existed among them; this was said by Qatadah.

The fourth: they are the covenants which Allah took from the People of the Book concerning belief in the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ); this was said by Ibn Jurayj, and we have already mentioned from him that the address is to the People of the Scripture.

The fifth: they are the contracts of people among themselves, such as sale and marriage, or a person's binding of himself by a vow or oath; this is the view of Ibn Zayd.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Lawful for you are the quadrupeds of livestock﴾: concerning "bahimat al-anʿam" there are three views.

The first: they are the unborn young of livestock found dead in the wombs of their mothers when the mothers are slaughtered; this was said by Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: they are camels, cattle, and sheep; this was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

al-Rabiʿ said: they are all livestock. Ibn Qutaybah said: they are camels, cattle, sheep, and all wild animals.

The third: they are the wild livestock, such as gazelles and wild oxen; this was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu Salih. al-Farraʾ said: bahimat al-anʿam are wild oxen, gazelles, and wild asses.

(p-269) al-Zajjaj said: it is called "bahimah" because it is unable to distinguish (ubhimat ʿan an tumayyiz), and every living thing that cannot distinguish is a bahimah.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿except for what is recited to you﴾: it was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: it is carrion and all that the Qur'an prohibits. Ibn al-Anbari said: what is recited to us of the prohibited is the verse that follows it, which is His words: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion﴾.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿not permitting hunting﴾: Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said: "fulfill the contracts, not permitting hunting," so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Others said: the meaning is: lawful for you are the quadrupeds of livestock, not permitting yourselves to hunt them while you are in the state of ihram. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-Ḥurum" means those in the state of ihram; the singular of ḥurum is ḥarām, as one says: a man ḥarām, and a people ḥurum. The poet said:

I said to her: "Turn back to me, for I am in ihram, and yet after that I am wise,"

(p-270) i.e., one who utters the talbiyah. His words, ﴿Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills﴾, meaning: the creation belongs to Him; He makes lawful what He wills for whom He wills, and forbids what He wills upon whom He wills.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 2:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not violate the rites of Allah﴾. There are two reports concerning the occasion of its revelation.

The first: "Shurayh ibn Dubay'ah came to Madinah, entered upon the Prophet ﷺ, and said: 'To what do you invite?' He said: 'To the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and that I am the Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'I have leaders behind me, and I will return to them and consult them.' Then he left. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'He entered with the face of a disbeliever and left with the heels of a treacherous man, and this man is not a Muslim.' Shurayh then passed by a herd belonging to the people of Madinah and drove it off. When the year of al-Hudaybiyah came, Shurayh went out toward Makkah to perform 'umrah (the lesser pilgrimage), and with him was merchandise. The owners of the herd wished to raid him as he had raided them, so they asked permission of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this verse was revealed." This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. Al-Suddi said: "His name was al-Hutam ibn Hind al-Bakri." He said: "When he drove off the herd, he began to chant:

Night has wrapped it with a driver, a crusher,
Not a shepherd of camels, nor of sheep,
Nor a butcher on the back of a... and a cleaver.
They lay down asleep, while the son of Hind did not sleep.
He kept driving them, a youth like an arrow-shaft,
Thick-calved, with smooth-soled feet.

The second: that some polytheists came intending the House on the day of the Conquest, in the state of ihram (the sacred state entered for pilgrimage) for 'umrah. The Muslims said: "We will not leave these people; rather we will raid them." So the verse was revealed: ﴿Nor those who make for the Sacred House﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: "The rites of Allah are that which Allah has made a sign of His obedience."

Concerning what is meant by them here, there are seven opinions.

The first: they are the rites of the Hajj. This was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas. Al-Farra' said: "Most of the Arabs did not regard al-Safa and al-Marwah as among the rites, and did not circumambulate between them. So Allah the Exalted said: Do not deem lawful the abandoning of that."

The second: they are what Allah the Exalted has forbidden while in the state of ihram. This was related by al-'Awfi from Ibn Abbas.

The third: the religion of Allah in its entirety. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: the limits of Allah. This was said by Ikrimah and Ata'.

The fifth: the sanctuary (haram) of Allah. This was said by al-Suddi.

The sixth: the sacrificial animals marked for the Sacred House of Allah. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Zajjaj.

The seventh: they are the markers of the sanctuary, forbidding them from passing beyond them while not in ihram when they wish to enter Makkah. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi and Qadi Abu Ya'la.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nor the sacred month﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "Do not deem lawful fighting in it."

Concerning what is meant by the sacred month, there are three opinions.

The first: it is Dhu al-Qa'dah. This was said by Ikrimah and Qatadah.

The second: what is meant is the sacred months (al-ashhur al-hurum). Muqatil said: "Junadah ibn 'Awf used to stand in the market of 'Ukaz every year and say: 'Verily I have made lawful such-and-such, and forbidden such-and-such.'"

The third: it is Rajab. This was mentioned by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

"Al-hady" (sacrificial offering): everything that is offered to the House of Allah the Exalted of anything. Concerning "the garlands" (al-qala'id), there are two opinions.

The first: they are the garlanded animals of the hady. This was related by al-'Awfi from Ibn Abbas.

The second: they are what the polytheists used to garland their camels and themselves with in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic age), so that they would be safe from their enemy, because war was constant among the Arabs except in the sacred months. Whoever met a person garlanding himself or his camel, or marking his animal, or driving a sacrificial animal, would not be molested. Ibn Abbas said: "Whoever wished to travel outside the sacred months would garland his camel with hair and wool, and he would be safe wherever he went." Malik ibn Mighwal related from Ata' who said: "They used to garland themselves with the bark of the trees of the sanctuary, and they would be safe with it when they left the sanctuary, so this verse was revealed." Qatadah said: "A man in the Jahiliyyah, when he left his home intending the Hajj, would garland himself with acacia (samur), and no one would confront him; and when he returned, he would garland himself with a garland of hair, and no one would confront him."

Al-Farra' said: "The people of Makkah garlanded themselves with the bark of trees, while the rest of the Arabs garlanded with wool and hair." Concerning the meaning of the statement, there are three opinions.

The first: do not deem lawful the garlanded animals of the hady. The second: do not deem lawful those who wear the garlands. The third: this is a prohibition to the believers from plucking anything from the trees of the sanctuary and garlanding themselves with it, as the polytheists used to do in their Jahiliyyah. This was related by 'Abd al-Malik from Ata', and Mutarrif and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said likewise.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nor those who make for the Sacred House, the Ka'bah﴾. "Al-amm" means the one who intends. "Fadl" means profit in trade. "Ridwan" from Allah is what they seek in their Hajj according to their claim. A parallel is His saying: ﴿And look at your god, to which you remained devoted﴾. It was said: seeking bounty is general, while seeking the good pleasure is specific to the believers.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾. Its wording is that of a command, but its meaning is permission. Its parallel is: ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse through the land﴾. It indicates a previous state of ihram.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And let not hatred ... lead you﴾. Al-Walid related from Ya'qub that it is read "yajrimannakum" with the letter nun (n) unvocalized and lightened. Ibn Abbas said: "Let it not bear you (la yahmilannakum)." Others said: "Let it not bring you into sin (al-jurm), as you say 'athamtuhu', meaning 'I made him enter into sin.'" Ibn Qutaybah said: "Let it not earn for you. It is said: 'Fulan jarim ahlihi,' meaning he is their earner, and likewise their jarimah." The Hudhali poet said, describing an eagle:

A jarimah of a fledgling on a cliff's top,
You see, for the bones it has gathered, a skeleton.

"Al-nahid" is her chick. He means: she earns for it, and brings it its sustenance. "Al-shana'an" means hatred. It is said: "shanii'tuhu, ash'uhu" when one hates him. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Al-shana'an" is hatred, and "al-sha'n" with a sukun on the nun is the one who is hated. The readers differed concerning the nun of "al-shana'an": Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read it with a vowel; Ibn 'Amir read it with a sukun; Hafs related from 'Asim the vowel, Abu Bakr from him the sukun; and it was likewise differed concerning Nafi'.

Abu 'Ali said: "Al-shana'an" has come as a description and has come as a noun. Whoever vocalizes it does so because it is a verbal noun (masdar), and the masdar often occurs in the form fa'alan, like al-nazawan. Whoever puts a sukun on it says it is a masdar, and the masdar has also come in the form fa'lan; you say: 'lawaytuhu daynahu laya'nan.' So the meaning in both readings is one, even if the wordings differ."

They differed concerning His saying: ﴿that they barred you﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a kasrah. The rest read it with a fathah. Whoever reads with a fathah makes the "sadd" (barring) a past verb, so the meaning is "because they barred you." Whoever reads with a kasrah makes it conditional, so the barring is anticipated. Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said: "The verb may be past even with a kasrah, as in His saying: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before﴾. The theft had already occurred in their view." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi recited:

When we claim lineage, a base woman did not bear me,
Nor did you find any way but to acknowledge it.

[The negation of birth is a past matter, yet he made it a condition, and a condition is only with the future, so the meaning is: if we claim lineage, you will not find me born of a base woman.] Ibn Jarir said: "The reading of the one who puts a fathah on the alif is clearer, because this surah was revealed after al-Hudaybiyah, and the barring had already occurred."

Based on this, there are two opinions concerning the meaning of the statement.

The first: let not the hatred of the people of Makkah, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, move you to transgress in it, so that you fight them and take their wealth when you enter it. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: let not the hatred of the people of Makkah and their barring you move you to transgress by committing what is not lawful for you, such as raiding the polytheist 'umrah pilgrims, according to what preceded concerning the occasion of the revelation of the verse.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety﴾. Al-Farra' said: "Let some of you help one another." Ibn Abbas said: "Righteousness (al-birr) is what you are commanded to do, and piety (al-taqwa) is abandoning what you are forbidden from. As for 'sin' (al-ithm), it is acts of disobedience. And 'transgression' ('udwan) is overstepping the limits of Allah." This was said by Ata'.

**Section**

The scholars of abrogation (al-nasikh wa al-mansukh) differed concerning this verse into two opinions.

The first: it is definitive (muhkam, not abrogated). It was related from al-Hasan that he said: "Nothing has been abrogated from al-Ma'idah." Likewise Abu Maysarah and others said. They said: "It is not permissible to violate the rites, nor the hady before the time of its slaughter." They differed concerning the "garlands": some said: it is forbidden to remove the garland from the hady until it is slaughtered. Others said: the Jahiliyyah used to garland with the trees of the sanctuary, so it was said to them: do not deem lawful taking garlands from the sanctuary, nor bar those who intend the House.

The second: it is abrogated, and concerning what is abrogated from it there are four opinions.

The first: all of it is abrogated. This is the opinion of al-Sha'bi.

The second: it was revealed concerning the polytheists who garlanded their hady and displayed the rites of Hajj, such as ihram and the talbiyah (the call "Labbayk"). The Muslims were forbidden by this verse from confronting them. Then that was abrogated by His saying: ﴿So kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾. This is the opinion of the majority.

The third: what was abrogated is His saying: ﴿Nor those who make for the Sacred House﴾, which was abrogated by His saying: ﴿They shall not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs﴾. This was related from Ibn Abbas and Qatadah.

The fourth: what is abrogated from it is the prohibition of the sacred month, and of those who intend the Sacred House when they are polytheists, and the hady of the polytheists when they have no safe-conduct from the Muslims. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

[p. 280] **"Al-mutaraddiyah"** (the animal that falls to its death) is the one that falls from a mountain or a wall, or into a well. It is said *taraddā* when it falls.

**"Al-nati'ah"** (the animal gored to death) is the one struck by a goat or a cow. It is a *fa'ilah* form with the meaning of *maf'ulah* (passive).

﴿And what the beast of prey has eaten﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Razin, Abu Mijlaz and Ibn Abi Layla read *al-sab'* with a sukun on the *ba'*. The intended meaning is what the predator has seized and eaten part of.

﴿Except what you have slaughtered﴾ means: except what you reach from all of this while it still has life in it, and then you slaughter it.

As for the exception, there are two opinions.

The first is that it refers back to what was mentioned from the words ﴿and the strangled﴾.

The second is that it refers only to what the beast of prey has eaten. The scholars hold the first view.

**Section on slaughter (dhakah)**

Al-Zajjaj said: The root meaning of *dhakah* in the language is the completion of a thing. From it comes *al-dhaka'* (intelligence) in the teeth, which is the completion of the teeth. Al-Khalil said: *al-dhaka'* is when an animal's incisors have completed a year, and this is the full completion of strength. From it also comes *al-dhaka'* in understanding, which is complete understanding, quick to accept. *Dhakaytu al-nar* means I completed its kindling.

It is narrated from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah that they said: If you reach its slaughter while there is an eye that blinks or a tail that moves, its flesh is lawful.

Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: The position of our companions (the Hanbali school) is that if the animal can live with its condition, it becomes lawful by slaughter. If it cannot live with its condition, you must examine it. If its life is not stable, and its movement is only the movement of one already slaughtered, such as when its belly is split open and its intestines are exposed and separated from it, its flesh is not lawful. If its life is stable and it can live a day or two, such as when its belly is split but the intestines are not cut, its flesh is lawful. Some people say that if there is any life in it at all, it becomes lawful by slaughter. The correct view is what we have mentioned, because if there is no stable life in it, it is in the status of the dead. Do you not see that if a man cuts the entrails of a human being and then another strikes his neck, the first is the killer, because life does not remain after the first act?

[p. 281] There are two narrations concerning what must be cut in slaughter.

One is that it is the windpipe (*al-hulqum*) and the gullet (*al-mari'*), and the two veins between them. If any of these is cut short, the animal is not eaten. This is the apparent meaning of Ahmad's words in the narration of 'Abd Allah.

[p. 282] The second is that cutting the windpipe and the gullet suffices. This is the apparent meaning of his words in the narration of Hanbal, and al-Shafi'i held this view. Abu Hanifah said: cutting the windpipe, the gullet and one of the two jugular veins suffices. Malik said: cutting the jugular veins suffices, even if the windpipe is not cut. Al-Zajjaj said: the windpipe is after the mouth, and it is the place of breath, and in it are branches that divide into the lungs. The gullet is the passage of food. The two jugular veins (*al-wadajan*) are the two veins that the slaughterer cuts.

As for the instrument with which slaughter is permitted, it is anything that makes the blood flow and cuts the jugular veins, except [p. 283] a tooth or a nail, whether they are detached or not detached. Abu Hanifah permitted slaughter with a detached tooth or nail. As for a camel that has run wild, or fallen into a well, it is in the position of game, and its slaughter is by wounding it. Malik said: its slaughter is the slaughter of an animal under one's control. If a man shoots at game and severs part of it, while it still has stable life, and then he slaughters it, or leaves it until it dies, its flesh is lawful. There are two narrations about eating the part that was severed.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And what is sacrificed on the stones (*nusub*)﴾. There are two opinions about *al-nusub*.

One is that they are idols that are set up and worshipped besides Allah. This is what Ibn 'Abbas, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said. On this view the meaning is: what was slaughtered in the name of the idols, or for their sake. Here *'ala* carries the sense of *li* (for), and the two interchange in speech, as in His saying: ﴿So peace be upon you (*fa-salamun laka*)﴾ (al-Waqi'ah 56:91), meaning "for you", and His saying: ﴿And if you do evil, it is for them (*fa-laha*)﴾ (al-Isra' 17:7).

[p. 284] The second is that they are stones upon which they used to slaughter and cut up meat and which they venerated. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj. Al-Hasan and Kharijah, from Abu 'Amr, read *'ala al-nasb* with a fatha on the *nun* and a sukun on the *sad*. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said *nusub*, *nusb* and *nasb*, and its plural is *ansab*.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And that you seek decisions by arrows (*al-azlam*)﴾. Ibn Jarir said: that is, that you seek knowledge of what has been apportioned to you, or not apportioned, by means of the arrows. It is the *istaf'altu* form from *al-qasm* (division) [the division of provision and needs]. Ibn Qutaybah said: *al-azlam* are the divining arrows (*al-qidah*); the singular is *zalam* or *zulam*. Seeking decisions by them means that they are struck and one acts upon what emerges from them of command or prohibition. When they wished to divide something among themselves, and wanted to know each person's share, they learned it from these arrows. So the term *istiqsam* is taken from *al-qism*, which is the share. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: *al-azlam* are white pebbles. When they intended to go out in the morning or in the evening, they wrote on two arrows, on one: "My Lord has commanded me," and on the other: "My Lord has forbidden me." Then they struck them, and whichever came out, they acted upon. Mujahid said: *al-azlam* are the arrows of the Arabs and the knucklebones of the Persians with which they gambled. Al-Suddi said: the arrows were kept by the soothsayers. Muqatil said: in the house of the idols. Some people said: they were kept by the custodians of the Ka'bah. Al-Zajjaj said: there is no difference between this and the words of the astrologers: "Do not go out because of such-and-such a star," or "Go out because of such-and-such a star."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿That is wickedness (*fisq*)﴾. There are two opinions about what the word "that" refers to.

One is that it refers to everything mentioned in the verse. This was transmitted by 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr held it.

[p. 285] The second is that it refers to seeking decisions by the arrows. This was transmitted by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. *Al-fisq* is departing from obedience to Allah into disobedience to Him.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion﴾. There are three opinions about "this day".

The first is that it is the day on which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered Makkah during the Farewell Pilgrimage. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: it was revealed on that day.

The second is that it is the Day of 'Arafah. This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

The third is that it does not refer to a specific day; the meaning is "now they have despaired," just as you say: "I have now grown old." This was said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: the Arabs apply "today" to a period that includes hours and nights. They say: "I was heedless, and today I have awakened," meaning "now." And they say: "So-and-so used to visit us, and today he shuns us," and by "today" they do not mean one specific day. A poet said:

[p. 286]
"A day for us and a day against us, a day that we are harmed and a day that we rejoice."

He meant: a time for us and a time against us, and he did not mean one single day to which nothing else is joined.

There are two opinions about the meaning of their despair.

One is that they despaired that the believers would return to the religion of the polytheists. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi.

The second is that they despaired of the nullification of Islam. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: they only despaired of nullifying the religion of the believers when Allah moved the fear of the Muslims toward them and their security toward the Muslims. They knew that they could not nullify the religion of the Muslims or uproot them. They fought them after that only because they thought their disbelief would remain.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So do not fear them﴾. Ibn Jurayj said: do not fear that they will prevail over you. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: do not fear that they will prevail over your religion, and fear Me in opposing My command.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾. Al-Bukhari and Muslim in their two *Sahih*s narrate from the hadith of Tariq ibn Shihab, who said: "A man from the Jews came to 'Umar and said: O Commander of the Believers, you recite a verse in your Book which, if it had been revealed to us Jews, we would have taken that day as a festival. He said: Which verse is it? He said: His saying: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you﴾. 'Umar said: I know the day on which it was revealed to the Messenger of Allah, and the hour in which it was revealed, and the place where it was revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who was standing at 'Arafah on a Friday." In another wording: "It was revealed on the evening of 'Arafah." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ lived after that eighty-one days.

As for His saying "today", there are two opinions.

One is that it is the Day of 'Arafah. This is the view of the majority.

The second is that it is not a specific day. This was transmitted by 'Atiyyah from Ibn 'Abbas, and we have mentioned this just above.

There are five opinions about the meaning of the perfecting of the religion.

The first is that it is the perfecting of its obligations and its limits, and no permission or prohibition was revealed after this verse. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi. On this view the meaning is: today I have perfected for you the laws of your religion.

The second is that it means the exclusion of the polytheists from the House, so that no polytheist made the pilgrimage with them that year. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah. Al-Sha'bi said: the perfection of the religion here is its might and its dominance, and the humiliation and effacement of polytheism, not the completion of the obligations and the sunnah, because these continued to be revealed until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died. On this view the meaning is: today I have perfected for you the victory of your religion.

[p. 288] The third is that it means the lifting of *naskh* (abrogation) from it. As for the obligations, they continued to be revealed until he died. This is also narrated from Ibn Jubayr.

The fourth is that it means the removal of fear of the enemy and dominance over them. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The fifth is that it made this Shari'ah secure from being abrogated by another after it, as it abrogated what came before it. There are three opinions about the completion of the favour.

One is the prevention of the polytheists from making the pilgrimage with them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah.

The second is guidance to faith. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third is the manifestation of victory over the enemy. This was said by al-Suddi.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Whoever is compelled (*fa-man idturra*)﴾, that is, he is driven by necessity to eat what has been forbidden to him. ﴿In a state of severe hunger (*makhmasah*)﴾, that is, famine. *Al-khamas* is hunger. A poet, censuring a man, said:

"He sees hunger as torment, and if he meets a full belly, his heart stays confused from the scarcity of concern."

This statement refers back to the forbidden things mentioned earlier, carrion and blood, and what was mentioned together with them.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Without inclining to sin (*mutajanif li-ithm*)﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: not inclining toward it. *Al-janaf* is inclination. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid said: not intentionally committing sin.

There are two opinions about the meaning of "inclining to sin".

One is that he takes from it after the necessity has passed. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and others.

[p. 289] The second is that he sets himself upon disobedience in his purpose. This was said by Qatadah. Mujahid said: whoever rebels and goes out in disobedience, eating it becomes unlawful for him. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: this is more sound than the first view, because the verse requires the combination of inclining to sin with necessity, and that can only hold in the case of the sinful traveller. It cannot be understood as taking more than what suffices to keep one alive, because the necessity has already ceased. Abu Sulayman said: the meaning of the verse is: whoever is compelled and eats it without inclining to sin, then Allah is ﴿Forgiving﴾, that is, He overlooks it, ﴿Merciful﴾, since He has made that lawful for the one under compulsion.

(p-290) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them﴾ — regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts.

One: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the killing of dogs, the people said: O Messenger of Allah, what has been made lawful for us from this community that you have commanded to be killed? So this verse was revealed." Abu 'Abd Allah al-Hakim reported it in his Sahih from the hadith of Abu Rafi', from the Prophet (ﷺ). The reason for the Prophet's (ﷺ) command to kill them was that "Jibril (peace be upon him) asked permission to enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)(p-291) and he was given permission, but he did not enter and said: 'We do not enter a house in which there is a dog or a picture.' So they looked, and in some of their houses there was a puppy."

The second: "'Adi ibn Hatim and Zayd al-Khayl, whom the Messenger of Allah named Zayd al-Khayr, said: O Messenger of Allah, we are a people who hunt with dogs and hawks; of what is caught, we sometimes reach its slaughter and sometimes we do not reach its slaughter, and Allah has forbidden carrion, so what is lawful for us of it? So this verse was revealed." This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the speech is: They ask you what has been made lawful for them? Say: What is good has been made lawful for you, and the game caught by the trained hunting animals that you have taught has been made lawful for you. The interpretation is that they asked about it, but the mention of "the game caught by what you have taught" was omitted, because the context indicates it.

Regarding "the good things" (al-tayyibat) there are two views.

One: that they are what is permissible of slaughtered animals.

The second: that they are what the Arabs found good, of what has not been forbidden.

As for "al-jawarih" (the trained hunting animals), they are the predatory beasts and birds used in hunting, such as the dog, the leopard, the falcon, the hawk, and the like, of what accepts training. Ibn 'Abbas said: Everything that hunts is a jarih.

(p-292) Regarding its being called "al-jawarih" there are two views.

One: because its owners earn by means of it. Ibn Qutaybah said: The root of al-ijtirah is earning; it is said: "a woman who has no jarih," meaning no earner.

The second: because they generally wound what they hunt; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: The sign of training is that when you call it, it answers; when you incite it, it becomes fierce and pursues its prey; and when it holds, it holds for you and not for itself. The sign of its holding for you is that it does not eat any of it. This applies to beasts and dogs; as for training hunting birds, it differs from beasts, because the bird is trained to hunt by eating, whereas the leopard, the dog, and similar animals are trained by refraining from eating. This is the difference between them.

Regarding His saying: ﴿mukallibin﴾ there are three views.

One: that they are the owners of dogs. Abu Salih reported it from Ibn 'Abbas; it is the view of Ibn 'Umar, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, and Ibn Qutaybah. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "a man is mukallib and kilabi," meaning one who hunts with dogs.

The second: that the meaning of "mukallibin" is "persisting in hunting," and this is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Mujahid.

The third: that "mukallibin" means "those who teach." Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: They were called mukallibin only because most of their hunting is done with dogs. Tha'lab said: al-Hasan and Abu Razin read "mukliBin" with the kaf sukun, it is said: "akalaba al-rajul" when his dogs became numerous, and "amsha" when his livestock became numerous; and the Arabs call a hunter "mukallib."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You teach them from what Allah has taught you﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: You discipline them for hunting (p-293). al-Farra' said: You discipline them so that they do not eat their catch. They differed on whether the hunter's restraint from eating is a condition for the validity of the training, or not, in three views.

One: that it is a condition for all trained animals; if it eats, it is not to be eaten. This was reported from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata'.

The second: that it is not a condition for all; it may be eaten even if it eats. This was reported from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Hurayrah, and Salman al-Farisi.

The third: that it is a condition for trained beasts, and not a condition for trained birds; this was the view of al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, and al-Suddi. It is the most sound, because we have explained that the trained bird is trained to eat, so what it eats is permitted, whereas the predatory beasts are trained to refrain from eating, so what they eat is not permitted.

Accordingly, if the dog or the leopard eats of the game, it is not permitted to eat it. As for what the falcon or hawk eats of it, it is permitted; this is the view of Abu Hanifah and his companions. Malik said: What the dog, the leopard, or the falcon eats of it is permitted to eat; if the dog kills and does not eat, it is permitted.

Abu Hanifah said: It is not permitted. If the hunter reaches the game while it still has life, and it dies before he slaughters it, then if that happens before he is able to slaughter it, it is permitted; if he was able to slaughter it and did not, it is not permitted. This was the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah said: It is not permitted in either case.

As for hunting with the dog of a Magian, it is reported from Ahmad that it is not disliked, and this is the view of most scholars; and it is reported from him that it is disliked, and this is the view of al-Thawri, due to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and what you have taught from the trained animals﴾, and this is addressed to the believers. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: Our companions prohibited hunting with the black dog, even if it is trained, because the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded its killing; and the command to kill prevents the establishment of possession and nullifies the ruling of the act, so its existence becomes like its non-existence, and therefore its game is not permitted.

(p-294) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So eat of what they hold for you﴾. al-Akhfash said: "min" is superfluous, like His saying: ﴿in which is hail from the mountains﴾ [al-Nur: 43].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and mention the name of Allah over it﴾. Regarding the pronoun "ha' al-kinayah" there are two views.

One: that it refers to the sending (of the animal). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi, and in our view the mention of Allah's name is a condition for the permissibility of the game.

The second: that it refers to the eating, so mentioning the name is recommended.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and fear Allah﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Do not deem lawful what the name of Allah has not been mentioned over.

(p-295) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you﴾. Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: It is possible that by "today" he means the very day on which the verse was revealed, and it is possible that he means the day mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion﴾, and in His saying: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾. It has also been said that it does not refer to any specific day. The discussion of "the good things" has already preceded, and he repeated their permissibility only for emphasis. As for the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab), they are the Jews and the Christians. Their food (ta'am) is their slaughtered animals (dhaba'ih). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and the majority. The meaning here is specifically the slaughtered animals, because the rest of their food does not differ depending on whether it is prepared by a Magian or a People of the Book. What differs is the ritual slaughter (dhaka). Since he singled out the People of the Book with this, it indicates that what is meant is the slaughtered animals. As for the slaughtered animals of the Magians (majus), there is consensus on their prohibition. They differed concerning the slaughtered animals of idol-worshippers who adhere to Judaism or Christianity. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked about the slaughtered animals of the Christian Arabs, and he said: "There is no harm in them," and he recited His saying: ﴿Whoever among you takes them as allies, then indeed he is one of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51]. This is also the view of al-Hasan, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, al-Sha'bi, Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Zuhri, al-Hakam, and Hammad. It has been narrated from 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and others that their slaughtered animals are not lawful. Al-Kharqi transmitted two narrations from Ahmad concerning the Christians of Banu Taghlib.

One of them: their slaughtered animals are permitted. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and Malik.

The second: they are not permitted. Al-Shafi'i said: Whoever enters the religion of the People of the Book after the revelation of the Qur'an, the eating of his slaughtered animal is not permitted.

(p-296) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And your food is lawful for them﴾. That is: your slaughtered animals are lawful for them. So if they buy something from us, the price is lawful for us and the meat is lawful for them. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: It has been made lawful for you that you feed them.

Section

Some people claimed that this verse necessitates the permissibility of the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book absolutely, even if they mentioned other than the name of God over them. So this would abrogate (naskh) His saying: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am: 121]. The correct view is that the verse grants permission for their slaughtered animals in general, because the default assumption is that they mention God, so their practice is interpreted in this light. If we are certain that they mentioned other than Him, then we do not eat, and there is no basis for abrogation. Ali, Ibn 'Umar, 'Ubadah, Abu al-Darda', al-Hasan and a group of others held the view that I have stated.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And chaste women from among the believing women﴾. Concerning them there are two views.

One: they are the chaste (al-'afa'if). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: they are free women (al-hara'ir). This was said by Mujahid.

Concerning His saying: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Book﴾ there are two views.

One: they are also free women. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they are the chaste. This was said by al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. According to this view, it is permissible to marry a free woman and a slave woman from among them.

Section

This verse permits marriage (nikah) to a woman of the People of the Book. It has been narrated from Uthman that he married Na'ilah bint al-Farafisah, who was a Christian, in addition to his other wives. And from Talhah ibn 'Ubayd Allah that he married (p-297) a Jewish woman. It has also been narrated from Umar and Ibn 'Umar that they disliked this. They differed concerning marrying a woman of the People of the Book who is a combatant (harbiyyah). Ibn 'Abbas said: It is not lawful. The majority hold the opposite view. They disliked it only because of His saying: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in God and the Last Day loving those who oppose God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadalah: 22], and marriage necessitates affection. They differed concerning marrying the women of Taghlib. It was narrated from Ali, may God be pleased with him, that it is prohibited, and Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Nakha'i said likewise. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is permitted. There are two narrations from Ahmad. They differed concerning the slave women of the People of the Book. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid that marrying them is not permitted, and this was the view of al-Awza'i, Malik, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, al-Shafi'i and our companions. It was narrated from al-Sha'bi and Abu Maysarah that it is permitted, and this was the view of Abu Hanifa. As for the Magians, the majority hold that they are not People of the Book. Whoever said that they are People of the Book is an outlier, and his view is refuted by the words of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Treat them as you would treat the People of the Book." As for "wages" (ujur), "chastity" (ihsan), "fornication" (sifah) and "secret lovers" (akhdan), these were discussed previously in Surat al-Nisa'.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in faith, his deeds have become void﴾. The occasion of revelation of this statement: When God, may He be exalted, granted the concession regarding marrying the women of the People of the Book, they said among themselves: "If God had not been pleased with us, He would not have permitted the believers to marry us." And the Muslims said: "How can a man among us marry a Christian or Jewish woman when she is not upon our religion?" So this was revealed: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in faith, his deeds have become void﴾. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: It was revealed concerning those women of the People of the Book whom the Muslims made chaste, meaning: the Muslims' making them chaste does not remove them from disbelief. Layth related from Mujahid regarding "whoever disbelieves in faith" that he said: faith in God, may He be exalted. Al-Zajjaj said: (p-298) The meaning of the verse: whoever makes lawful what God has prohibited, or prohibits what God has made lawful, is a disbeliever. Abu Sulayman said: Whoever denies what God has revealed of the laws of faith, and what He has made known of the lawful and the unlawful, his previous deeds have become void. I heard al-Hasan ibn Abi Bakr al-Nisaburi, the jurist, say: God, mighty and majestic, only permitted the women of the People of the Book because some Muslims may be attracted by their beauty, so He warned the one who marries them against inclining toward their religion, by His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in faith, his deeds have become void﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 6:**

(p-298)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When you rise to prayer﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is "when you intend to rise to prayer," like His saying: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 98]. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is like your saying: "If you seek brotherhood, then seek the people of noble lineage, and if you trade, then trade in cloth." He said: It is also possible that the speech is in front and back order, its implied meaning being: "When you have washed your faces and completed the purification, then rise to prayer." The scholars have two views on the intended meaning of the verse.

One: "When you rise to prayer while in a state of minor impurity (ḥadath), then wash." Thus the impurity becomes implied in the obligation of wudu' (ablution). This is the view of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn Abbas, and the jurists.

(p-299)

The second: The speech is in its general sense without any implied element, so wudu' is obligatory upon everyone who wishes to pray, whether in a state of impurity or not. This is narrated from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), Ikrimah, and Ibn Sirin. He reported from them that this ruling is not abrogated (naskh). He also reported from a group of scholars that it was obligatory and then abrogated by the Sunnah, namely what Buraydah narrated: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed five prayers on the day of the Conquest with one wudu'. Umar said to him: 'You have done something you did not used to do?' He said: 'I did it deliberately, O Umar.'" Others said: In the verse there is inversion and reordering (taqdim wa ta'khir), and its meaning is: "When you rise to prayer from sleep, or one of you comes from the place of relieving himself, or you have touched women, then wash your faces."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and your hands up to the elbows﴾. "Ila" (up to) is a particle set for the limit (al-ghayah, the end point). The limit may sometimes be included and sometimes not included. Since the impurity is certain, it is not lifted except by an equally certain thing, namely washing the two elbows. As for the head, it is narrated from Ahmad that wiping all of it is obligatory, and this is the view of Malik. It is also narrated from him that wiping most of it is obligatory. Two narrations are reported from Abu Hanifa:

One: that it is limited to a quarter of the head. The second: to the extent of three fingers.

(p-301)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and your feet up to the two ankles﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Hamzah, and Abu Bakr, from Asim, read it with a kasra on the lam, as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the wiping of the head. Nafi', Ibn Amir, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from Asim, and Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the lam, as a conjunction on the washing, so it would be of the reordered type. Al-Zajjaj said: The leg is from the root of the thigh to the foot. When the ankles are stated as the limit, it is known that the washing ends at them. The limit by the two ankles indicates the obligation of washing, just as the limit "up to the elbows" came in the case of the hand. Nothing in the case of wiping came with a limit. It is also possible that washing is intended even with the kasra reading, because the limit by the two ankles indicates washing, so it is joined to the washing by being conjoined with the wiping. The poet said:

"Would that your husband had become one who wears a sword and carries a spear."

The meaning is: "and carrying a spear." Another said:

"I fed them straw and cold water."

The meaning is: "and I gave them cold water to drink." Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said: The genitive (jarr) is permitted by the principle of following (itba'), and the meaning is washing, (p-302)

like the saying: "A ruined lizard's hole." Ibn al-Anbari said: Since the feet came after the heads, they were conjoined to them because of proximity and nearness, and in meaning they are conjoined to the faces, like the saying: "A ruined lizard's hole." It is also possible that they are conjoined to the heads, because the Arabs call washing "wiping," since washing does not occur without a kind of wiping. Abu Ali said: Whoever reads with the genitive has as his argument that he found two governing elements in the speech: one is the washing, and the other is the preposition "bi" (in). When two governing elements come together, the speech is to be taken according to the nearer of them rather than the more distant. This is "bi" here. The evidence has also been established that by wiping is meant washing, for two reasons.

One: Abu Zayd said: "Masḥ" is a light washing. They say: "I wiped myself (tamassahtu) for prayer." Abu Ubaydah said: "fa-ṭafiqa masḥan bi-l-sūq," meaning "striking." So wiping in the verse is like a light washing. If it is said: Then is the preferred practice repetition three times? It is said: The verse only brought what is obligatory, not what is prescribed as Sunnah.

The second reason: the limit and time-setting came only with the washed part, not with the wiped part. When the limit came together with wiping, it is known that it has the ruling of washing, since it agrees with washing in the limit. The argument of the one who reads with the accusative (naṣb) is that he took that as washing, because the jurists of the cities agree on washing.

(p-303)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿up to the two ankles﴾. "Ila" here means "ma'a" (with). The two ankles (al-ka'bān) are the two protruding bones on either side of the foot.

(p-304)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you are in a state of janabah (major impurity), then purify yourselves﴾. That is: "then cleanse yourselves (fa-tatahharu)." The ta' was assimilated into the ta' (ṭa'), because they are from the same point of articulation, and a hamzah was introduced as a means of reaching the pronunciation of a sukun (unvoweled letter). Allah, mighty and majestic, has explained the purification of the one in janabah in the surah of al-Nisa' by His saying: ﴿until you wash (taghtasilu)﴾ [al-Nisa': 43]. We have already discussed there the speech about the rest of the verse, up to His saying: ﴿Allah does not want to place upon you any hardship﴾. "Al-ḥaraj" means constriction. Allah made the religion broad when He granted the concession of tayammum (dry ablution).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But He wants to purify you﴾. That is: He wants to purify you. Muqatil said: From minor and major impurities. Others said: From sins and misdeeds, because wudu' expiates sins.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and to complete His favor upon you﴾. Regarding that by which the favor is completed, there are four views.

One: by the forgiveness of sins. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: Abdullah ibn Darah narrated to me, from Himran, who said: "I passed by Uthman with a jug of water, so he called for it and performed wudu' and did it well. Then he said: 'Had I not heard it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) once, or twice, or three times, I would not have related it to you. I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "No servant performs wudu' and does it well, then rises to prayer, except that what is between him and the next prayer is forgiven him."'" Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: Whenever I heard a hadith, I sought it in the Qur'an, and I found this in His saying: ﴿Indeed We have granted you a clear victory, that Allah may forgive you your past and future sins and complete His favor upon you﴾ [al-Fath: 1-2]. So I knew that Allah did not complete the favor upon him until He forgave him his sins. Then I recited the verse in al-Ma'idah: ﴿When you rise to prayer﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and to complete His favor upon you﴾, and I knew that He did not complete the favor upon them until He forgave them.

(p-305)

Two: by guidance to faith and the perfection of the religion. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Three: by the concession of tayammum. This was said by Muqatil and Abu Sulayman.

Four: by clarifying the laws of the sharia. Some exegetes mentioned this.

Allah's saying: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾ — meaning, all the blessings. In this is an exhortation to gratitude. Regarding the covenant (al-mithaq) there are four opinions.

The first: that it is the affirmation of every believer of what he believed in. Ibn 'Abbas said: When Allah sent down the Book and sent the Messenger, and they said, "We believe," He reminded them of His covenant which they had affirmed against themselves, and commanded them to fulfill it.

The second: that it is the covenant which He took from the children of Adam when He brought them forth from his loins. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid and Ibn Zayd also said so.

The third: that it is what He bound upon the believers, through the tongue of His Prophet ﷺ, of the command to fulfill what they had affirmed of faith. This meaning was related by 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: that it is the covenant taken from the Companions to hear and obey in the Pledge of 'Aqaba and the Pledge of al-Ridwan. Some exegetes mentioned this.

Allah's saying: ﴿And fear Allah﴾ — Muqatil said: fear Him in breaking the covenant. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾ — that is, of what is in them of faith and doubt.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

The first: it was revealed also concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh, whose mention has already preceded in His saying: ﴿And do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness﴾ [sic: ﴿and let not the enmity of a people, that they obstructed you from al-Masjid al-Haram, incite you to transgress﴾]. Abu Salih related something similar to this from Ibn Abbas, and Muqatil said it.

The second: Quraysh sent a man to kill the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so Allah informed His Prophet of that, and this verse and the one after it were revealed. This is the saying of al-Hasan.

The third: "The Prophet (ﷺ) went to the Jews of Banu al-Nadir seeking their help regarding a blood-money payment, so they intended to kill him, and this verse was revealed." This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah. The meaning of the verse: be persistently standing firm for Allah with the truth, and let not the hatred of a people move you to abandon justice. ﴿Be just﴾ toward the friend and the enemy alike. ﴿It is nearer to righteousness﴾, i.e., nearer to taqwa (God-consciousness). The meaning: it is closer to your being among those who are mindful of Allah. And it was said: it is closer to guarding against the Fire.

One of them: the meaning is that Allah promised them that He would forgive them and reward them, and He was satisfied with what He mentioned of this meaning.

The second: the meaning is that He promised them, so He said: ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾. We have explained in (al-Baqarah) the meaning of "al-Jahim" (الجَحِيمِ, the blazing Fire).

One of them: the meaning is that Allah promised them that He would forgive them and reward them, and He was satisfied with what He mentioned of this meaning.

The second: the meaning is that He promised them, so He said: ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾. We have explained in (al-Baqarah) the meaning of "al-Jahim" (الجَحِيمِ, the blazing Fire).

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 11:

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you when a people determined to extend their hands toward you﴾. Regarding its occasion of revelation (sabab nuzul), there are four opinions.

The first: "A man from Muharib said to his people, 'Shall I not kill Muhammad for you?' They said, 'And how will you kill him?' He said, 'I will treacherously strike him (afteku bihi).' So he approached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with his sword in his lap. He took it and began to shake it and intended to strike him, but Allah repelled him. Then he said, 'O Muhammad, do you not fear me?' He said, 'No.' He said, 'Do you not fear me while the sword is in my hand?' He said, 'Allah protects me from you.' So he sheathed the sword, and this verse was revealed." This was narrated by al-Hasan al-Basri from Jabir ibn Abdullah. In some wordings: "The sword fell from his hand." In another wording: "The Prophet ﷺ said nothing to him and did not punish him." The name of this man was Ghawrath ibn al-Harith from the Muharib of Khasafah.

The second: The Jews resolved to treacherously attack the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but Allah sufficed him against their evil.

Ibn Abbas said: "They prepared food for him, and he was informed by revelation of their plan, so he did not go." Mujahid and Ikrimah said: "He went out to them seeking their help regarding blood money (diyah). They said, 'Sit until we give you (what you need).' So he sat, he and his companions. They withdrew to confer with one another and said, 'You will not find Muhammad closer to you than he is now. Who will climb onto this house and drop a stone upon him?' Amr ibn Jihash said, 'I will.' He came to a large millstone to drop it upon him, but Allah restrained his hand. Jibril came and informed him, and he left, and this verse was revealed."

The third: "The Banu Tha'labah and the Banu Muharib intended to treacherously attack the Prophet and his companions while they were at Batn Nakhlah during the seventh expedition (ghazwat) of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. They said, 'They have a prayer which is dearer to them than their fathers and mothers. When they prostrate, we will fall upon them.' So Allah informed His Prophet of that, (p-310) and He revealed the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf), and this verse was revealed." This is the statement of Qatadah.

The fourth: It was revealed concerning the Jews when they backed the polytheists against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This is the statement of Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾. Abu al-'Aliyah said: Allah took their covenant that they would make their worship sincerely for Him and not worship other than Him. Muqatil said: that they would act in accordance with what is in the Torah.

Regarding the meaning of the naqib (chief/representative), there are three opinions.

The first: that he is the guarantor (damin). This was said by al-Hasan, and its meaning is that he is a guarantor so as to know the circumstances of those under his authority, and he cannot be a guarantor on their behalf for their fulfilment (of the covenant), because such a guarantee is not valid. Ibn Qutaybah said: he is the surety (kafil) over the people. The office of naqabah is similar to that of 'arafah (the office of the 'arif, the overseer).

The second: that he is the witness (shahid). This was said by Qatadah. Ibn Faris said: the naqib is the witness of the people and their guarantor.

The third: that he is the trustworthy one (amin). This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas and al-Yazidi, and these opinions are close in meaning. Al-Zajjaj said: The naqib in the language is like the amin and the kafil. It is said: "naqaba al-rajulu 'ala al-qawm yanqubu" when a man becomes a naqib over the people, and his office is naqabah. Likewise, "'arafa 'alayhim" when he becomes an 'arif. It is also said of the first thing that appears of mange: al-nuqbah, and its plural is nuqab and nuqb. The poet said:

Disheveled, his good qualities appear, he places the tar (hana') on the places of the mange (nuqb).

It is also said: "Fulan has noble qualities (manaqib jamilah)." The root meaning of the whole word is an impression that has depth and penetration. From this comes "naqabtu al-ha'it," meaning I reached its far end in boring, and al-nuqbah from mange is a disease of severe penetration. It is said "naqib" because he knows the inner matter of the people, recognizes their noble qualities, and it is the path to knowing their affairs. It is related that Allah, exalted is He, commanded Musa and his people to travel to the Holy Land, which was inhabited by the tyrants. Allah, exalted is He, said: "O Musa, go out to it (p-312) and strive against the enemy within it, and take from your people twelve naqibs, one naqib from each tribe, who will be a guarantor over his people for fulfilling what they were commanded," so they chose the naqibs.

Regarding what they were sent for, there are two opinions.

One: that Musa sent them to Bayt al-Maqdis to bring him news of the tyrants. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The second: that they were sent as guarantors over their people for fulfilling their covenant. This was said by al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq. Regarding their prophethood there are two opinions. The more correct of them: they were not prophets.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah said﴾. In the speech there is an omitted element. Its estimation: And Allah said to them.

Regarding those to whom it was said, there are two opinions.

One: that they are the Children of Israel. This was said by the majority.

The second: that they are the naqibs. This was said by al-Rabi' and Muqatil. The meaning of ﴿Indeed I am with you﴾ is: with help and support. Regarding the meaning of ﴿and you support them﴾ there are two opinions.

One: that it is aid and support. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The second: that it is honouring and respect. This was said by 'Ata', al-Yazidi, Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you lend Allah a goodly loan﴾. Regarding this lending there are two opinions.

One: that it is the obligatory zakah. The second: voluntary charity. We have explained the meaning of the goodly loan in (al-Baqarah).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever disbelieves after that among you﴾ refers to the covenant, ﴿then he has certainly strayed from the sound way﴾, meaning: he has missed the intended path.

(p-312) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant﴾ — there is an elided element in the speech; its estimate is: "So they broke it, and for their breaking [of it] We cursed them." Regarding what is meant by this curse there are three opinions.

The first: it is punishment through the jizya (poll tax). This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it is punishment through transformation (maskh, into animal forms). This is related from al-Hasan and Muqatil. The third: it is removal from mercy. This is related from ʿAta' and al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made their hearts hard﴾ — Ibn Kathir, Nafi', ʿAsim, Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿAmir read "qasiyah" with an alif, from the verb qasat, so it is qasiyah. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and al-Mufaddal from ʿAsim read "qasiyyah" without an alif, with the yaʾ doubled, because the pattern fa'il and fa'il may come in the same sense, like shahid and shahid, and ʿalim and ʿalim. The "qaswah" (hardness) is the opposite of softness and tenderness. We have mentioned this in (al-Baqarah).

As for their distortion of the words (tahrif al-kalim), there are three opinions.

The first: changing the limits (hudud) of the Torah. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: changing the description of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is related from Muqatil. The third: interpreting it in a way other than what was revealed. This is related from al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿from their places﴾ — this is explained in Surah (al-Nisa').

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of﴾ — "forgetting" (al-nisyan) here means deliberate abandonment. And "portion" (hazz) means share. Mujahid said: "They forgot the Book of Allah that was revealed to them." Others said: "They abandoned their share of the covenant that was taken from them." Regarding the meaning of ﴿they were reminded of﴾ there are two opinions:

One: they were commanded. The second: they were instructed.

(p-314) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them﴾ — al-Aʿmash read "ʿala khiyanatin minhum" (upon betrayal from them). Ibn Qutaybah said: al-khaʾinah means al-khiyanah (betrayal). It may also be a description of the traitor, as one says "rajul taghiyah" and "rawiyah lil-hadith" (a man who is extremely rebellious; a great transmitter of hadith). Ibn ʿAbbas said: this is like the breaking of the covenant of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by the Banu Qurayzah, and the going out of Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf to the people of Makkah to incite them against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿Except a few of them﴾ — they did not break the covenant; they are ʿAbdullah ibn Salam and his companions. It is also said: rather, the few are those among them who did not believe.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So pardon them and overlook﴾ — the scholars differed about whether it has been abrogated, on two views:

One: it has been abrogated. This is the view of the majority. They differed about its abrogating verse on three views:

The first: it is the verse of the sword. The second: His saying: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29]. The third: His saying: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people﴾ [al-Anfal: 58].

The second: it was revealed concerning a people who had a covenant with the Prophet (ﷺ), then they betrayed it and intended to kill the Prophet (ﷺ), but Allah made him prevail over them, and then Allah revealed this verse. It was not abrogated.

Ibn Jarir said: it is permissible that they be pardoned for a treachery they committed, so long as they do not take up war and do not refuse to pay the jizya and acknowledge subjugation; therefore abrogation does not apply.

(p-315) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And from those who say, "We are Christians," We took their covenant﴾. Al-Hasan said: He only said "those who say, 'We are Christians'" and did not say "from the Christians," to indicate that they were not truly upon the method of the Christians, and they are those who followed al-Masih (the Messiah). Qatadah said: They were in a village called Nasirah, and so they were named by this name. Muqatil said: A covenant was taken from them, just as a covenant was taken from the People of the Torah that they would believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), but they abandoned what they were commanded.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We stirred up among them﴾. An-Nadr said: We incited. Al-Mu'arrij said: We set some of them against others. Az-Zajjaj said: We attached that to them. It is said: "I adhered to the man" (gharaytu bil-rajuli gharan, maqsuran) when you clung to him; this is the statement of al-Asmai. Other than al-Asmai said: "gharraytu bihi ghira'" (with a long vowel), and this ghira' is the adhesive with which things are stuck. The meaning of "We stirred up among them enmity and hatred" is that they became sects, each of which declares the others to be unbelievers. Regarding the ha' and mim in His saying "among them" (baynahum), there are two views.

One: they refer to the Jews and the Christians; this was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, and as-Suddi.

The second: they refer to the Christians specifically; this was said by ar-Rabi'. Az-Zajjaj said: They are the Christians, among them the Nestorians, the Jacobites, and the Melkites, and each sect among them opposes the other. And in the completion of the verse there is a severe warning for them.

(p-316) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O People of the Scripture﴾ — regarding whom there are two opinions.

One of them: they are the Jews. The second: the Jews and the Christians. And the Messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He makes clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they concealed the verse of stoning (rajm) and the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his description. ﴿And He pardons much﴾ — He overlooks it, so He does not inform them of their concealment. If it is said: how could he refrain from clarifying a truth that they concealed? There are two answers to this.

One of them: he was receiving what he was commanded; when he was commanded to make known something of their affairs, he made it known and held them to it, and otherwise he remained silent.

The second: the dhimmi covenant (ʿaqd al-dhimma) was made on the basis that they would remain upon their religion. When they concealed much of what they had been commanded, and took something other than it as their religion, He made known to them what they had concealed of his description and the sign of his prophethood, so that his miracle would be established for them. They also brought the matter of stoning before him for judgment, so he made known what they had concealed that agreed with his law, and he remained silent about other matters so that their acceptance of their religion would be established.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There has certainly come to you from Allah a light﴾. Qatadah said: by the light is meant the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ).

Others said: it is Islam. As for the ﴿clear Book﴾, it is the Qur'an.

The Arabic says "وَ "السُّبُلُ"" — translated below as part of the flow.

"As-subul" (the paths): the plural of sabil. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Subul al-salam" (the paths of peace) is the religion of Islam. Al-Suddi said: "Al-salam" is Allah, and "subuluhu" (His paths) is His religion which He prescribed. Al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that "subul al-salam" means the path of safety, whoever travels it is safe in his religion; and it is permissible that "al-salam" is one of the names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so the meaning would be: the paths of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He brings them out of darknesses﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means: disbelief (kufr), ﴿into the light﴾, meaning: faith (iman), ﴿by His permission﴾, i.e., by His command, ﴿and guides them to a straight path﴾, which is Islam. Al-Hasan said: the path of truth.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Certainly, they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary."﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: These are the Christians of Najran, and that is because they took him as a god.

﴿Say, "Who then has any power against Allah if He wished to destroy the Messiah, the son of Mary"﴾ That is: who is able to repel from Him any of His punishment?

﴿...if He wished to destroy the Messiah, the son of Mary﴾ That is: if he were a god as you claim, he would be able to turn back the command of Allah when it comes to him, to destroy him or to destroy his mother. When the command of Allah came down upon his mother, he was not able to repel it from her.

His saying, ﴿He creates what He wills﴾ is a refutation of them, when they said to the Prophet: "Then bring us the like of him without a father."

If it is said: Why did He say, ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ and not say "what is between them" (in the feminine dual form, "baynahunna")? The answer: the meaning is what is between these two kinds of things, as said by Ibn Jarir.

(p-318) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the Jews and the Christians said﴾. Muqatil said: They are the Jews of Madina and the Christians of Najran. Al-Suddi said: They said: Indeed Allah, exalted is He, revealed to Israel: "Your offspring are firstborn among children, so I will make them enter the Fire, where they will remain forty days until I purify them and consume their sins. Then a caller will call out: Bring forth every circumcised one of the Children of Israel." It was also said: When they said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," the meaning of their statement ﴿We are the sons of Allah﴾ was: one of us is the son of Allah. As for His saying: ﴿Say: Why then does He punish you for your sins?﴾, it is a refutation of their claim, because a father does not punish his son, and a beloved does not punish his beloved; yet they say that Allah punishes us with the Fire for forty days.

(p-319) It was also said: the meaning of the speech is: "Why then did He punish some of you by transforming them into apes and swine?" These are the people of the Sabbath and the table-spread.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Rather, you are human beings among those He has created﴾, that is: you are like the rest of the children of Adam, who are repaid for good and evil. ʿAtaʾ said: "He forgives whom He wills, and they are the monotheists, and He punishes whom He wills, and they are the polytheists."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 19:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has come to you Our Messenger﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, and 'Uqbah ibn Wahb said: 'O assembly of the Jews, fear Allah! By Allah, you know that he is the Messenger of Allah; you used to mention him to us before his mission, and describe him by his attributes.'

Then Wahb ibn Yahudha and Rafi' said: 'We did not say this to you, and Allah did not send down any Book after Moses, nor did He send any messenger bearing good tidings or warning [after him],' so this verse was revealed." This is related from Ibn 'Abbas.

As for "al-fatrah" (the interval between messengers), its root meaning is stillness. It is said: "fatara al-shay'" (the thing slackened) yafturu futuran, when its sharpness subsides and it ceases from what it was upon. A "fatir" glance is one that is not sharp. And "al-futur" is weakness. Regarding the length of the interval between 'Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, there are four opinions.

(p-320) The first: there were six hundred years between 'Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and Salman al-Farisi and Muqatil also said so.

The second: five hundred and sixty years, said by Qatadah.

The third: four hundred and some thirty years, said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: five hundred and forty years, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. Abu Salih said from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning ﴿in a lull between the messengers﴾, that it means: a cessation from them. He said: between the birth of 'Isa and the birth of Muhammad ﷺ were five hundred and ninety-nine years, and that is the interval. After 'Isa there were four messengers, and this is His saying: ﴿When We sent to them two, and they denied them, so We strengthened them with a third﴾ [Ya-Sin: 14]. He said: "As for the fourth, I do not know who he is." Between those years there were a hundred years, and thirty-four prophethoods, and the rest was an interval. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: "The fourth, and Allah knows best, is Khalid ibn Sinan, of whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'A prophet whom his people neglected.'"

(p-321) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿lest you say﴾. Al-Farra' said: "lest you say: ﴿there came to us no bearer of good tidings﴾," like His saying: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa': 176]. Others said: "lest you say," and it has been said: "out of aversion that you say."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 20:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When He made among you prophets﴾, there are two opinions concerning them.

One of them: they are the seventy whom Musa (Moses) chose and who set out with him to the mountain. God made them prophets after Musa and Harun (Aaron). This is the view of Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil.

The second: they are the prophets who were sent from the Children of Israel after Musa. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. And with what did He make them kings? Concerning this there are eight opinions.

The first: with the manna, the quail, and the stone. The second: by His giving a man among them a wife and a servant. The third: with the wife, the servant, and the house. These three were related from Ibn 'Abbas, and this third is the choice of al-Hasan and Mujahid. The fourth: with the servant and the house, said by Ikrimah. The fifth: by their being given ownership of servants, and they were the first to own servants, and "whoever takes a servant is a king," said by Qatadah. The sixth: by their being free, so that a person owns from among them himself, his family, and his property, said by al-Suddi. The seventh: by spacious dwellings in which there are flowing waters, said by al-Dahhak. The eighth: by His giving them kingship and authority, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds﴾, they differed concerning who was addressed by this, on two opinions.

One of them: they are the people of Musa, and this is the position of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Ibn 'Abbas said: by "the worlds" is meant those who were among them in their time. Concerning what He gave them there are three opinions.

The first: the manna, the quail, the stone, and the cloud, related by Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, and he held this view.

The second: that it is the house, the servant, and the wife, related by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Jarir said: no one among the worlds was given blessings in the time of the people of Musa like what they were given.

The third: the abundance of prophets among them, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The second: that the address is to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is the position of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik.

One of the two meanings: "the purified." This is said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Zajjaj, who said: It was also said that the bucket (al-saṭl) is called al-qadas, because it is used for purification (yutatahharu minhu). The Holy House (Bayt al-Maqdis) is so named because one is purified from sins within it. It was also said: He named it "sacred" (muqaddasah) because it was purified from polytheism and made a dwelling for the prophets and the believers.

The second: al-Muqaddasah means "the blessed." This is said by Mujahid.

Regarding the referent of "that land," there are four opinions.

The first: it is Ariha (Jericho). This was transmitted by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd also said so. Al-Suddi said: Ariha is the land of Bayt al-Maqdis. It is narrated from al-Dahhak that he said: the intended land is Iliya' and Bayt al-Maqdis. Ibn Qutaybah said: I read in the supplication of Musa that he said: "O God, You have chosen from the livestock the ewe, from the birds the dove, and from the houses Makkah and Iliya'; and from Iliya', Bayt al-Maqdis." This indicates that Iliya' is the land in which Bayt al-Maqdis is situated. I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur, the linguist, that Iliya' is Bayt al-Maqdis, and that it is an arabized word. Al-Farazdaq said:

"Two houses: the House of God, of which we are its custodians, and a house on the heights of Iliya' that is exalted."

The second opinion: it is al-Tur and what surrounds it. Mujahid transmitted this from Ibn 'Abbas and held it.

The third: it is Damascus, Palestine, and part of Jordan. Abu Salih transmitted this from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: it is the whole of al-Sham (Greater Syria). This was said by Qatadah.

Regarding His, the Exalted, words: ﴿which God has prescribed for you﴾ there are three opinions.

The first: it means "He commanded you and obligated you to enter it." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi.

The second: it means "God granted it to you." This was said by Muhammad ibn Ishaq. Ibn Qutaybah said: He made it yours.

The third: He wrote it in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) that it would be your dwellings.

If it is asked: how can He say ﴿for it is forbidden to them﴾ when He had prescribed it for them? There are two answers to this.

The first: He granted it to them on the condition of obedience, and when they disobeyed, He forbade it to them.

The second: He prescribed it for the children of Israel, and it passed to them; Musa did not mean that God prescribed it for those individuals who were commanded to enter it by their own persons. Ibn Jarir said: It is possible that the statement came in a general form while a specific group was intended, so it was written for some of them, and Yusha' and Kalib entered it.

Regarding His, the Exalted, words: ﴿and do not turn back on your heels﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: do not turn back from the command of God to His disobedience. The second: do not turn back to associating partners with Him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 22:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, in it are a people of great strength (jabbarin)﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The jabbar (tyrant, overbearing one) among human beings is the one who compels people to do what he wills.
