It is said: jabbar, meaning one clearly possessing jabariyyah (compulsion, domineering power), and al-jibriyyah with a kasra on the jim and the ba', and al-jabarut, al-jubburah, al-tajbar and al-jabarut (all denoting the same quality of domineering force).

Regarding the meaning of describing these people as jabbarin, there are three opinions.

The first: that they were people of strength; this is related from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that they were people of great stature and bodies; this is related from Qatadah. The third: that they were fighters; this is related from Muqatil.

(p-325) Reference to the story

Ibn 'Abbas said: When Musa and his people came to the city of the jabbarin, he sent twelve men to bring him news of them. A man from the jabbarin met them, put them in his garment, brought them to the city, and called out to his people, and they gathered. They said to them: "Where are you from?" They said: "We are the people of Musa; he sent us to come to him with news of you." So they gave them a single grape that would burden a man, and said to them: "Tell Musa and his people: measure the measure of their fruit." When they returned, they said: "O Musa, indeed in it are a people of great strength (jabbarin)." Al-Suddi said: The one who met them was called 'Aj, that is, 'Awj ibn 'Anaq. He took the twelve, put them in his chamber with a bundle of firewood on his head, and went with them to his wife, and said: "Look at these, who claim that they want to fight us." He threw them down before her and said: "Shall I not crush them with my foot?" His wife said: "No, rather release them until they inform their people of what they saw." When they went out, they said: "O people, if you inform the Children of Israel of the news of the people, they will apostatize from the Prophet of Allah." So they took a covenant among themselves to conceal that. Ten of them broke it, and two concealed it.

Mujahid said: When the nuqaba' (chiefs) saw the jabbarin, they found that two of them could enter the sleeve of one of them, and that five or four were needed to carry one cluster of their grapes, and five or four could enter a half of a pomegranate once its seeds were removed. So all the nuqaba' returned, forbidding their tribes from fighting them, except Yusha' and the son of Yuqanna.

(p-326) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Two men from among those who feared said﴾. Concerning the two men there are three opinions.

The first: they were Yusha' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yuqinna (Caleb). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: Ibn Yuqanna. Both were among the chiefs (nuqaba').

The second: they were among the giants (jabbarin) and embraced Islam. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: they were in the city of the giants, and they were upon the religion of Musa. This is the view of al-Dahhak. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Raja' and Ayyub recited "yukhafuna" with a dammed yaa', meaning that the two were from the enemy and came out as believers.

Concerning the phrase "their fear" (khawfihim) there are three opinions.

The first: they feared God alone. The second: they feared the giants, but their fear did not prevent them from speaking the truth. The third: "he fears from them," according to the reading of Ibn Jubayr.

Concerning what God bestowed upon them there are four opinions.

The first: Islam, the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The second: righteousness, virtue and certainty, the view of 'Ata'. The third: guidance, the view of al-Dahhak. The fourth: fear, mentioned by Ibn Jarir from some of the early generation (al-salaf).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Enter upon them through the gate﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: The two men said: Enter upon them through the gate of the town, for they have been filled with terror and dread from us.

(p-327) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Go, you and your Lord, and fight, while we sit here﴾. Ibn Zayd said: They said to him, "Look at what your Lord did to Pharaoh and his people, so let Him do the same to these." Muqatil said: "Go, you, and ask your Lord for victory." Others said: "Go, you, and let your Lord help you."

Ibn Mas'ud said: "I witnessed from al-Miqdad a stance that I would rather have been his companion in than anything else that might be exchanged for it. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was supplicating against the polytheists, and said: 'We will not say to you what the people of Musa said to Musa: ﴿Go, you and your Lord, and fight, while we sit here﴾. Rather, we will fight on your right and on your left, before you and behind you.' So I saw the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brighten at that, and he was pleased with it."

Anas said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) consulted the people on the day he set out for Badr. Abu Bakr gave him his opinion, then he consulted them again, and Umar gave him his opinion, but he remained silent. A man from the Ansar said: 'He only wants you (to speak).' So they said: 'O Messenger of Allah! We will not say to you what the Children of Israel said to Musa: ﴿Go, you and your Lord, and fight, while we sit here﴾. Rather, by Allah, if you were to drive your mounts to Bark al-Ghimad, we would go with you.'"

(p-328) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I have no power except over myself and my brother﴾, concerning which there are two opinions.

One of them: "I have no power except over myself, and my brother has no power except over himself."

The second: "I have no power except over myself and over my brother," meaning: and I have power over my brother's obedience, because when his brother obeys him, he is like a king to him. This is figurative, as it is related that "the Prophet ﷺ said: 'No wealth has benefited me as much as the wealth of Abu Bakr.' Abu Bakr wept and said: 'Am I and my wealth not but yours, O Messenger of Allah?' He meant: I am at your disposal wherever you direct me, and your command over my wealth is permitted."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So separate us from the defiantly disobedient people﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Judge between us and them." Abu 'Ubayda said: "Keep far away, distinguish, and set apart." Regarding the meaning of ﴿al-fasiqin﴾ (the defiantly disobedient, i.e., those who deliberately transgress the bounds of obedience), there are three opinions.

(p-329) One of them: the disobedient, related from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the liars, related from Ibn Zayd. The third: the disbelievers, related from Abu 'Ubayda. Al-Suddi said: "Musa became angry when they said to him: 'Go, you and your Lord,' so he invoked against them, and it was a hastiness from Musa, which he hastened."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 26:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then indeed it is forbidden to them﴾ The reference is to the Holy Land. The meaning of its being forbidden to them is that they were prevented from it. As for the accusative case of "forty" (arba'in), al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative by the verb "forbidden" (al-tahrim), and it is also permissible for it to be in the accusative by "they will wander" (yatihuna). Al-Zajjaj said: it cannot be in the accusative by "forbidden," because the exegesis has come that it is forbidden to them forever. I say: The exegetes differed on this. The majority, among them 'Ikrimah and Qatadah, held the view of al-Zajjaj, that it was forbidden to them forever. 'Ikrimah said: "Then indeed it is forbidden to them forever; they will wander in the land for forty years." Another group, among them al-Rabi' ibn Anas, held that it was forbidden to them for forty years, after which they were commanded to set out toward it, and this is the preference of Ibn Jarir. He said: It was only put in the accusative by "forbidden," and the prohibition applied generally to all of them, and none of them entered it during that period. When it ended, those among them who remained were permitted to enter together with their offspring. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the meaning of "yatihuna" is: they will go astray and be lost.

(p-330) The reference is to their story.

Ibn 'Abbas said: God forbade those who disobeyed from entering the House of the Holy (Bayt al-Maqdis), so they remained in their wandering for forty years, and they died in the wandering. Musa and Harun died, and none entered Bayt al-Maqdis except Yusha' and Kalib, among the sons of the people. Yusha' set out with those who remained with him against the city of the giants (al-Jabbarin) and conquered it. Mujahid said: They wandered for forty years, rising in the morning where they had been at evening, and being at evening where they had risen in the morning. Al-Suddi said: When God imposed the wandering upon them, Musa regretted his supplication against them, and they said to him: "What have you done with us? Where is the food?" So God sent down the manna. They said: "Where is the drink?" So Musa was commanded to strike the rock with his staff. They said: "Where is the shade?" So the cloud shaded them. They said: "Where is the clothing?" Their garments grew longer with them as children's grow, and no garment of theirs tore. Musa was taken (died), and none remained of those who refused to enter the town of the giants except that he died, and he did not witness the conquest. There is another opinion: that when the forty years had passed, Musa brought the Children of Israel out of the wandering and said to them: (Enter this town, and eat from it wherever you wish, abundantly, and enter the gate prostrating, and say: "Hittah" ...) to the end of the story. This is the saying of al-Rabi' ibn Anas and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: This is the correct view, and that Musa is the one who conquered the city of the giants together with the righteous among the Children of Israel, because the people of the biography (ahl al-sirah) agreed that Musa is the slayer of 'Awj, and 'Awj was their king, and Bal'am ibn Ba'ura' was among those whom Musa captured and killed. None of their former leaders entered with Musa except Yusha' and Kalib, and it was only forbidden to those who did not obey. There are two opinions on the extent of the land of the wandering.

One of them: nine farsakh, said by Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil said: this is its width, and its length is thirty farsakh. The second: six farsakh in length by twelve farsakh, also related by Muqatil.

(p-331) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So do not grieve over the defiant people﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: Do not grieve over a people whose concern is sins and opposing the messengers. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said "asiitu 'ala kadha," meaning "I grieved over such," so I grieve (ana aasi), with grief (asan).

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 5, verse 27:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam, in truth﴾. *An-naba'* means news or report. There are two views concerning "the two sons of Adam."

The first: they were his own sons by his loins, namely Qabil (Cain) and Habil (Abel). This was said by Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Qatādah.

The second: they were two brothers from the Children of Israel, and they were not the sons of Adam by his loins. This is the view of al-Ḥasan. The scholars hold the first view, and it is the more sound, because of His saying: ﴿So that he might show him how to conceal his brother's shame﴾ [al-Māʾidah 5:31]. Had they been from the Children of Israel, he would have known how to bury. Also, because the Prophet ﷺ said about him: "Indeed, he was the first to establish killing." (ﷺ)

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿in truth﴾ means: just as it was.

*Al-qurbān* (an offering brought near to God, a sacrifice) is on the pattern *fuʿlān* from *al-qurb* (nearness). We have discussed it in (Āl ʿImrān).

Concerning the cause for which they offered it, there are two views.

The first: Ādam, peace be upon him, had been forbidden to let a woman marry her twin brother, but he was permitted to marry her to someone other than her brothers. Each birth produced a male and a female. A daughter was born to him who was beautiful, and another who was plain. The brother of the plain one said to the brother of the beautiful one: "Marry me to your sister, and I will marry you to my sister." The brother of the beautiful one said: "I am more entitled to my sister." The brother of the beautiful one was a farmer, and the brother of the plain one was a herder of sheep. He said: "Come, let us each offer a sacrifice, and whichever of us has his sacrifice accepted is more entitled to her." So the herder brought a white, large-eyed, horned ram, and the farmer brought a heap of food. The ram was accepted, and God stored it in Paradise for forty autumns. It is the one that Ibrāhīm slaughtered. Then the farmer killed him. All of Adam's offspring come from that disbeliever. This was narrated by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second: they offered it without a cause. al-ʿAwfī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that the two sons of Adam were sitting one day, and they said: "If only we offered a sacrifice." The herder brought the best and fattest of his sheep, and the other brought some of his crops. Fire descended and consumed the sheep and left the crops. Then he said to his brother: "Will you walk among the people when they know that your sacrifice was accepted and that you are better than me? I will surely kill you."

They differed over whether Qabil and his sister were born before Habil and his sister, or after them, and there are two views on this. They also differed over whether Qabil was a disbeliever or a sinner who was not a disbeliever, and there are two views on this.

Concerning the reason his sacrifice was accepted, Habil's, there are two views.

The first: he was more God-fearing than Qabil. The second: he drew near (to God) with the best of his property, while Qabil drew near with the worst of his property.

Concerning whether their sacrifice was by the command of Ādam or on their own initiative, there are two views.

The first: it was while Ādam had gone to visit the House (the Kaʿbah). The second: Ādam had commanded them to do so.

Concerning whether Habil was killed after the marriage of Qabil's sister, or not, there are two views.

The first: he killed him before that, so that she would not be joined to him. The second: he killed him after marrying her.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "I will surely kill you."﴾ Zayd narrated from Yaʿqūb: "La-aqtulanka" with the *nūn* sukūn and lightened. The speaker is the one whose offering was not accepted. al-Farrāʾ said: he omitted mentioning him because the meaning indicates him. Similar to this in speech is when you say: "If you see the oppressor and the oppressed, help (the oppressed)," and "When the foolish and the forbearing gather, the forbearing is praised." That is because the meaning is not ambiguous. But if you said: "A man and a woman passed by me, so I helped," while you meant one of them, it would not be permissible, because there is no sign indicating what you intend.

Concerning the meaning of ﴿the God-fearing﴾, there are two views.

The first: they are those who guard against sins. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second: they are those who guard against shirk. This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 28:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I will not extend my hand toward you to kill you﴾. Concerning this there are two views.

One: "I will not retaliate on my own behalf." This is related from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: "I would not be the one to initiate against you." This is related from Ikrimah. Concerning the reason for his refraining from defending himself against him, there are two views.

One: His scrupulousness prevented him, although he was able to defend himself and it was permissible for him to do so. This is related from Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-335) The second: For a person to defend himself was not permissible at that time. This is related from al-Hasan and Mujahid. Ibn Jarir said: "There is no evidence in the verse that the one who was killed knew of the killer's determination to kill him and then abandoned defending himself. It has been mentioned that he was killed by stealth, so one should not claim what is not in the verse except with evidence."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 29:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin﴾, there are two opinions concerning it.

The first: "Indeed, I want you to return with the sin of my killing and your sin that is upon your neck." This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak.

The second: that you bear my sin for my wrongdoings, and your sin for your killing of me. This is also narrated from Mujahid. Ibn Jarir said: "The sound position from Mujahid is the first view." Al-Bukhari and Muslim have related in their two Sahihs, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam bears a share of its blood, because he was the first to establish killing." Now if it is asked: how could Habil, who was among the believers, want Qabil to bear the sin, which is disobedience, when the believer loves for his brother what he loves for himself? In answer to this there are three responses.

The first: he did not want his brother to commit the sin; rather he meant: if you kill me, I want you to bear the sin. This is the meaning to which al-Zajjaj went.

The second: that there is an elision in the speech, its implied sense being: "Indeed, I want that you not bear my sin and your sin," so the "not" (la) is omitted, as in His saying: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it should shake with you﴾ [Luqman: 10], meaning: lest it should not shake with you. From this is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"I said: By God's oath, I will not cease sitting, even if they cut off my head and my limbs before you."

He meant: "I will not cease." This is the view of Tha'lab.

The third: that the meaning is: "I want the removal of your bearing my sin and your sin, and the nullification of your bearing my sin and your sin," so that is omitted and "an" (that) takes its place, as in His saying: ﴿And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 93], meaning: the love of the calf. This is mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari, and the one before it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers﴾: the reference is to companionship with the Fire.

The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 30:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So his soul permitted to him the murder of his brother﴾. Regarding this there are five opinions.

The first: it made him follow [his inclination] to kill his brother. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it encouraged him, related from Mujahid. The third: it made it appealing to him, related from Qatada. The fourth: it made it easy for him, related from Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash. The fifth: that "tawwaʿat" is from "al-tawʿ" (obedience), and the Arabs say: "Ṭāʿa li-hādhihi al-ẓabyati uṣūlu hādhā al-shajar" and "ṭāʿa lahu kadhā," meaning it came to him willingly. This is related by al-Zajjaj from al-Mubarrad. Ibn Qutayba said: it complied with him and submitted to him; it is said, "My tongue does not comply (lā yaṭūʿu) with such-and-such," meaning it does not submit. These meanings are close to one another.

Regarding the manner of his killing there are three opinions.

The first: that he stoned him until he killed him; this was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: that he struck his head with a rock while he was asleep; this was narrated by Mujahid from Ibn ʿAbbas, and by al-Suddi from his shaykhs.

The third: that he crushed his head between two stones. Ibn Jurayj said: He did not know how to kill him, so Iblis appeared to him, took a bird, placed its head upon a stone, and then crushed it with another stone; he did this to him in this way. Habil was twenty years old at that time. Regarding the place where he was slain there are three opinions.

The first: on Mount Thawr, said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: at Basra, said by Jaʿfar al-Sadiq. The third: at the pass of Hira, related by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

Regarding His saying: ﴿So he became among the losers﴾ there are three opinions.

The first: among the losers in both this world and the Hereafter. His loss in this world was that he angered his parents and remained without a brother; his loss in the Hereafter was that he angered his Lord and went to the Fire. This is said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: that he became among those who lost the good deeds; said by al-Zajjaj. The third: among those who lost themselves by destroying them; said by al-Qadi Abu Yaʿla.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 31:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then Allah sent a crow scratching the ground﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: [Qabil] carried him on his shoulder, so whenever he walked, his hands and feet would drag on the ground, and whenever he sat, he would set him down beside himself, until he saw two crows fighting, and one of them killed the other. Then it scratched the earth for it until it buried it, after he had carried him for years. Mujahid said: He carried him on his shoulder for a hundred years. ʿAtiyya said: He carried him until he became exhausted. Muqatil said: He carried him for three days. Regarding the meaning of ﴿the corpse of his brother﴾ there are two views.

One of them: the private parts of his brother. The second: the corpse of his brother.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So he became among the regretful﴾. If it is said: Is not regret a repentance? Why was it not accepted from him? There are four answers to this.

The first: it is possible that regret was not a repentance for those before us, but it is a repentance for this community, because it was given distinctions in which it was not shared with others. This was said by al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl.

The second: he regretted carrying him, not killing him. The third: he regretted that he did not bury him when he killed him. The fourth: he regretted the loss of his brother, not the committing of the sin. In this story there is a warning against envy, for it is what destroyed Qabil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 32:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Because of that﴾. Al-Dahhak said: "Because of the son of Adam who killed his brother unjustly." Abu 'Ubayda said: "Because of the crime of that, and because of the course of that." The poet said:

؎ And the people of a tent, whose mutual affairs are sound, have fought over a matter whose consequence I shall bear.

That is: its perpetrator, and that (act) brought it upon them. Others said: the statement is connected to what precedes it, and the meaning is: "He became among the regretful because of that." On this reading, it is good to pause here; on the first reading, it is not good to pause. The first is more sound. And "We prescribed" (kataba-na) means: We made obligatory. The meaning of ﴿whoever kills a soul, not for a soul﴾ is: he kills it unjustly, while it has not killed a soul. ﴿Or corruption in the land﴾: "corruption" (fasad) is coordinated with "soul"; the meaning is: or without corruption that deserves killing. It was also said: by corruption here is meant polytheism (shirk). Regarding His saying ﴿it is as if he had killed all mankind﴾, there are five opinions.

The first: that he bears the sin of one who kills all mankind; this was said by al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj.

The second: that he will burn in the Fire by killing a Muslim, as if he had killed all mankind; this was said by Mujahid and 'Ata'. Ibn Qutayba said: he is punished as the killer of all mankind is punished.

The third: that he owes retaliation (qisas) as if he had killed all mankind; this was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: that the meaning of the statement is that all people should assist the guardian of the slain man until they exact retaliation from him, as if he had killed all of their guardians; this was mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

The fifth: that the meaning is: whoever kills a prophet or a just imam, it is as if he had killed all mankind; this was narrated by 'Ikrima from Ibn 'Abbas. The view of generality is more sound. If it is asked: if the sin of killing one person is like the sin of one who kills all mankind, does this indicate that there is no sin upon him for killing whoever he kills after killing the one, until people perish? The answer: the measure deserved by one who kills all mankind is known and fixed with God; so one who kills one person incurs that known sin, one who kills two incurs twice that, and whenever he kills more, God increases his sin. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160]. The good deed's reward is known with God, so its doer is given ten times that same amount. This answer is to the question of one who asks: if whoever gives life to one soul has the reward of one who gives life to mankind, what is the reward of one who gives life to all mankind? All of this is transmitted from the exegetes. What I think is that the comparison with a thing is an approximation of it, because it is not possible that the sin of killing two persons equals the sin of killing one person; rather the comparison occurred with "as if" (ka'annama) because all creation came from one person, so from the one slain there can be imagined the multiplication of the number of all created beings.

His saying: ﴿and whoever gives it life﴾ has five opinions.

The first: he rescues it from destruction; this was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid. Al-Hasan said: whoever saves it from drowning, burning, or destruction. In the narration of 'Ikrima from Ibn 'Abbas: whoever strengthens the arm of a prophet or a just imam, it is as if he had given life to all mankind.

The second: he abstains from killing a soul that is forbidden to be killed; narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid said so in one narration.

The third: that the guardians of the slain man pardon from retaliation; said by al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Qutayba.

The fourth: that he restrains and forbids killing it.

The fifth: that he helps the guardian in executing retaliation, because in retaliation there is life; al-Qadi Abu Ya'la mentioned these two. Regarding His saying ﴿it is as if he had given life to mankind﴾, all together, there are two opinions.

One: he has the reward of one who gives life to all mankind; said by al-Hasan and Ibn Qutayba.

The second: upon all mankind is his thanks, as if he had given them life; mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And certainly Our messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾, meaning: the Children of Israel who were mentioned.

[p. 344] Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾. There are four opinions about the occasion of its revelation.

The first is that it was revealed concerning some people from 'Uraynah who came to Madinah and found its climate unsuitable. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent them out with the camels of the zakat and instructed them to drink from their milk and urine, and they did so and recovered. Then they apostatized from Islam, killed the herdsman, and drove off the camels. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent after them, and they were brought back. He cut off their hands and feet on alternate sides, branded their eyes with hot iron, and threw them onto al-Harrah, where they died. Then this verse was revealed. This was narrated by Qatadah from Anas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi also held this view.

The second is that a people from the People of the Book had a covenant and pact with the Prophet ﷺ, but they broke the covenant and spread corruption on the earth. So Allah gave His Messenger the choice through this verse: if he wished, he could kill them, or if he wished, he could cut off their hands and feet on alternate sides. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak also held this view.

[p. 344] The third is that companions of Abu Burdah al-Aslami cut off the road to a people who had come seeking to embrace Islam, and so this verse was revealed. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: Abu Burdah, whose name was Hilal ibn 'Uwaymir, had made a truce with the Prophet ﷺ that he would neither help against him nor be helped against him, and that whoever came to him from among the Muslims would not be harmed, and whoever passed by Hilal on his way to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would not be harmed. Then a group from the Banu Kinanah who wanted to embrace Islam passed by some people of Hilal's tribe, and they attacked them, killed them, and took their property. Hilal was not present, and so this verse was revealed.

The fourth is that it was revealed concerning the polytheists. This was narrated by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan also held this view. Know that the mention of "waging war" (muharabah) against Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in the verse is figurative (majaz).

[p. 345] Regarding its meaning, scholars have two views.

The first is that He called them those who wage war against Him by way of comparison with those who genuinely wage war, because the one who opposes is a warrior even if he does not fight. So the meaning is: they oppose Allah and His Messenger through acts of disobedience.

The second is that the intended meaning is: they wage war against the allies of Allah and the allies of His Messenger. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: by waging war against Allah and His Messenger He meant disbelief after Islam. Muqatil said: He meant polytheism. As for "corruption" (fasad), it is killing, wounding, seizing property, and terrorizing the road.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿that they be killed or crucified﴾. The scholars differed as to whether this punishment is applied in sequence (tartib) or by choice (takhyir). The position of Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, is that it is in sequence: if they kill and take property, or kill without taking property, they are killed and crucified; if they take property without killing, their hands and feet are cut off on alternate sides; and if they neither take property nor kill, they are exiled. Ibn al-Anbari said: according to this view, the particle "aw" (أوْ) is distributive (mubi'idah, i.e., it divides the cases), so the meaning is: some of them are treated in this way and some in that way. A similar usage is found in His saying: ﴿Be Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:135], meaning: some said this, and some said that. This view is the choice of most of the linguists.

Al-Shafi'i said: if they kill and take property, they are killed and crucified; if they kill without taking property, they are killed but not crucified; and if they take property without killing, their hands and feet are cut off on alternate sides. Malik said: the imam has the choice to implement whichever of the prescribed punishments (hudud) he wishes, whether they killed or did not kill, took property or did not take property, and crucifixion follows killing. Abu Hanifah and Malik said: he is crucified and pierced with a spear until he dies. They differed regarding the length of time for crucifixion. Our companions hold that he is crucified for as long as his crucifixion becomes known. The companions of al-Shafi'i differed: some said three days, which is the position of Abu Hanifah, and some said he is left until his pus flows. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the meaning of "on alternate sides" (min khilaf) is that his right hand and left foot are cut off, with the cutting of the two set apart from each other. As for "exile" (nafy), its root meaning is driving away and banishing.

Regarding the manner of their exile, there are four views.

The first is that they are banished from the lands of Islam to the abode of war (dar al-harb). This was said by Anas ibn Malik, al-Hasan, and Qatadah. This applies only to a polytheist who wages war, whereas a Muslim should not be compelled to this.

The second is that they are pursued so that the prescribed punishments may be carried out upon them, and so they are driven away. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

The third is that they are expelled from their city to another city. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Malik said: they are exiled to a land other than their own, where they are imprisoned.

The fourth is that exile means imprisonment. This was said by Abu Hanifah and his companions. Our companions said: the manner of exile is that they are kept on the move and not allowed to settle in any land, so that whenever they settle in one land, they are expelled to another.

Regarding "disgrace" (khizy) there are two views. The first is that it is punishment. The second is public humiliation (fadihah).

As for whether the ruling of those who wage war applies to them within a city (misr), or not: the apparent meaning of our companions' words is that it does not apply to them within a city, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Yusuf said: the city and the open countryside are the same, and in the property taken, the minimum amount (nisab) must be reached, just as it is considered in the case of the thief, unlike Malik's view.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 34:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Except for those who repent﴾. Most of the exegetes said: this exception concerns the warring polytheists who repent of their polytheism, their warring and their corruption, and believe before they fall into one's power; for them there is no liability for what they took of property or blood, and there is no disagreement about this. As for Muslim muharibun (those who wage war against society), the scholars differed concerning them. The position of our companions (the Hanbali school) is that the hudud (fixed punishments) of God fall away from them, namely the obligation of execution, crucifixion, amputation and banishment. As for the rights of human beings concerning wounds and property, repentance does not drop them, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i.

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿And seek the means of nearness to Him﴾.

Regarding *al-wasilah* (the means), there are two opinions. (p-348) The first is that it means nearness (*al-qurbah*). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Mujahid, and al-Farra' (a grammarian and Qur'an scholar). Qatadah said: "Draw near to Him by means of what pleases Him." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "It is said: *tawassaltu ilayhi*, meaning I drew near to him." He recited:

*When the slanderers are heedless, we return to our union,*
*and the purity between us returns, and the means (of reconciliation).*

The second opinion is that it means love (*al-mahabbah*). It is said: "Make yourselves beloved to God." This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 38:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: It was revealed concerning Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq, and his story has already passed in Surat (al-Nisa'). "Thief" (al-sariq): he is only called a thief because he takes an item in secrecy, and "istaraqa al-sam'" means when he listens stealthily while hiding. Al-Mubarrad said: "al-sariq" here is in the nominative as the subject of a sentence (mubtada'), because the intention is not a specific individual; it is like your saying: "Whoever steals, cut off his hand." Ibn al-Anbari said: The fa' (fa') entered because the sentence carries the meaning of a conditional, its estimate being: "Whoever steals, then cut off his hand." Al-Farra' said: He said ﴿cut off their hands﴾ because every singular limb of the human body, when mentioned as attached to two or more, is put in the plural; you say: "I have smashed their heads, and filled their backs and bellies with blows," and similarly ﴿your hearts have inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. The plural was preferred over the dual because the limbs of a human are most often in pairs: the two hands, the two feet, the two eyes. Since most of them follow this pattern, the singular of them, when attached to two, takes the course of the dual, though their dual form is also permissible. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"So they exchanged their two souls with thrusts like the holes of the cracked waterskins that are not mended."

Section

This verse necessitates the amputation for every thief, and the Sunnah has clarified that the intended thief is one who steals a nisab from a place of safekeeping (hirz) appropriate to its kind, just as He said: ﴿Kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], while the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade killing women, children, and the people of the monasteries. The amount of the nisab has been disputed. The position of our companions (the Hanbalis) is that theft has two nisabs: one, of gold, a quarter of a dinar, and of silver, three dirhams, or the value of three dirhams in goods. This is also the view of Malik. Abu Hanifa said: no amputation until the theft reaches ten dirhams. Al-Shafi'i said: the criterion in this is a quarter of a dinar, and other things are valued by it; so if he steals two dirhams whose value is a quarter of a dinar, he is amputated. If he steals a nisab of unminted gold, the amputation applies. Abu Hanifa said: no amputation until that amount is in minted form. If he steals a handkerchief that is not worth a nisab, with a dinar in its corner while he does not know it, there is no amputation. Al-Shafi'i said: he is amputated. If he steals the covering of the Ka'bah, he is amputated, contrary to Abu Hanifa. If he steals a small free child, he is not amputated, even if the child has jewelry on him. Malik said: he is amputated in every case. When a group shares in stealing a nisab, they are all amputated, and Malik said likewise, except that he required that the stolen item be heavy, needing some of them to help others in removing it. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said: there is no amputation for him in any case.

And the amputation for the one who denies a loan (ariyyah) is obligatory according to us, and this is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Layth ibn Sa'd, contrary to most jurists.

Section

As for the place of safekeeping (hirz), it is whatever is made for dwelling and for guarding property, such as houses, tents, and the pitched tents in which people live and keep their belongings. All of that is a hirz, even if there is no guard in it or with it, and whether it is stolen from while its door is open, or it has no door but is enclosed by building. As for what is in neither a building nor a tent, it is not in a hirz unless there is someone with it who guards it. Al-Maymuni transmitted from Ahmad: if the place is shared in entering it, like a bathhouse or a tent, the thief is not amputated from it, and the guard is not considered. Ibn Mansur transmitted from him: the thief of a bathhouse is not amputated unless there is a guarding hired worker over the goods. As for the grave-robber (al-nabbash), Ahmad said in the narration of Abu Talib: he is amputated, and this is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ibn Abi Layla. Al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, and Abu Hanifa said: he is not amputated.

Section

As for the place of amputation of the thief, it is from the joint of the palm and from the joint of the foot. As for the left hand and the right foot, it is narrated from Ahmad that they are not amputated, and this is the view of Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali, and Abu Hanifa; and it is narrated from him that they are amputated, and this is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. The amputation is not established except by his confession twice, and this is the view of Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Shubrumah, and Abu Yusuf. Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Shafi'i said: it is established with one confession. The amputation and the compensation combine, whether he is wealthy or poor. Abu Hanifa said: they do not combine; if the item itself remains, its owner takes it, and if it has been destroyed, there is no liability. Malik said: he compensates for it if he is wealthy, and there is nothing upon him if he is poor.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿As a punishment from Allah﴾. We have already discussed "nakal" (exemplary punishment) in (al-Baqarah).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Mighty in His retribution, Wise in that He ruled with amputation. Al-Asma'i said: I recited this verse while a Bedouin was beside me, and I said by mistake: "And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful." The Bedouin said: Whose speech is this? I said: The speech of Allah. He said: Repeat it. I repeated: "And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful," and he said: This is not the speech of Allah. I became alert and said: "And Allah is Mighty and Wise." He said: You are right; this is the speech of Allah. I said to him: Do you recite the Qur'an? He said: No. I said: How did you know that I had erred? He said: O man, He is Mighty, so He ruled and amputated; had He forgiven and shown mercy, He would not have amputated.

(p-355) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "A woman had committed theft, and she said, 'O Messenger of Allah, is there repentance for me?' So this verse was revealed." This was related by ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing﴾, that is, after his theft, and amends his conduct, then indeed Allah will pardon him. Indeed Allah is Forgiving of what he did before repentance, Merciful to whoever repents.

(p-355) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "A woman had committed theft, and she said, 'O Messenger of Allah, is there repentance for me?' So this verse was revealed." This was related by ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing﴾, that is, after his theft, and amends his conduct, then indeed Allah will pardon him. Indeed Allah is Forgiving of what he did before repentance, Merciful to whoever repents.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 41:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O Messenger, let not those who race to disbelief grieve you﴾. The scholars differed concerning who it was revealed about, on five views.

The first: "The Prophet ﷺ passed by a Jew whom they had blackened (tahmim) and flogged. He said: 'Is this how you find the punishment for the adulterer in your Book?' They said: 'Yes.' So he summoned a man of their scholars and said: 'I adjure you by God, who sent down the Torah to Moses: is this how you find the punishment for the adulterer in your Book?' He said: 'No, but it became widespread among our nobles, so we would leave the noble and inflict it on the lowly. So we said: Come, let us agree on something we apply to both noble and lowly, and we agreed on blackening and flogging.' The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'O God, I am the first to revive Your command when they have caused it to die.' He then ordered him to be stoned, and this verse was revealed." This was narrated by al-Bara' ibn 'Azib.

The second: It was revealed concerning Ibn Suriya, who believed and then disbelieved. This meaning is also related from Abu Hurayrah.

The third: It was revealed concerning a Jew who killed a Jew, then said: "Ask Muhammad: if he was sent with the blood-money (diyah), we will have our dispute brought to him; but if he was sent with execution, we will not go to him." This was said by al-Sha'bi.

The fourth: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

The fifth: A man of the Ansar was pointed to by the Qurayzah on the day of their siege: "On what should we come down?" He gestured to them that it was slaughter. This was said by al-Suddi. Muqatil said: he was Abu Lubabah ibn 'Abd al-Mundhir. The Qurayzah said to him: "Shall we come down under the judgment of Sa'd?" He gestured with his hand that it was slaughter, and he was their ally. Abu Lubabah said: "I knew that I had betrayed God and His Messenger, so this verse was revealed." The meaning of the statement is: let not the racing of those who race to disbelief grieve you, from among those who say "We believe" with their mouths while they are not believers, namely the hypocrites, and from among those who are Jews.

﴿Listeners to falsehood﴾. Sibawayh said: it is in the nominative by way of the inceptive (mubtada'). Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said: it is also permissible that its nominative status be in the sense of: "And among those who are Jews are listeners to falsehood." Concerning its meaning there are four views.

One: listeners to you in order to lie about you. Two: listeners to falsehood, i.e., those who accept it from him. Three: listeners to the falsehood which they altered in their Torah. Four: listeners to falsehood, i.e., those who accept it; from this is the saying "God hears whoever praises Him," meaning He accepts.

(p-358) Concerning His saying ﴿Listeners for another people who have not come to you﴾ there are two views.

One: they listen on behalf of those others, so they are spies for them. Two: they are listeners from another people, namely their leaders who altered the Torah.

Concerning the listeners to falsehood and the other people there are two views.

One: "the listeners to falsehood" are the Jews of Medina, and "the other people [who did not come to the Messenger of God ﷺ]" are the Jews of Fadak. The second is the reverse of this.

Concerning their distorting of words there are five views.

One: it is altering the limits of God in the Torah, for they changed the stoning; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and the majority. Two: altering what they heard from the Prophet ﷺ by lying about him; this was said by al-Hasan. Three: concealing the description of the Prophet ﷺ. Four: dropping retaliation (qawad) after it became due. Five: bad interpretation. Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is that they distort the ruling of the words, and the mention of the ruling was omitted because the listeners know it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿after their places﴾. al-Zajjaj said: i.e., after God had placed it in its places, so He made lawful what is lawful and forbade what is forbidden.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They say: If you are given this, take it﴾. Concerning those who say this there are two views.

One: they are the Jews, because a man and a woman of their nobles committed adultery, and their punishment was stoning; the Jews disliked stoning them, so they sent to the Prophet ﷺ asking him about his judgment regarding the two adulterers if they were married, and they said: "If he orders you to flog, take it; and if he orders you to stone, do not act upon it." This is the view of the majority. (p-359) Two: they are the hypocrites. Qatadah said: this was because "the Banu al-Nadir did not give the Qurayzah retaliation when they killed from among them, but gave them only blood-money; when the Qurayzah killed from the Nadir, they would not accept anything but retaliation, out of arrogance towards them. So the Banu al-Nadir killed a man of the Qurayzah intentionally, and they wished to bring this to the Prophet ﷺ. A man of the hypocrites said: 'Your slain is a deliberate killing, and if you bring this to Muhammad I fear retaliation for you; if he accepts blood-money from you, then pay, and otherwise be wary of him.'" Concerning the meaning of "beware" there are three views.

One: beware of acting upon his harsh word. Two: beware of informing him of what is in the Torah, lest he make you act upon it. Three: beware of asking him after this.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whomever God wills to test﴾. Concerning "fitnah" there are three views.

One: it means misguidance; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Two: punishment; this was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. Three: disgrace; al-Zajjaj mentioned it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿you will not avail him anything from God﴾. That is: you cannot avail him, nor can you rescue him. In this is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ regarding his grief over their racing to disbelief.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿God does not intend to purify their hearts﴾. al-Suddi said: this means the hypocrites and the Jews; He did not intend to purify their hearts from the filth of disbelief and the stain of polytheism with the purity of faith and Islam.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾. As for the disgrace of the hypocrites, it is by the exposure of their concealment and the Prophet's being informed of their disbelief; and the disgrace of the Jews is by their humiliation in the exposure of their lie when they concealed the stoning, and by the taking of the jizyah from them. Muqatil said: the disgrace of the Qurayzah was by their killing and captivity, and the disgrace of the Nadir was by their expulsion.

(p-360) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They are listeners to falsehood﴾. Al-Hasan said: this means the judges of the Jews, who listen to lies from the one who lies before them in his claim, and when he brings them a bribe, they take it. Abu Sulayman said: they are the Jews who listen to lies, which is the saying of some of them to others: "Muhammad is a liar, he is not a Prophet, and there is no stoning in the Torah," while they know their own lying.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Devourers of the unlawful gain﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far read "al-suhuta" with a damma on the ha' and a shaddah. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Hamzah read "al-suht" with a sukun on the ha' and no shaddah. Kharijah ibn Mus'ab related from Nafi': "akkalina lil-sahti," with a fatha on the sin and a sukun on the ha'. Abu 'Ali said: al-suht and al-suhut are two dialects, and both are nouns for the thing that is gained unlawfully, not verbal nouns. As for the one who reads the sin with a fatha, it is the verbal noun of sahata, and he has applied the name of the verbal noun to the thing that is gained, just as they apply "al-darb" to the thing struck in their saying: "this dirham is the mint (darb) of the amir." There are three opinions concerning the meaning of al-suht.

The first: bribery in judgment. The second: bribery in religion; both of these opinions are from Ibn Mas'ud. The third: that it is every earning that is not lawful, as said by al-Akhfash.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾. Concerning whom this speech was intended there are two opinions.

One: the two Jews who committed adultery, said by al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The second: two men from Qurayzah and al-Nadir, one of whom killed the other, said by Qatadah. Ibn Zayd said: Huyayy ibn Akhtab had made the blood-money for the man from al-Nadir two diyat, and for the man from Qurayzah one diyah, because he was from al-Nadir. So Qurayzah said: "We will not accept the judgment of Huyayy; we will bring our dispute to Muhammad." Then God, exalted is He, said to His Prophet: ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them﴾, the verse.

Section

The scholars of tafsir differed regarding this verse into two opinions.

One: that it is abrogated. This is because the People of the Book, when they brought their disputes before the Prophet ﷺ, he had the choice: if he wished he judged between them, and if he wished he turned away from them. Then this was abrogated by His saying: ﴿And judge between them by what God has revealed﴾, so judgment became obligatory and the choice was removed. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Suddi.

The second: that it is muhkam (not abrogated), and that the Imam and his deputies in judgment have the choice when disputants come before them: if they wish they judge between them, and if they wish they turn away from them. This is related from al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i and al-Zuhri, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said it. It is the sound view, because there is no contradiction between the two verses: the one gives the choice between judging and leaving it, and the second explains how to judge when one does judge.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 43:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And how would they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah?﴾ The exegetes said: This is an expression of wonder from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to His Prophet regarding the Jews' seeking his judgment, after they knew what the Torah says concerning the ruling of the matter they came to him about, and it is a rebuke to the Jews, for they seek judgment from one whose prophethood they deny, and they abandon the ruling of the Torah, whose authenticity they believe in.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in which is the judgment of Allah﴾ has two views.

The first: the judgment of Allah concerning stoning (rajm), and it was concerning this that they sought judgment. This is said by al-Hasan.

The second: His judgment concerning retaliation (qawad), and it was concerning this that they sought judgment. This is said by Qatada.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿then they turn away after that﴾ has two views.

The first: after the judgment of Allah in the Torah. The second: after your judgment.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and those are not believers﴾ has two views.

The first: they are not believers because of their distortion of the Torah. The second: they are not believers that your judgment is from Allah, because of their denial of your prophethood.

(p-363) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which was guidance and light﴾. The commentators said: The occasion of the revelation of this verse was that the Jews asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for a ruling concerning the two adulterers, and this has already been mentioned. "Guidance" (al-huda) means clarification (al-bayan). So the Torah clarifies the truth of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, and clarifies what they took to it for judgment. "Light" (al-nur) is the illumination that disperses doubts and makes difficulties clear.

Regarding "the prophets who submitted" (alladhina aslamu), there are three opinions.

The first: they are the prophets from the time of Musa to the time of Isa. This is what most of them said.

According to this opinion, there are four views concerning the meaning of "aslamu" (submitted).

The first: they submitted to the judgment of Allah and were content with His decree. The second: they yielded to the judgment of Allah and so did not conceal it, as those (others) concealed it. The third: they surrendered themselves to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The fourth: they submitted to what is in the Torah and adhered to it, because there were among them those who did not act upon everything in it, such as Isa, peace be upon him. Ibn al-Anbari said: Regarding "al-muslim" (the one who submits) there are two opinions.

One of them: he was so named for his submission and yielding to his Lord. The second: for his sincerity toward his Lord, from His saying: ﴿and a man belonging wholly to one man﴾ [al-Zumar: 29], meaning, purely devoted to him.

(p-364) The second opinion: the intended "prophets" is our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. This is said by al-Hasan and al-Suddi, and that was when he ruled over the Jews concerning stoning. He mentioned it in the plural form, as in His saying: ﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?﴾ [al-Nisa: 54].

Regarding what he judged by from it, there are two opinions. One: stoning and retaliation (qawad). The second: judging by the rest of it, so long as nothing in his law contradicts it. The third: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and the prophets before him, may the blessings of Allah be upon them all. This is said by Ikrimah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿for those who were Jews﴾. Ibn Abbas said: they repented from disbelief. al-Hasan said: they are the Jews. al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that there is an inversion of order in the verse, meaning: Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which was guidance and light, for those who were Jews; the prophets who submitted judge by it. As for "al-Rabbaniyyun" (the rabbis), their mention has already passed in (Al ʿImran). As for "al-Ahbar" (the scholars), they are the learned, whose singular is habr and hibr; the plural is ahbar and hubur. al-Farra' said: Most of what I have heard the Arabs say for the singular of ahbar is hibr, with a kasra on the ha'. Regarding the derivation of this name there are three opinions.

One: it is from al-habar, which is good effect (al-athar al-hasan), said by al-Khalil. The second: it is from al-hibr with which one writes, said by al-Kisa'i. The third: it is from al-hibr, which is beauty and splendor. In a hadith: "A man will come out of the Fire whose hibr and sibr have gone," meaning his beauty and splendor. So the scholar is radiant with the beauty of knowledge. This is the saying of Qutrub.

Is there a difference between al-Rabbaniyyun and al-Ahbar or not? There are two opinions.

One: there is no difference, and all are scholars. This is the saying of most, including Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj. It has been narrated from Mujahid that he said: al-Rabbaniyyun are the jurists and scholars, and they are above the ahbar. al-Suddi said: al-Rabbaniyyun are the scholars, and al-ahbar are the readers. Ibn Zayd said: (p-365) "al-Rabbaniyyun" are the rulers, and "al-ahbar" are the scholars. It was also said: al-Rabbaniyyun are the scholars of the Christians, and al-ahbar are the scholars of the Jews.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿because they were entrusted with the Book of Allah﴾. Ibn Abbas said: because they were entrusted with the Book of Allah, which is the Torah. Regarding the meaning of the statement there are two opinions.

One: they judge by the ruling of what they were entrusted with. The second: they are scholars of what they were entrusted with. Ibn Jarir said: the "ba'" in His saying ﴿bima istuhfizu﴾ is connected to al-ahbar.

Regarding His saying: ﴿and they were witnesses to it﴾ there are two opinions.

One: and they were witnesses to what is in the Torah concerning stoning; narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: they were witnesses for Muhammad, peace be upon him, by what he said, that it is true. Narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So do not fear the people, but fear Me﴾. Ibn Kathir, Asim, Hamzah, Ibn Amir, and al-Kisa'i read "wakhshawni" without a ya' both in pause and in continuation. Abu 'Amr read it with a ya' in continuation and without it in pause, and both are good. We have already pointed to this in (Al ʿImran). Then, regarding those addressed by this, there are two opinions.

One: they are the leaders of the Jews. It was said to them: So do not fear the people in making known the description of Muhammad and acting upon stoning, and fear Me in concealing that. Abu Salih narrated this meaning from Ibn Abbas. Muqatil said: The address is to the Jews of Medina. It was said to them: Do not fear the Jews of Khaybar lest you inform them of the stoning and the description of Muhammad, and fear Me in concealing it.

The second: they are the Muslims. It was said to them: Do not fear the people as the Jews feared the people, so they did not speak the truth. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi mentioned this.

(p-366) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾. Regarding what is meant by "the signs" there are two opinions.

One: they are the description of Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an. The second: the rulings and obligations. The small price is mentioned in (al-Baqarah).

As for His saying: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has sent down, those are the disbelievers﴾, and His saying after it: ﴿those are the wrongdoers﴾ and ﴿those are the defiant﴾. The scholars differed concerning whom these were revealed about, into five opinions.

One: they were revealed about the Jews specifically; narrated by Ubayd ibn Abd Allah from Ibn Abbas, and Qatadah said likewise. The second: they were revealed about the Muslims; Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas a similar meaning. The third: they are general, concerning the Jews and this community; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, and al-Suddi. The fourth: they were revealed about the Jews and the Christians; this was said by Abu Mijlaz. The fifth: the first is about the Muslims, the second about the Jews, and the third about the Christians; this was said by al-Sha'bi.

Regarding the meaning of the disbelief mentioned in the first verse there are two opinions.

One: it is disbelief in Allah, Exalted. The second: it is disbelief in that ruling, which is not a disbelief that removes one from the religion.

The decisive matter is that whoever does not judge by what Allah has sent down while denying it, knowing that Allah sent it down, as the Jews did, then he is a disbeliever. And whoever does not judge by it out of inclination toward desire without denial, then he is a wrongdoer and defiant. Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: (p-367) Whoever denies what Allah has sent down has disbelieved, and whoever acknowledges it but does not judge by it is defiant and a wrongdoer.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 45:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We prescribed﴾, i.e., We made obligatory (ʿalayhim), i.e., upon the Jews (fīhā), i.e., in the Torah. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "And We prescribed for them therein that a life is for a life. So what is wrong with them that they oppose it, killing two souls for one soul, and gouging out two eyes for an eye?" The law for the Children of Israel was retaliation (qiṣāṣ) or pardon, and there was no blood-money (diyah) among them for a life or for a wound. So God lightened it for the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) through blood-money.

Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir read: "the life for the life, and the eye for the eye, and the nose for the nose, and the ear for the ear, and the tooth for the tooth," putting all of that in the accusative (naṣb), and they read "wa-l-jurūḥa" (and the wounds) in the nominative (rafʿ). Nafiʿ, ʿAsim, and Hamza all put all of that in the accusative. Al-Kisa'i read "anna al-nafsa bi-l-nafs" in the accusative, and put what follows it in the nominative. Abu ʿAli said: his argument is that the waw is for coordinating sentences (ʿaṭf al-jumal), not for sharing the same governing element (al-ishtirak fi al-ʿamil). It is also possible that he treated the speech as governed by its meaning (ḥamala al-kalām ʿalā al-maʿnā), because the meaning of "And We prescribed for them" is "We said to them: the life is for the life," so he took "the eye" along with this, and this is the argument of the one who reads "al-jurūḥ" in the nominative. It is also possible that it is a new (mustaʾnaf) statement, not something prescribed for the people, but rather the beginning of an obligation (ibtidāʾ ījāb).

Qadi Abu Yaʿla said: His saying, "the eye for the eye," does not mean plucking out the eye in exchange for the eye, because it is impossible to achieve exact equivalence, since we cannot determine the exact limit to which the eye must be removed. Rather, retaliation is due in the case where its light has gone while the eye remains intact. The manner of this is that the eye of the one who inflicts it is bound, and a mirror is heated, and then he approaches the eye in which the retaliation is owed until its light is gone. As for the nose: if the cartilage (al-maarin), which is the soft part, is cut off while its bony core (qaṣaba) is left, then retaliation is due for it. But if it is cut off from its root, there is no retaliation for it, because retaliation cannot be carried out, just as if someone cut off a hand from the middle of the forearm. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: there is retaliation for it if it is cut off entirely. As for the ear, retaliation is due if it is cut off entirely and the extent is known. There is no retaliation for a bone except in the case of a tooth: if it is pulled out, a similar tooth is pulled out; and if part of it is broken, it is filed down to the corresponding amount. His saying, "and the wounds are subject to retaliation," requires that retaliation be obligatory for all wounds in which an equivalent can be carried out.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever forgoes it﴾ refers to retaliation.

﴿it is an expiation for him﴾ — concerning the pronoun "lahu" (for him), there are two opinions.

One is that it refers to the wounded person: when he forgoes retaliation, he is expiated of his sins. This is the view of Ibn Masʿud, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, al-Hasan, and al-Shaʿbi.

The second is that it refers to the one who inflicted the injury: if the wounded person pardons him, the offense he committed is expiated for him. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and Muqatil, and it is understood to apply when the offender has repented of his offense, because if he persists, the punishment for persistence remains.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 46:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We sent, following in their footsteps, Jesus, son of Mary﴾. That is: We caused to follow in the footsteps of the prophets who had submitted (aslamu) ﴿Jesus﴾, and We made him follow their traces, ﴿confirming﴾, that is: We sent him as one confirming ﴿what was before him﴾. ﴿And We gave him the Gospel, in which was guidance and light, and confirming﴾. This is not a repetition of the first, because the first (confirming) refers to Jesus and the second refers to the Gospel, since Jesus used to call to the affirmation of the Torah, and the Gospel was revealed containing mention of the affirmation of the Torah.

The Words of Allah: ﴿Let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein﴾. Most of the readers recited it with the lām jazm (sukūn on the lām), understanding it as an imperative. Its implied sense is: "And We commanded its people that they judge by what Allah revealed therein."

Al-A'mash and Hamzah recited it with a kasrah on the lām and a fatḥah on the mīm, understanding it in the sense of "kay" (in order that). So it is as if He said: "And We gave him the Gospel so that the People of the Gospel might judge by what Allah revealed therein."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 48:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿in truth﴾ (bi-l-haqq), i.e., with truthfulness, ﴿confirming what came before it of the Book﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "It means every Book that Allah Exalted has sent down." Regarding "al-muhaymin" (the guardian/witness) there are four opinions.

The first: that it means "al-mu'aymin" (the trustworthy). This was narrated by al-Tamimi from Ibn Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, Ata' and al-Dahhak also said so. Al-Mubarrid said: "Muhaymin" has the sense of "mu'aymin," except that the ha' is a substitute for the hamza, as they say: "araqtu al-ma'" and "harqtu," and "iyyaka" and "hiyyaka."

The proponents of this view say: the meaning is that the Qur'an is entrusted over the Books before it. However, Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid: "and muhaymin over it," and he said: "Muhammad is entrusted over the Qur'an." According to his statement, there is an omitted element in the speech, as if he said: "And We made you, O Muhammad, a muhaymin over it," so that the pronoun in "over it" refers to the Qur'an. According to other than Mujahid's view, it refers to the previous Books.

The second: that it means the witness (al-shahid). This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Muqatil also said so.

The third: that it means the one who confirms what He reported about the Books. This is the view of Ibn Zayd, and it is close to the first opinion.

The fourth: that it means the vigilant guardian (al-raqib al-hafiz). This was said by al-Khalil.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So judge between them﴾, referring to the Jews, ﴿by what Allah has sent down﴾ to you in the Qur'an, ﴿and do not follow their desires, away from the truth that has come to you﴾. Abu Sulayman said: the meaning is: "so that you would turn away from what has come to you." Ibn Abbas said: "Do not adopt their desires regarding the flogging of a married person (muhsan)."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For each of you We have made a law (shir'ah) and a way (minhaj)﴾. Mujahid said: "al-shir'ah" is the sunnah, and "al-minhaj" is the path. Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-shir'ah" and "al-shari'ah" are one and the same, and "al-minhaj" is the clear path. If it is asked: How is "al-minhaj" conjoined to "al-shir'ah" when both have one meaning? To this there are two answers.

The first: that there is a difference between them in two respects. One is that "al-shir'ah" is the beginning of the path, while "al-minhaj" is the continuous path, as said by al-Mubarrid. The second is that "al-shir'ah" is the path which may or may not be clear, while "al-minhaj" is the path which is only ever clear, as mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. Thus, since there is a difference between "al-shir'ah" and "al-minhaj," it is apt to conjoin one to the other.

The second: that "al-shir'ah" and "al-minhaj" have one meaning, and one was conjoined to the other only because the two words differ. Al-Hutay'ah said:

Ah, how lovely is Hind, and the land in which is Hind, and Hind, between her and us stand distance and remoteness.

So he conjoined "al-bu'd" (remoteness) to "al-na'y" (distance) when they differed in wording, even though they agree in meaning, as mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. The proponents of the first view answered this, saying: "al-na'y" is whatever its distance is small or great, as if it were separation, whereas "al-bu'd" is only used of that whose distance of separation is great.

The commentators have two opinions regarding the meaning of the speech.

The first: for each religious community We have made a law and a way: the People of the Torah have a law, the People of the Gospel have a law, and the People of the Qur'an have a law. This is the view of most. Qatadah said: the address is to the three nations: the nation of Moses, the nation of Jesus, and the nation of Muhammad. For the Torah there is a law, for the Gospel there is a law, and for the Criterion (al-Furqan) there is a law in which Allah makes lawful what He wills and makes unlawful what [He wills] as a trial, so that He may know who obeys Him from among those who disobey Him. [But] the one religion that is not accepted other than it is tawhid and sincere devotion to Allah, which the Messengers brought.

The second: that the meaning is: for each one who entered the religion of Muhammad, We made the Qur'an a law and a way. This is the view of Mujahid.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one community﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions.

The first: He would have gathered you upon the truth.

The second: He would have made you upon one religious community. ﴿But to test you﴾, i.e., to examine you, ﴿in what He has given you﴾ of the Books, and has explained to you of the religious communities. If it is asked: if the one meant by His saying "For each of you We have made a law" is our Prophet Muhammad along with all the prophets before him, then who is the addressee in His saying "to test you"? The answer: it is an address to our Prophet, and what is intended is all the prophets and nations. Ibn Jarir said: it is among the habits of the Arabs that when they address an absent party and wish to report about him, they make the addressee prevail, and thus they express the report about both of them in the form of address.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾. Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak said: this is an address to the nation of Muhammad, peace be upon him. Muqatil said: "al-khayrat" are the righteous deeds. ﴿To Allah is your return﴾ in the Hereafter, ﴿and He will inform you of what you used to dispute﴾ regarding religion. Ibn Jarir said: He has explained that in this world through evidences and proofs, and tomorrow He will explain it through recompense.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 49:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "A group of the Jews, among them Ka'b ibn Usayd, 'Abd Allah ibn Suriya, and Shas ibn Qays, said to one another: 'Come, let us go to Muhammad; perhaps we can seduce him from his religion.' So they came to him and said: 'O Muhammad, you know that we are the rabbis (ahbar) and nobles of the Jews, and that if we follow you, the Jews will follow you. Between us and a people there is a dispute, and we will bring it before you, and you will rule for us against them, and we will believe in you.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ refused that, and this verse was revealed." This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil mentioned that (p-375) a group of Banu al-Nadir said to him: "Would you rule for us against our fellows, the people of Qurayza, in the matter of blood-wit, as we were accustomed to before, and we will pledge allegiance to you?" So this verse was revealed. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: This verse is not a repetition of what preceded it; rather, the two were revealed concerning two different matters: one concerning the stoning (rajm), and the other concerning equalization in blood-money (diyat), until they brought their disputes to him in both matters.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And beware of them lest they seduce you﴾, i.e., divert you ﴿from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾. There are two views concerning this.

One: it is the stoning (rajm); this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it is the matter of retaliation (qisas) and blood, the view of Muqatil.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if they turn away﴾. There are two views concerning this.

One: from your judgment. The second: from faith. Know that their turning away is because Allah intends to punish them for some of their sins. Concerning the mention of "some" there are two views.

One: it is to be taken literally, and He only afflicts them with some of what they deserve.

The second: what is meant is the whole, just as the singular word is mentioned while the plural is meant, as in His saying: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1], while what is meant is all Muslims. Al-Hasan said: He meant what He hastened for them of the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir and the killing of Banu Qurayza.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, many of the people are defiant wrongdoers (fasiqun)﴾. The exegetes said: He meant the Jews.

Concerning the meaning of fisq (defiant disobedience) here there are three views. One: disbelief (kufr), the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The second: lying (kadhib), the view of Ibn Zayd. The third: acts of disobedience (ma'asi), the view of Muqatil.

(p-376) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do they then seek the judgment of the Time of Ignorance?﴾ The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yabghuna" with the letter ya', because what precedes it is in the third person, namely His saying: ﴿And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient.﴾ Ibn 'Amir read "tabghuna" with the letter ta', meaning: Say to them. The occasion of its revelation: "When the Prophet ﷺ ruled for stoning against the two Jews, Banu Qurayza clung to Banu al-Nadir and said: O Muhammad, these are our brethren; our father is one and our religion is one. If they kill one of us, they give us seventy wasq of dates, and if we kill one of them, they take from us one hundred and forty wasq. If we kill a man of theirs, they kill two men in return, and if we kill a woman of theirs, they kill a man in return. So judge between us with justice. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Banu al-Nadir have no superiority over Banu Qurayza in blood-money or in life.' Banu al-Nadir said: By Allah, we will not accept your judgment, nor obey your command, and we will certainly hold to our former custom. Then this verse was revealed." Narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the verse is: Do the Jews seek a judgment that Allah did not command, though they are the People of the Book of Allah, just as the Time of Ignorance does?!

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And who is better than Allah in judgment?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: And who is more just?!

Regarding His saying: ﴿for a people who have certainty﴾ there are two opinions.

One: they have certainty in the Qur'an; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: they have certainty in Allah; this was said by Muqatil. Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever has certainty perceives the justice of Allah in His judgment.

(p-377) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

The first: it was revealed concerning Abu Lubabah, when he said to the Banu Qurayzah, when they accepted the judgment of Sa'd, "It is the slaughter." This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the view of 'Ikrimah.

The second: "'Ubadah ibn al-Samit said: O Messenger of Allah, I have Jewish clients, and I disavow to Allah the alliance of the Jews. 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy said: I am a man who fears misfortunes, and I will not disavow to Allah the alliance of the Jews. So this verse was revealed." This was stated by 'Ata' al-'Awfi.

The third: when the Battle of Uhud took place, a group of people feared that the disbelievers would gain the upper hand over them. One man said to his companion, "As for me, I will join so-and-so the Jew, and take safe-conduct from him, (p-378) or I will become a Jew along with him." So this verse was revealed. This was stated by al-Suddi and Muqatil. Al-Zajjaj said: "Do not make them your guardians in religion." Others said: "Do not seek their support, nor seek their help," ﴿some of them are allies of others﴾ in aid and support.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then he is indeed one of them﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: whoever takes them as allies in religion, then he is one of them in disbelief.

The second: whoever takes them as allies in covenant, then he is one of them in opposing the command.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 52:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them﴾. The exegetes said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites. Then, regarding this, there are two statements.

One of them: The Jews and Christians used to supply the hypocrites with provisions (yamiruna) and lend to them, and so they showed them affection. When ﴿Do not take the Jews and Christians as allies﴾ was revealed, the hypocrites said: "How can we cut off the friendship of a people who, if a year of drought strikes us, have been generous to us?" So this verse was revealed. Abu Salih related it from Ibn 'Abbas. Among those who said it was revealed concerning the hypocrites without specifying [a particular incident] were Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: that it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy. This was said by 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi.

Regarding the meaning of "disease" (maradh) there are two statements.

One of them: that it is doubt (shakk); this was said by Muqatil. The second: that it is hypocrisy (nifaq); this was said by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding His saying ﴿hastening toward them﴾ there are three statements.

The first: they hasten in their allegiance to them and their giving of sincere counsel; this was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: in seeking their approval; this was said by Ibn Qutaybah. The third: in aiding them against the Muslims; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding the meaning of "the calamity" (al-da'irah) there are two statements.
