One of them: drought and famine; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Qutaybah said: "We fear that fate may turn against us with some misfortune," meaning drought, so that they will not trade with us, and [we will not obtain provisions from them], so they will not supply us.

The second: the turning of the state to the Jews over the Muslims; this was said by Muqatil.

Regarding the meaning of "the victory" (al-fath) there are four statements.

One of them: the conquest of Makkah; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi. The second: the conquest of the villages of the Jews; this was said by al-Dahhak. The third: the victory of the Prophet (ﷺ) over those who opposed him; this was said by Qatadah and al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: relief (al-faraj); this was said by Ibn Qutaybah. Regarding "the command" (al-amr) there are four statements.

One of them: the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir and the seizure of their wealth, and the killing of Qurayzah and the taking captive of their offspring; this was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil. The second: the jizyah; this was said by al-Suddi. The third: fertility and abundance; this was said by Ibn Qutaybah. The fourth: that the Prophet (ﷺ) be commanded to make manifest the matter of the hypocrites and to kill them; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding "what they concealed" (asarru) there are two statements.

One of them: their allegiance to them. The second: their saying, "Perhaps Muhammad will not be victorious."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 53:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who believe will say﴾. Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha on the lam (yaqula, "say"), meaning: "and it is hoped that he will say" (ʿasā an yaqūla). The rest read it with a damma, making the sentence a fresh start (mustaʾnafan). Ibn Kathir, (p-380) Nafi', and Ibn 'Amir read yaqulu without a waw, with a damma on the lam, and likewise it is so in the codices (maṣāḥif) of the people of Makkah and Madinah. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) expelled the Banu al-Nadir, this weighed heavily on the hypocrites, and they began to lament their departure. A hypocrite would say to his believing relative, when he saw him zealously opposing the Jews: 'Is this their reward from you? By Allah, they have long filled your belly!' When Qurayza was killed, none of the hypocrites could contain what was in his soul, and they began to say: 'Four hundred were reaped in a single night!' When the believers saw what had become apparent from the hypocrites, they said: ﴿Are these the ones who swore by Allah with the utmost of their oaths?﴾, meaning the hypocrites." Ibn 'Abbas said: they went to excess in their oaths. Muqatil said: "the utmost of their oaths" is swearing by Allah. Al-Zajjaj said: they strove to exaggerate in swearing an oath. ﴿Indeed, they are with you﴾ against your enemy. ﴿Their deeds have become void﴾ because of their hypocrisy.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 54:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whoever among you turns back from his religion﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read yartadda, with the first dal assimilated into the second (idgham). Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read yartaddid, with two dals. Al-Zajjaj said: "yartaddid is the original form, because when the second of the doubled letters is vowelled with sukun, the doubling becomes apparent. As for yartadda, the first dal was assimilated into the second and the second was given a fatha, because of the meeting of two unvowelled letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn)." Al-Hasan said: God knew that a people would revert from Islam after the death of their Prophet, peace be upon him, so He informed them that He would bring a people whom He loves and who love Him.

Regarding who these people are, there are six opinions.

The first: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and his companions who fought the people of apostasy (ahl al-ridda). This was said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Hasan, peace be upon them both, and by Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj. Anas ibn Malik said: "The Companions disliked fighting those who withheld zakat, and said: 'They are people of the qiblah.' So Abu Bakr girded on his sword and went out alone, and they had no choice but to go out following him."

The second: Abu Bakr and 'Umar. This is also related from al-Hasan.

The third: they are the people of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. 'Iyad al-Ash'ari narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "They are the people of this one," meaning Abu Musa.

The fourth: they are the people of Yemen. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid also said so.

The fifth: they are the Ansar. This was said by al-Suddi.

The sixth: the Muhajirun and the Ansar. This was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Ibn Jarir said: Allah has fulfilled what He promised, and brought about in the time of 'Umar a people who were better in their standing in Islam than those who apostatized.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿humble toward the believers﴾. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, said: they are tender toward those of their own religion and severe toward those who oppose them in their religion. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "adhillah" is that their side is gentle toward the believers, not that they are abased.

﴿They strive in the way of Allah and do not fear the blame of any blamer﴾. Because the hypocrites court the disbelievers, support them, and fear their blame, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed that the sincere believer does not fear the blame of any blamer in (the cause of) Allah. Then He informed that this is not possible except by His enabling success, so He said: ﴿That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills﴾, meaning: their love for Allah, their gentleness toward the Muslims, and their severity toward the disbelievers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 55–56:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Your only protector is Allah, and His Messenger, and those who believe﴾. The scholars differed concerning whom it was revealed about, in four opinions.

The first: "Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'Indeed, a people have shown us enmity, and we cannot sit with your companions because of the distance of our dwellings.' (p-383) Then this verse was revealed. They said: 'We are content with Allah, His Messenger, and the believers.' Bilal called the adhan for the prayer, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out, and there was a poor man asking the people. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Has anyone given you anything?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'What?' He said: 'A silver ring.' He said: 'Who gave it to you?' He said: 'That one standing,' and behold, it was Ali ibn Abi Talib, who gave it to me while he was bowing. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this verse." This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and Muqatil also said this.

Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning Ali ibn Abi Talib, who gave charity while he was bowing.

The second: When Ubadah ibn al-Samit disavowed his Jewish allies, this verse was revealed concerning him. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas.

The third: It was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. This was said by Ikrimah.

The fourth: It was revealed concerning those among the Muslims who had passed away and those who remained among them. This was said by al-Hasan.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they give zakat while bowing﴾. In this there are two opinions.

One: They did this during their bowing, and this is the charity of Ali, peace be upon him, with his ring during his bowing. The second: It is among their characteristics to give zakat and to perform bowing.

(p-384) Concerning the meaning of "bowing" there are three opinions.

The first: It is the bowing itself, as narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. It was also said: the verse was revealed while they were in the bowing position. The second: It is voluntary prayer by night and day, and He singled out bowing for mention to honor it; this is also narrated from Ibn Abbas.

The third: It is humility and submissiveness, and they recited:

"Do not humiliate the poor man, perhaps you will bow one day while time has raised him up."

This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. As for "the party of Allah" (ḥizb Allah), al-Hasan said: they are the soldiers of Allah. Abu Ubaydah said: the helpers of Allah. Then there are two opinions concerning it.

One: They are the Emigrants (muhajirun) and the Helpers (ansar), said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: They are the Helpers alone, mentioned by Abu Sulayman.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 55–56:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Your only protector is Allah, and His Messenger, and those who believe﴾. The scholars differed concerning whom it was revealed about, in four opinions.

The first: "Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'Indeed, a people have shown us enmity, and we cannot sit with your companions because of the distance of our dwellings.' (p-383) Then this verse was revealed. They said: 'We are content with Allah, His Messenger, and the believers.' Bilal called the adhan for the prayer, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out, and there was a poor man asking the people. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Has anyone given you anything?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'What?' He said: 'A silver ring.' He said: 'Who gave it to you?' He said: 'That one standing,' and behold, it was Ali ibn Abi Talib, who gave it to me while he was bowing. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this verse." This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and Muqatil also said this.

Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning Ali ibn Abi Talib, who gave charity while he was bowing.

The second: When Ubadah ibn al-Samit disavowed his Jewish allies, this verse was revealed concerning him. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas.

The third: It was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. This was said by Ikrimah.

The fourth: It was revealed concerning those among the Muslims who had passed away and those who remained among them. This was said by al-Hasan.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they give zakat while bowing﴾. In this there are two opinions.

One: They did this during their bowing, and this is the charity of Ali, peace be upon him, with his ring during his bowing. The second: It is among their characteristics to give zakat and to perform bowing.

(p-384) Concerning the meaning of "bowing" there are three opinions.

The first: It is the bowing itself, as narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. It was also said: the verse was revealed while they were in the bowing position. The second: It is voluntary prayer by night and day, and He singled out bowing for mention to honor it; this is also narrated from Ibn Abbas.

The third: It is humility and submissiveness, and they recited:

"Do not humiliate the poor man, perhaps you will bow one day while time has raised him up."

This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. As for "the party of Allah" (ḥizb Allah), al-Hasan said: they are the soldiers of Allah. Abu Ubaydah said: the helpers of Allah. Then there are two opinions concerning it.

One: They are the Emigrants (muhajirun) and the Helpers (ansar), said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: They are the Helpers alone, mentioned by Abu Sulayman.

(p-385) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game﴾. The occasion of its revelation: Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut and Suwayd ibn al-Harith had both outwardly professed Islam, then turned hypocrite, and some men among the Muslims were friendly with them. So this verse was revealed. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas. As for their taking the religion as a mockery and a game, it is their displaying Islam while concealing disbelief, and their toying with the religion. "Those who were given the Book" are the Jews and the Christians, and "the disbelievers" are the worshippers of idols. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read "wal-kuffara" in the accusative, meaning: do not take the disbelievers as allies. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "wal-kuffari" in the genitive, because the phrase is close to the governing preposition. Abu 'Amr also pronounced the alif with imalah (inclination). ﴿And fear Allah﴾, that you should make them your allies.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 58:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you call to prayer﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts.

The first: "The caller of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would, when he called to prayer and the Muslims rose to it, the Jews would say: 'Let them rise, may they not rise! Let them pray, may they not pray!' mocking and laughing. So this verse was revealed." This was related by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second: "When the disbelievers heard the adhan, they envied the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims for it, and said: 'O Muhammad, you have innovated something we have not heard of among the previous nations. If you claim prophethood, then you have opposed the prophets before you in this adhan. How ugly this sound is, and how vile this matter!' So this verse was revealed." This was mentioned by some of the exegetes. And al-Suddi said: "There was a man from the Christians in Medina who, whenever he heard the caller calling, 'I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,' would say: 'May the liar be burned.' One night his servant came to him with a fire while he was asleep and his family were sleeping, and a spark fell and burned the house, and he and his family were burned."

Al-munada (the call) is the adhan (the call to prayer). Their taking it as mockery (huzuwan) is their laughing at it and winking at one another. ﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾: they do not understand what benefit lies in answering the prayer, nor what harm befalls them through mocking it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 59:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, do you resent us for anything except that we have believed in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before, and that most of you are defiantly disobedient?"﴾ The occasion of its revelation: "A group of the Jews came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about which of the messengers he believed in. He mentioned all the prophets, and when he mentioned Jesus, they denied his prophethood and said: 'By Allah, we know of no religion worse than your religion.' Then this verse and the one after it were revealed." This is related by Ibn ʿAbbas.

al-Hasan and al-Aʿmash read "tanqamūna" (تَنْقَمُونَ) with a fatha on the qaf. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said "naqamtu ʿalā al-rajul anqimu" and "naqimtu ʿalayhi anqamu," and the first is better. The meaning of "naqimtu" is that I went to great lengths in disliking something. The meaning is: Do you dislike in us anything except our faith and your own defiant disobedience? Because you know that we are upon the truth, and that you are defiantly disobedient.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 60:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Shall I inform you of something worse than that as requital from Allah?﴾ The exegetes said: The occasion of its revelation was the statement of the Jews to the believers: "By Allah, we know no people with less fortune than you in this world and the Hereafter, nor a religion more evil than your religion." Regarding His saying ﴿something worse than that﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: something worse than the believers. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: something worse than what you resent of our faith. This was said by al-Zajjaj. As for "al-mathuba" (requital), it is reward. Al-Zajjaj said: The position of "man" in His saying ﴿those whom Allah has cursed﴾ may be in the nominative or the genitive, as you wish. Whoever puts it in the genitive makes it a substitute (badal) for "sharr" (worse), so the meaning is: "Shall I inform you of those whom Allah has cursed?" Whoever puts it in the nominative does so by supposing a hidden "huwa" (he/it), as if someone said: "Who is that?" and it was said: "He is the one whom Allah has cursed." Abu Salih said, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: "Those whom Allah has cursed" means those cursed through the poll-tax (jizya), and upon whom He was angry for worshipping the calf; so they are worse in requital with Allah. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the two transformed groups from the People of the Sabbath were: the young men of them transformed into apes, and their elders into swine. Others said: the apes are the People of the Sabbath, and the swine are the disbelievers of the Table of 'Isa. Ibn Qutayba used to say: "I think these apes and swine are the very transformed ones, who have reproduced." He said: "I have argued from His saying Exalted is He: ﴿and made from them apes and swine﴾, for the entry of the definite article (alif and lam) indicates definiteness, and that they are the apes that are observed. Had He intended something that became extinct and passed away, He would have said: 'and made from them apes and swine,' unless the hadith of Umm Habiba concerning the 'transformed' is authentic, in which case it would be as he said, upon him be peace." I say: As for the hadith of Umm Habiba in the "Sahih," it was related by Muslim alone, that "a man asked the Prophet ﷺ, saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, are the apes and swine among those who were transformed?' The Prophet ﷺ said: '[Indeed Allah] has not transformed a people or destroyed a people such that He would give them offspring or a successor, and the apes and swine existed before that.'" We have mentioned in Surat al-Baqara further explanation of this from Ibn 'Abbas, so one should not heed the opinion of Ibn Qutayba.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and worshipped the Taghut﴾. There are twenty readings for it. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Nafi' and al-Kisa'i recited: "wa 'abada" with a fatha on the 'ayn, the ba' and the dal, and a nasb on the ta' of "al-Taghut," and there are two aspects for it.

The first: the meaning is: "and made from them apes and swine, and those who worshipped the Taghut."

The second: the meaning is: "those whom Allah has cursed and who worshipped the Taghut." Hamza recited: "wa 'abuda al-taghuti" with a fatha on the 'ayn and the dal, a damma on the ba', and a khafd on the ta' of "al-Taghut." Tha'lab said: it has no aspect except that "fa'l" is pluralized as "fa'ul." Al-Zajjaj said: its aspect is that the noun is patterned on "fa'ula," as you say "'alima Zayd" and "rajul hadhar," meaning one who is exceedingly cautious. So the meaning is: "there were made from them the servants of the Taghut and those who attained the utmost in obedience to the Taghut." Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited: "wa 'abadu" with a fatha on the 'ayn and the ba', and a raf' on the dal as a plural, "al-Taghuta" in the accusative. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited: "wa 'abada" with a fatha on the 'ayn, the ba' and the dal, except that both of them kasra'd the ta' of "al-Taghut." Al-Farra' said: they intended "'abada" (servants), and dropped the ha'. Anas ibn Malik recited: "wa 'abid" with a fatha on the 'ayn and the dal, and a ya' after the ba', with a khafd on the ta' of "al-Taghut." Ayyub and al-A'mash recited: "wa 'uబbada" with a damma on the 'ayn, a nasb on the ba' and the dal with the ba' shaddada, and a kasra on the ta' of "al-Taghut." Abu Hurayra, Abu Raja' and Ibn al-Sumayf recited: "wa 'abid" with an alif, the ba' kasra'd, the dal fatha'd, with a kasra on the ta' of "al-Taghut." Abu al-'Aliya and Yahya ibn Wathhab recited: "wa 'ubud" with a damma on the 'ayn and the ba', and a fatha on the dal, with a kasra on the ta' of "al-Taghut." Al-Zajjaj said: it is the plural of "'abid" and "'ubud," like "raghif" and "ruguf," and "sarir" and "surur," and the meaning is: "and made from them the servants of the Taghut." Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, Muriq al-'Ijli and al-Nakha'i recited: "wa 'ubida" with a damma on the 'ayn, a kasra on the ba' lightened, a fatha on the dal, with a damma on the ta' of "al-Taghut." Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza' and 'Ikrima recited: "wa 'abbada" with a fatha on the 'ayn and the dal, and a shadda on the ba', with a nasb on the ta' of "al-Taghut." Al-Hasan, Abu Mijlaz and Abu Nahik recited: "wa 'abda" with a fatha on the 'ayn and the dal, and a sukun on the ba' lightened, with a kasra on the ta' of "al-Taghut." Qatada and Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil recited: "wa 'abada" with a fatha on the 'ayn, the ba' and the dal, and a ta' in pronunciation, nasbed after the dal, "al-Tawaghit," with an alif, a waw and a ya' after the ghayn, in the plural. Al-Dahhak and 'Amr ibn Dinar recited: "wa 'ubada" with a damma on the 'ayn, a fatha on the ba' and the dal, with the ba' lightened, and a kasra on the ta' of "al-Taghut." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Sha'bi recited: "wa 'abda" like Hamza, except that they raised the ta' of "al-Taghut." Yahya ibn Ya'mar and al-Jahdari recited: "wa 'abudu" with a fatha on the 'ayn, a raf' on the ba' and the dal, with a kasra on the ta' of "al-Taghut." Abu al-Ashhab al-'Utaridi recited: "wa 'ubda" with a damma on the 'ayn, a sukun on the ba', and a nasb on the dal, with a kasra on the ta' of "al-Taghut." Abu al-Simak recited: "wa 'abadatu" with a fatha on the 'ayn, the ba' and the dal, and a ta' in pronunciation after the dal, raised, with a kasra on the ta' of "al-Taghut." Mu'adh al-Qari' recited: "wa 'abid," like the reading of Abu Hurayra, except that he damma'd the dal. Abu Haywa recited: "wa 'ubbad" with a shadda on the ba' and an alif after it, with a raf' on the 'ayn, and a fatha on the dal. Ibn Hadhlam and 'Amr ibn Fa'id recited: "wa 'abbad," like Abu Haywa, except that the 'ayn is fatha'd and the dal is damma'd.

The word "al-Taghut" has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqara. Regarding its meaning here there are two opinions. The first: the idols. The second: Satan.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are worse in position﴾, meaning: these whom we have described are worse in position than the believers, and there is no evil in the position of the believers; but the speech is built upon the words of the opponents, when they said to the believers: "We know of no one worse than you," so it was said: "whoever has this attribute is worse than them."

Allah says: ﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe."﴾ Qatadah said: These are people from among the Jews who would enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and inform him that they believed in what he had brought, while they remained holding fast to their misguidance.

(p-391) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they had entered with disbelief﴾ means: they entered as disbelievers and they left as disbelievers. So disbelief was with them in both of their states. ﴿And Allah is most knowing of what they were concealing﴾ of disbelief and hypocrisy.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 62:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you see many of them﴾, meaning: the Jews, ﴿hastening﴾, that is, hurrying, ﴿into sin﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: it is the acts of disobedience; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it is disbelief (kufr); this was said by al-Suddi. As for ʿudwan, it is injustice (zulm).

Regarding "al-suht" (forbidden gain) there are three views.

The first: bribery in judgment. The second: bribery in religion. The third: usury (riba).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 63:

﴿Why do the rabbis (rabbaniyyun) and the scholars (ahbar) not forbid them?﴾ "Law la" (لَوْلا) is here in the sense of "halla" (هَلّا), meaning "why not" or "would that". "Al-Rabbaniyyun" (الرَّبّانِيُّونَ) is mentioned in (Al 'Imran), and "al-Ahbar" (الأحْبارُ) has already been mentioned in this surah. This verse is among the most severe verses against those who abandon enjoining good (al-amr bil-ma'ruf) and forbidding evil (al-nahy 'an al-munkar), because Allah the Exalted combined the doer of evil and the one who abandons denouncing it in censure. Ibn 'Abbas said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more severe in rebuke than this verse."

God's words: ﴿The Jews say, "God's hand is chained up."﴾ Abu Salih reported from Ibn Abbas: it was revealed concerning Fanhas the Jew and his companions, who said, "God's hand is chained up." Muqatil said: Fanhas, Ibn Suluba, and Azar ibn Abi Azar.

There are three opinions regarding the reason for their saying this.

The first: God had expanded their provision, but when they disobeyed God regarding the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and disbelieved in him, He withheld some of what He had expanded for them, so they said, "God's hand is chained up." This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and Ikrima also said this.

The second: God had asked them for a loan, as He had asked this community for a loan, so they said, "God is stingy, and His hand is chained up, so He asks us to lend to Him." This was said by Qatada.

The third: when the Christians helped Bukhtnasar the Magian (Nebuchadnezzar) in destroying Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), the Jews said, "If God were righteous, He would have prevented us from him. So His hand is chained up." Qatada also mentioned this.

Al-maghlulah means the one that withholds and constricts. Regarding what they meant by saying that it withholds, there are two opinions.

One: it withholds the giving. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Farra', Ibn Qutayba, and al-Zajjaj.

The second: it withholds from punishing us, so He punishes us only to the extent of the fulfilment of the oath (tahillat al-qasam), in proportion to our worship of the calf. This was said by al-Hasan.

Regarding God's words ﴿Their hands are chained up﴾ there are three opinions.

One: they are chained up in Hell. This was said by al-Hasan. The second: they have withheld from good. This was said by Muqatil. The third: they were made stingy, so they are the stingiest of people. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Ibn al-Anbari said: This is a report that God informed creation of, that this has befallen them. Its position is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). Its implied meaning: the Jews said this in the state of God's judgment by chaining up their hands and His cursing them (p-393), and it is permissible that the meaning is: so their hands were chained up. It is also permissible that it is a supplication, meaning: God's teaching us how we should invoke curses upon them, like His words: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ [al-Masad: 1], and His words: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if God wills, in security﴾ [al-Fath: 27].

Regarding God's words ﴿and they were cursed for what they said﴾ there are three opinions.

One: they were removed far from God's mercy. The second: they were punished in this world with the jizya (poll tax), and in the Hereafter with the Fire. The third: they were transformed into apes and swine.

Ibn Abbas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever curses something that is not deserving of the curse, the curse returns upon the Jews, with the curse of God upon them."

Al-Zajjaj said: Some people have gone to the view that the meaning of "God's hand" is His blessing. This is an error, refuted by His words: ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾. So the meaning according to their saying would be "His two blessings," whereas the blessings of God are too many to be counted. The intended meaning of His words ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾ is that He is generous, spending as He wills. Ibn al-Anbari also went to this view. Ibn Abbas said: If He wills, He expands provision, and if He wills, He restricts it.

God's words: ﴿And what has been sent down to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief﴾

Al-Zajjaj said: Whenever something is sent down to you, they disbelieve in it, so their disbelief increases. Here, "transgression" (al-tughyan) means excess in disbelief. Muqatil said: What has been sent down to you from your Lord regarding the matter of stoning and blood will increase the Banu al-Nadir in transgression and disbelief.

(p-394) God's words: ﴿And We have cast among them enmity and hatred﴾. Regarding who is meant by this there are two opinions.

One: the Jews and the Christians. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Muqatil. If it is asked: where is the mention of the Christians? The answer: it has already preceded in His words: ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾. The second: they are the Jews. This was said by Qatada.

God's words: ﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it﴾. The mention of kindling fire is a parable struck for their striving in warfare. It was said: the origin of using the name of fire for war is that when a tribe of the Arabs wished to wage war against another, they would kindle fire on the tops of mountains and elevated places, so that their readiness for war would be known, and whoever wished to assist them would prepare. It was also said: when they made a firm pact to be serious in their war, they would kindle a fire and make their alliance.

Regarding the meaning of the verse there are two opinions.

One: every time they gathered for war against the Prophet (ﷺ), God scattered them. The second: every time they schemed a plot, God turned it back.

God's words: ﴿And they strive in the land to cause corruption﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions.

One: through sins. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Muqatil. The second: by erasing the mention of the Prophet (ﷺ) from their books, and by repelling Islam. This was said by al-Zajjaj. The third: through disbelief. The fourth: through wrongdoing. Al-Mawardi mentioned these two.

Allah's saying: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed﴾, meaning the Jews and the Christians, ﴿and feared Allah﴾ by avoiding shirk, ﴿We would have removed from them their misdeeds﴾ that had already passed.

(p-395) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they acted in accordance with what is in them. "And what was sent down to them from their Lord" has two interpretations. One: the books of the prophets of the Children of Israel. The second: the Qur'an, because when they were addressed by it, it was being sent down to them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾. Concerning this there are two views.

One: they would have eaten from the rain of the sky and the growth of the earth. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and Qatada.

The second: the meaning is that provision would have been widened for them, as one says: "So-and-so is in ease from his horn to his foot." This was mentioned by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. And by this God, Exalted is He, has informed that piety is a cause of the widening of provision, as He said: ﴿Had the people of the towns believed and been mindful of God, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 96], and He said: ﴿And He will provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 3].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾. He means: from among the People of the Book, and they are those among them who embraced Islam; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. And al-Qurazi said: they are those who said, "The Messiah is the servant of God and His messenger." And "iqtisad" (moderation) is uprightness in speech and action, without excess or deficiency.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 67:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O Messenger, deliver what has been sent down to you﴾. The commentators mentioned that this verse was revealed on account of several occasions. Al-Hasan narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah sent me with His message, I was distressed by it, and I knew that some of the people would deny me." And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in awe of the Quraysh, the Jews and the Christians, so Allah revealed this verse.

Mujahid said: When there was revealed ﴿O Messenger, deliver what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾, he said: "My Lord, how shall I act? I am alone, and the people will gather against me." So Allah revealed ﴿And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message. And Allah will protect you from the people﴾.

Muqatil said: When he called the Jews and was insistent with them, they began to mock him, so he remained silent toward them, and he was urged by this verse.

Ibn Abbas said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to be guarded. Abu Talib would send with him, every day, men from the Banu Hashim to guard him, until this verse was revealed to him, and he said: 'O uncle, indeed Allah has protected me from the jinn and mankind.'"

Abu Hurayrah said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) once rested under a tree and hung his sword upon it. A man came and took it and said: 'O Muhammad, who will prevent me from you?' He said: 'Allah.' So there was revealed his saying: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾."

Aisha said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stayed awake one night, so I said: 'What is the matter with you?' He said: 'Is there not a righteous man who will guard me tonight?' While we were in that, I heard the sound of weapons. He said: 'Who is this?' The reply came: 'Sa'd and Huthayfah; we have come to guard you.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) slept until I heard his snoring, and then there was revealed ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then put his head out of a leather tent and said: 'Disperse, O people, for Allah, Exalted is He, has protected me.'"

Al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿deliver what has been sent down to you﴾ means: deliver all of what has been sent down to you, and do not fear anyone, nor leave out any part of it for fear that some harm will befall you. If you leave out any part of it, then you have not delivered.

Ibn Qutaybah said: What indicates this omitted element is His saying ﴿And Allah will protect you﴾. Ibn Abbas said: If you conceal a single verse, then you have not conveyed My message.

Others said: The meaning is: deliver all of what has been sent down to you openly; if you conceal any part of it out of fear of harm that would reach you, it is as if you had delivered nothing.

Abu Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "risalatahu" (His message) in the singular. Nafi' read "risalatihi" (His messages) in the plural.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: That is, He will prevent you from them. The protection (ʿiṣmah) of Allah is His preventing the servant from sins. It is said: "food that does not protect (lā yaʿṣimu)," meaning it does not prevent hunger. If it is said: Where is the guarantee of protection when his forehead was split, his incisor was broken, and harm was pushed to the extreme against him? There are two answers to this.

One: He protected him from being killed, taken captive, and from the destruction of the whole, whereas incidental harms do not contradict the protection of the whole. The second: this verse was revealed after that had befallen him, since al-Ma'idah is among the last of what was revealed.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾. There are two views concerning this.

One: He does not guide them to Paradise. The second: He does not help them to attain their aim.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 68:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, you do not stand upon anything"﴾. The occasion of its revelation (sabab al-nuzul): "The Jews said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'Do you not believe in what we have of the Torah, and bear witness that it is true?' He said: 'Yes, but you have introduced innovations and denied what is in it, so I am innocent of your innovations.' They said: 'We are upon guidance, and we hold to what is in our hands, and we do not believe in you.' So this verse was revealed." This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

As for "the People of the Scripture" (ahl al-kitab), what is meant by them is the Jews and the Christians. And His saying, ﴿you do not stand upon anything﴾, meaning: you do not stand upon anything of the true religion until you establish the Torah and the Gospel (al-Injil). Their establishment (iqamah) is acting upon what is in them, and among that is belief in Muhammad ﷺ. Regarding "that which has been sent down to them from their Lord" there are two opinions, which have already passed, and likewise the rest of the verse.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 69:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews and the Sabians﴾. We have already mentioned its tafsir in (al-Baqarah). Likewise, they differed concerning its muhkam (clear, unabrogated) and its naskh (abrogation), as we explained there. As for the raf' (nominative case) of "al-Sabi'un" (the Sabians), al-Zajjaj reported from the Basrans, among them al-Khalil and Sibawayh, that His saying "wa-al-Sabi'un" (and the Sabians) is treated as postponed (in its place) and is marked nominative by being the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'). The meaning is: indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews, whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteous deeds, there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve. And the Sabians and the Christians are likewise. They recited:

؎ Otherwise, know that we and you are transgressors (bughat) as long as we remain in dissension (shiqaq).

The meaning: know that we are transgressors as long as we remain in dissension, and you are likewise.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 70:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾. Muqatil said: He took their covenant in the Torah, that they would act in accordance with what is in it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Among those they called liars were Muhammad and ʿIsa, and among those they killed were Zakariyya and Yahya. Al-Zajjaj said: As for the denial (al-takdhib), the Jews and the Christians share in it. As for the killing (al-qatl), it is specific to the Jews.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 71:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they thought there would be no trial﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "takūna" (takūna) with the accusative (naṣb). Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "takūnu" (takūnu) with the nominative (raf'). They did not differ on the nominative of "fitnatun" (fitnatun).

Makki ibn Abi Talib said: whoever reads with the nominative makes "an" (an) a lightened form of the heavy "inna" (inna), and supplies the pronoun "al-ha'" (al-hā') with it, and takes "ḥasibū" (ḥasibū) to mean "they were certain" (ayqanū). This is because "an" is for emphasis, and emphasis is only permissible with certainty. The implied meaning is: "that there would be no trial." Whoever reads with the accusative makes "an" the particle that governs the verb in the subjunctive, and takes "ḥasibū" to mean "they thought" (ẓannū). If the verb before "an" is one that does not suit doubt, then "an" can only be a lightened form of the heavy particle, and it does not govern the verb in the accusative, as in His saying: ﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them?﴾ [Ṭa-Ha: 89] and ﴿He knew that there would be among you the sick﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20].

Abu 'Ali said: verbs are of three kinds. One kind indicates the establishment and settledness of a thing, such as knowledge and certainty. A second kind indicates the opposite of establishment and settledness. A third kind is drawn to this meaning at one time and to that meaning at another. Whatever carries the meaning of knowledge is followed by the heavy "anna" (anna), because its meaning is the establishment and settledness of a thing, as in His saying: ﴿And they know that Allah is the Manifest Truth﴾ [al-Nur: 25] and ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ [al-'Alaq: 14]. Whatever is not of the sense of establishment and settledness, such as "aṭma'" (I hope/desire), "akhaf" (I fear) and "arju" (I hope), is followed by the light "an" (an), as in His saying: ﴿If you fear that they will not keep the limits of Allah﴾ [al-Baqara: 229], ﴿You fear that the people will snatch you away﴾ [al-Anfal: 26], ﴿So we feared that it would overburden them﴾ [al-Kahf: 80], and ﴿I hope that He will forgive me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 82]. Whatever wavers between the two states, like "ḥasibtu" (ḥasibtu) and "ẓanantu" (ẓanantu), is treated at one time as equivalent to knowledge and at another time as equivalent to "arju" and "aṭma'". Both readings in ﴿And they thought there would be no trial﴾ have been transmitted by revelation. The position of the one who reads with the accusative is like His saying: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them﴾ [al-Jathiya: 21], ﴿Or do those who do evil deeds think that they will outrun Us?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 4], and ﴿Do the people think that they will be left?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2]. The position of the one who reads with the nominative is like His saying: ﴿Do they think that what We extend to them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55] and ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secret?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 80].

Ibn 'Abbas said: they thought that Allah would not punish them, nor test them by their killing of the prophets and their denial of the messengers.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they became blind and deaf﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: this is a parable, its interpretation being that they did not act upon what they heard and saw of the signs, so they became like the blind and the deaf.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then Allah turned to them in forgiveness﴾. Concerning this there are two views.

The first: He removed the affliction from them. This is said by Muqatil. Others said it is their victory over their enemies, and this is mentioned in His saying: ﴿Then We gave you the return of victory over them﴾ [al-Isra': 6].

The second: the meaning of "tāba 'alayhim" is that He sent Muhammad to them, informing them that Allah had turned to them if they believed and were sincere. This is said by al-Zajjaj. Concerning His saying: ﴿Then many of them became blind and deaf again﴾ there are two views.

The first: they did not repent after the removal of the affliction. This is said by Muqatil.

The second: they did not believe after the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Many of them﴾, that is, many of them became blind and deaf, as you say: "Your people came to me, most of them." Ibn al-Anbari said: this verse was revealed concerning a people who were upon disbelief before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent. When he was sent, they denied him out of rebellion and envy, and they assumed that this deed would not be ruinous for them or a crime against them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they thought there would be no trial﴾, that is, they thought that no trial would befall them through persisting in disbelief, so they became blind and deaf by turning away from the truth. ﴿Then Allah turned to them﴾, that is, He exposed them to repentance by sending Muhammad (ﷺ), even though they did not repent. Then, after the truth was made clear through Muhammad, many of them became blind and deaf again. He singled out some of them with the latter action, because they did not all unite in opposition to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

(p-402) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Certainly those have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary."﴾ Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran, who said that.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the Messiah said﴾ meaning: the Messiah had said to them while he was among them, "Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah, Allah has forbidden Paradise to him."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 73:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three."﴾ Mujahid said: They are the Christians. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: When Jesus was born, no idol remained but that it fell on its face. So the devils gathered before Iblis and informed him. He went and traversed the regions of the earth, then returned and said: "This newborn who was born without a male, I wanted to look at him. I found the angels had surrounded his mother. Let two of your rebellious ones remain with me." When morning came, he went out with the two of them in the form of men, and they came to the Mosque of the Children of Israel while they were talking about the matter of Jesus and saying: "A child born without a father." Iblis said: "This is not a human being, but Allah wished to take on a form in a woman in order to test the servants." One of his two companions said: "How great is what you have said! Rather, Allah wished to take a son." The third said: "How great is what you have said! Rather, Allah intended to make a god on the earth." They cast this speech onto the tongues of the people, then dispersed, and the people spoke with it.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: When Jesus was raised, a hundred of the scholars of the Children of Israel gathered and selected four from among them. One of them said: "Jesus is Allah; he was on the earth as he willed, then he ascended to heaven, for none gives life to the dead, heals the blind and the leper, except Allah." The second said: "It is not so, for we have known Jesus and we have known his mother. Rather, he is the son of Allah." The third said: "I do not say as you two have said, but his mother brought him forth from a deed other than righteous." The fourth said: "You have spoken abominably. Rather, he is the servant of Allah and His messenger, and His word." Then they left, and each of them was followed by a group of people. The exegetes said: The meaning of the verse is that the Christians said: divinity is shared between Allah, Jesus and Mary, and each one of them is a god. There is an ellipsis in the verse; the meaning is: "the third of three gods," and the word "gods" was omitted because the meaning is understood, since one does not disbelieve who says: "He is the third of three" without intending "gods," for there is no two but that He is the third of them. What indicates the omitted word is His saying: ﴿And there is no god except one God.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of "third of three" is that He is one of three. The "min" entered in His saying ﴿And there is no god﴾ for emphasis.

"Those of them who disbelieved" are those who persist in this statement. Ibn Jarir said: The meaning is: "Those who say, 'The Messiah is Allah,' and those who say, 'Indeed, Allah is the third of three,' and every disbeliever who follows their path, will surely be touched by a painful punishment."

"His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Will they not then turn in repentance to Allah?﴾ Al-Farra' said: its wording is that of a question, but its meaning is a command, like His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91]."

(p-404) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger﴾. In this there is a refutation of the Jews in their denial of his prophethood, and of the Christians in their claim of his divinity. The meaning is that he is not a god; his ruling is the ruling of those messengers who came before him. And in His saying: ﴿and his mother was a truthful woman﴾ there is a refutation of those Jews who attributed to her immorality. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Siddiqa means one who is intensive in truthfulness, and siddiq is on the pattern "fi'il," one of the intensive forms, just as you say: "So-and-so is sikkit," meaning one who is intensive in silence.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿they both used to eat food﴾, there are two opinions.

The first: that it shows they both live by nourishment, and whoever cannot sustain himself except by eating food is not a god. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: that by mentioning eating food He alerted to its consequence, which is excretion (al-hadath), since whoever eats food must necessarily excrete. This was said by Ibn Qutayba. He said: And His saying: ﴿Look how We make the signs clear to them﴾ is among the most subtle forms of metaphor (kinaya). And "yu'fakun" means: they are turned away from the truth and deviated. It is said: "afika al-rajulu 'an kadha" when the man turned away from such-and-such; and "ard ma'fukah" means a land deprived of rain and vegetation, as if that had been turned away from it and deviated.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 76:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Do you worship, besides Allah, that which holds no power to harm you or benefit you?﴾ Muqatil said: Say to the Christians of Najran: "Do you worship, besides Allah," meaning: Jesus, son of Mary, who does not possess for you any harm in this world, nor any benefit in the Hereafter. And Allah is the All-Hearing of their saying: "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and "the third of three," the All-Knowing of their statement.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 77:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, do not exceed the limits in your religion beyond the truth"﴾. Muqatil said: They are the Christians of Najran. The meaning is: do not go to extremes (ghuluww) in your religion, so that you say what is not the truth about Jesus. We have already explained the meaning of "ghuluww" at the end of Surat al-Nisa'.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before and led many astray and strayed from the right way﴾. Abu Sulayman said: "before" means before you go astray. Regarding them there are two opinions.

One of them: they are the leaders of misguidance among the Jews.

The second: they are the leaders of the Jews and the Christians. The verse is addressed to those who were in the time of our Prophet (ﷺ), and they were forbidden to follow their predecessors in what they innovated by their own desires.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 78:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed﴾. There are two opinions regarding their being cursed.

The first: it is the curse itself, and its meaning is distancing from mercy. Ibn 'Abbas said: They were cursed upon the tongue of Dawud (David), so they became apes, and they were cursed upon the tongue of 'Isa (Jesus) in the Injil (Gospel). Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that Dawud and 'Isa informed that Muhammad (ﷺ) is a prophet, and cursed whoever disbelieves in him.

The second: it is transformation (maskh), as said by Mujahid: They were cursed upon the tongue of Dawud, so they became apes, and upon the tongue of 'Isa, so they became swine. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: The people of the Sabbath were cursed upon the tongue of Dawud, for when they transgressed, Dawud said: "O Allah, curse them and make them a sign," so they were transformed into apes. And the people of the Table were cursed upon the tongue of 'Isa, for when they ate from it and did not believe, 'Isa said: "O Allah, curse them as You cursed the people of the Sabbath," so they were made into swine.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is because they disobeyed﴾. That is, that curse was for their disobedience to Allah, the Exalted, in opposing His command and His prohibition, and for their transgression in exceeding the limits He set for them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 79:

His saying, Most High: ﴿They did not forbid one another from any wrong they committed﴾. At-tanahi (mutual forbidding) is a form of tafa'ul (reciprocal form) derived from an-nahy (forbidding), meaning: they did not forbid one another from the wrong (munkar).

The exegetes mentioned three opinions regarding this munkar (wrong).

The first: hunting fish on the Sabbath. The second: taking bribes in judgment.

The third: consuming riba (usury) and the price of fats. The mention of the wrong in indefinite form (munkaran) indicates generality, and prevents restricting it to this limited set. What we have said is also supported by what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, when a man from the Children of Israel saw his brother committing a sin, he would forbid him from it out of admonition. Then, on the next day, what he had seen from him did not prevent him from being his companion, his dining partner and his drinking partner. When Allah, Most High, saw this from them, He set the hearts of some of them against others, and cursed them through the tongue of Dawud and Isa, son of Maryam."

His saying, Most High: ﴿Evil indeed was what they used to do﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the lam (la) has entered for oath and emphasis, and the meaning is: evil indeed is the deed they did.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 80–81:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You see many of them﴾ — regarding those referred to, there are two opinions.

The first: they are the hypocrites (munafiqun). This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and Mujahid.

The second: they are the Jews. This was said by Muqatil, along with others. According to this opinion, the connection between the verses is evident. According to the first, the discourse returns to His saying: ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them﴾. Regarding ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ there are two opinions. The first: they are the Jews, as said by the proponents of the first view. The second: they are the polytheists of the Arabs, as said by the proponents of this second view.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Evil is that which their souls have put forth for them﴾ — meaning: evil is what they have sent ahead for their return (to the Hereafter). ﴿That Allah has become angry at them﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "An" may be in a position of nominative case (raf') by the implied pronoun "huwa," as if it were said: "It is that Allah has become angry at them."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 80–81:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You see many of them﴾ — regarding those referred to, there are two opinions.

The first: they are the hypocrites (munafiqun). This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and Mujahid.

The second: they are the Jews. This was said by Muqatil, along with others. According to this opinion, the connection between the verses is evident. According to the first, the discourse returns to His saying: ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them﴾. Regarding ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ there are two opinions. The first: they are the Jews, as said by the proponents of the first view. The second: they are the polytheists of the Arabs, as said by the proponents of this second view.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Evil is that which their souls have put forth for them﴾ — meaning: evil is what they have sent ahead for their return (to the Hereafter). ﴿That Allah has become angry at them﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "An" may be in a position of nominative case (raf') by the implied pronoun "huwa," as if it were said: "It is that Allah has become angry at them."

(p-408) His words, Exalted is He: ﴿You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward those who believe to be the Jews﴾. The commentators (mufassirun) said: this verse and what follows it that relates to it were revealed concerning al-Najashi (the Negus) and his companions. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: al-Najashi sent a group of people to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they embraced Islam, so this verse and the one after it were revealed concerning them. We will mention their story later. Al-Zajjaj said: the lam in ﴿لَتَجِدَنَّ﴾ is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), and the nun (nun al-tawkid, the emphatic nun) entered to separate the present from the future. ﴿عَداوَةً﴾ is in the accusative as a specifying accusative (tamyiz). The Jews supported the polytheists against the believers out of envy toward the Prophet (ﷺ).

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who associate partners with Allah﴾ means: the worshippers of idols. As for those who said, "We are Christians," is this general to all Christians, or specific? On this there are two views.

One of them: it is specific, and then there are two views regarding it.

One of them: it refers to al-Najashi and his companions when they embraced Islam. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr.

The second: they are a group of Christians who adhered to the sharia (religious law) of Jesus, and when Muhammad, peace be upon him, came, they embraced Islam. This is the view of Qatada.

The second view: it is general. Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible that it refers to the Christians, because they were less supportive of the polytheists than the Jews were.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿That is because among them are qissisun (priests)﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: al-qiss and al-qissis are among the leaders of the Christians. Qutrub said: al-qissis is one who knows the language of the Romans. As for al-ruhban (monks), they are the worshippers, the lords of the monasteries (sawami'). Ibn Faris said: al-tarahhub means devotion (ta'abbud). If it is asked: how did He praise them by saying that among them are priests and monks, when that is not part of our sharia? The answer: He praised them for adhering to the religion of Jesus, when they applied to the matter of Muhammad what had been taken from them in their Book, (p-409) and monasticism had been regarded as commendable in their religion. The meaning is: among them are scholars of what Jesus enjoined concerning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). Qadi Abu Ya'la said: a person may ignorantly think that this verse praises the Christians, but this is not so, because it only praises those among them who believed, and what follows confirms this. There is no doubt that the saying of the Christians is more corrupt than the saying of the Jews.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And that they are not arrogant﴾, that is: they do not act arrogantly toward following the truth.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger﴾. Ibn Abbas said: when the companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him, were present before al-Najashi and recited the Qur'an, the priests and monks heard it, and their tears flowed because of what they recognized of the truth. Then Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿That is because among them are priests﴾ up to His words: ﴿with the witnesses﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "al-Najashi sent thirty men from his best companions to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited the Qur'an to them, and they wept and softened, and said: 'By Allah, we recognize it,' and they embraced Islam. They went to al-Najashi and informed him, and he embraced Islam. Then Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger﴾, the verse." Al-Suddi said: they were twelve men: seven of the priests and five of the monks. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an to them, they wept and believed, and this verse was revealed concerning them.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So record us with the witnesses﴾, that is: with those who bear witness to the truth. The commentators have four views on what is meant by "the witnesses" here.

One of them: Muhammad and his community. This was narrated by Ali ibn Abi Talha and Ikrima from Ibn Abbas.

The second: the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. The third: those who bear witness to faith. This was said by al-Hasan. The fourth: the prophets and the believers. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Qutrub said: al-qissis is one who knows the language of the Romans. As for al-ruhban (monks), they are the worshippers, the lords of the monasteries (sawami'). Ibn Faris said: al-tarahhub means devotion (ta'abbud). If it is asked: how did He praise them by saying that among them are priests and monks, when that is not part of our sharia? The answer: He praised them for adhering to the religion of Jesus, when they applied to the matter of Muhammad what had been taken from them in their Book, (p-409) and monasticism had been regarded as commendable in their religion. The meaning is: among them are scholars of what Jesus enjoined concerning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). Qadi Abu Ya'la said: a person may ignorantly think that this verse praises the Christians, but this is not so, because it only praises those among them who believed, and what follows confirms this. There is no doubt that the saying of the Christians is more corrupt than the saying of the Jews.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And that they are not arrogant﴾, that is: they do not act arrogantly toward following the truth.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger﴾. Ibn Abbas said: when the companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him, were present before al-Najashi and recited the Qur'an, the priests and monks heard it, and their tears flowed because of what they recognized of the truth. Then Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿That is because among them are priests﴾ up to His words: ﴿with the witnesses﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "al-Najashi sent thirty men from his best companions to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited the Qur'an to them, and they wept and softened, and said: 'By Allah, we recognize it,' and they embraced Islam. They went to al-Najashi and informed him, and he embraced Islam. Then Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger﴾, the verse." Al-Suddi said: they were twelve men: seven of the priests and five of the monks. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an to them, they wept and believed, and this verse was revealed concerning them.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So record us with the witnesses﴾, that is: with those who bear witness to the truth. The commentators have four views on what is meant by "the witnesses" here.

One of them: Muhammad and his community. This was narrated by Ali ibn Abi Talha and Ikrima from Ibn Abbas.

The second: the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. The third: those who bear witness to faith. This was said by al-Hasan. The fourth: the prophets and the believers. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 84–86:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And why should we not believe in Allah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: Their people blamed them for believing, so they said this. Regarding "the righteous people" there are three opinions.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 87–88:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are three reports.

The first: "Some men from among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), among them ʿUthman ibn Maẓʿun, made unlawful for themselves meat and women, and they intended to castrate themselves so that they might devote themselves to worship. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I was not commanded to do that.' And this verse was revealed." This was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas. Abu Salih related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: They were ten: Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, ʿUthman ibn Maẓʿun, al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa, Salman al-Farisi, Abu Dharr, and ʿAmmar ibn Yasir. They gathered in the house of ʿUthman ibn Maẓʿun and pledged themselves to this. The news reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me." And this verse was revealed (p-411). Al-Suddi said: The cause of their resolve to do this was that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sat one day and did not add to them beyond warning, so the people softened and wept, and these men resolved upon this and swore to what they had resolved. ʿIkrimah said: ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Masʿud, ʿUthman ibn Maẓʿun, al-Miqdad, and Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa, among his companions, devoted themselves to asceticism, sat in their houses, withdrew from women, wore woolen garments, and made unlawful the good things of food and clothing, except what the wanderers of the Children of Israel eat and wear, and they considered castration, and resolved to stand in prayer at night and fast by day. So this verse was revealed.

The second: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'When I eat this meat, I become inclined toward women, so I have made it unlawful for myself.' So this verse was revealed." This was related by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: "A guest stayed with ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawaha, and he was not present. When he came, he said to his wife: 'Has the guest eaten?' She said: 'I have been waiting for you.' He said: 'You have held back my guest on my account? Your food is unlawful to me.' She said: 'And it is unlawful to me if you do not eat it.' The guest said: 'And it is unlawful to me if you do not eat it.' When Ibn Rawaha saw that, he said: 'Bring your food near, eat in the name of Allah.' Then he went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of that, and he said: 'You have done well.' And this verse was revealed (p-412)," and he recited until he reached ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths﴾. This was related by ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd from his father.

As for "the good things" (al-tayyibat), they are the delicious things that souls desire, of what has been permitted.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And do not transgress﴾, there are five opinions.

The first: Do not castrate yourselves. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibrahim.

The second: Do not commit what Allah has forbidden. This was said by al-Hasan. The third: Do not conduct yourselves in a manner other than the way of the Muslims, such as abandoning women and perpetually fasting and standing in prayer. This was said by ʿIkrimah. The fourth: Do not make unlawful what is lawful. This was said by Muqatil. The fifth: Do not usurp unlawfully acquired wealth. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 89:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths﴾. The occasion of its revelation: when the verse ﴿Do not make unlawful the good things which Allah has made lawful for you﴾ was revealed, the people who had made women and meat unlawful said: "O Messenger of Allah, how should we deal with our oaths which we have sworn to?" Then this verse was revealed. Al-'Awfi narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas. The meaning of "al-laghw" has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

The words of the Most High: ﴿for what you have bound by oaths﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Hafs from 'Asim read "'aqqadtum" without an alif, with the qaf doubled. Abu 'Amr said: its meaning is "wakkadtum" (you confirmed). Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read "'aqadtum" lightly, without an alif, and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading. Ibn Jarir said: its meaning is "awjabtumuha 'ala anfusikum" (you made them obligatory upon yourselves). Ibn 'Amir read "'aqadtum" with an alif, like "'ahadtum" (you covenanted). Al-Qadi Abu Ya'la said: this doubled reading admits only the binding of speech, whereas the light reading admits both binding of the heart and binding of speech.

The exegetes mentioned two views regarding the meaning of the statement.

One: "but He will hold you accountable for what you have bound your hearts to in deliberately swearing an oath," as said by Mujahid.

The second: "for what you have bound your hearts to, that it is a lie," as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The words of the Most High: ﴿its expiation﴾. Ibn Jarir said: the pronoun refers to "ma" in the words ﴿for what you have bound﴾.

Section

As for feeding the poor, it is narrated from Ibn 'Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and others that for each poor person is a mudd of wheat, and this is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i.

It is narrated from 'Umar, 'Ali, 'A'ishah, and others: for each poor person is half a sa' of wheat. 'Umar and 'A'ishah said: or a sa' of dates, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah. The position of our companions regarding all expiations in which there is feeding, such as the expiation of oaths, zihar, the ransom for harm, and one who neglected making up Ramadan, is a mudd of wheat, or half a sa' of dates or barley. Among the conditions for the validity of the expiation is transferring ownership of the food to the poor; if he provides them with lunch and dinner, it does not suffice him. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hakam, and al-Shafi'i. al-Thawri and al-Awza'i said: it suffices him, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah and Malik. It is not permissible to give two mudds to one poor person, nor to pay the value in expiation, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah said: it is permissible. al-Zajjaj said: the masculine wording occurs with "al-masakin" (the poor), and had they been women it would have sufficed, because the masculine prevails in Arabic speech. Regarding the words ﴿from the middle of what you feed your families﴾ there are two views.

One: from its middle in quantity, as said by 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid.

The second: from the middle of the kinds of food, as said by Ibn 'Umar, al-Aswad, 'Ubaydah, al-Hasan, and Ibn Sirin. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the people of Madinah [used to say:] a free person's share of sustenance is more than that of a slave, and an adult's share is more than a child's, so ﴿from the middle of what you feed your families﴾ was revealed, meaning not the best of it nor the worst of it. Regarding their clothing there are five views.

One: it is one garment, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Tawus, 'Ata', and al-Shafi'i. The second: two garments, as said by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, and al-Dahhak. The third: a waist-wrap, a cloak, and a shirt, as said by Ibn 'Umar. The fourth: an all-encompassing garment like a milhafah, as said by Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. The fifth: clothing in which prayer is valid, as said by Malik. The position of our companions: if he clothes a man, he clothes him with one garment, and a woman with two garments, a shirt and a headscarf, which is the least in which prayer is valid. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-Jawza', and Yahya ibn Ya'mur read "aw kiswatuhum" with a dammah on the kaf. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-'Aliyah, Abu Nuhayk, and Mu'adh al-Qari read "awka'isawatihim" with a kasrah on the hamzah, a fathah on the kaf, and a kasrah on the ta' and the ha'. Ibn al-Sumayfa' and Abu 'Imran al-Jawzi read the same, except that they gave the hamzah a fathah. The author said: I do not consider this reading permissible, because it drops a fundamental element of the expiation.

The words of the Most High: ﴿or the freeing of a slave﴾. Its liberation is manumission, and by "raqabah" (slave) is meant the whole person. They agreed on the condition of faith in the slave in the expiation for killing, due to the explicit text.

They differed regarding whether faith is required in the slave mentioned in this expiation, on two views.

One: it is a condition, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, because Allah the Most High specified the mention of faith in the expiation for killing, so the unrestricted must be read in light of the restricted.

The second: it is not a condition, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah. From Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, there are two narrations regarding the faith of the freed slave in the expiation for oaths, the expiation for zihar, the expiation for intercourse, and the vowed expiation.

The words of the Most High: ﴿but whoever does not find [means]﴾. They differed regarding one who cannot find it and fasts, on five views.

One: that if he does not find two dirhams he fasts, as said by al-Hasan. The second: three dirhams, as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The third: if he does not find except the amount with which he would expiate, he fasts, as said by Qatadah. The fourth: two hundred dirhams, as said by Abu Hanifah. The fifth: if he has only the amount of his sustenance and the sustenance of his dependents for his day and night, as said by Ahmad and al-Shafi'i. As for the consecutiveness of the three days, there are two views.

One: it is a condition, and Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud used to recite: (fasting three days consecutively). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Tawus, 'Ata', Qatadah, and Abu Hanifah, and it is the position of our companions.

The second: it is not a condition, and separation is permissible, and this is the view of al-Hasan and Malik, and al-Shafi'i has two opinions on it.

The words of the Most High: ﴿That is the expiation of your oaths when you swear﴾. There is an implied element in it, its estimated meaning being: when you swear and break them. Regarding the words ﴿and guard your oaths﴾ there are three views.

(p-416) One: reduce them, and his words support this: ﴿and do not make Allah an obstacle to your oaths﴾, and they recited:

"Few in oaths, guarding his oath."

The second: guard yourselves from breaking them.

The third: be mindful of them so that you pay the expiation when you break them.

The Qur'anic phrase is: ﴿O you who believe, indeed intoxicants (khamr) and gambling (maysir)...﴾ There are four opinions regarding its occasion of revelation.

The first: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas came to a group of the Muhajirun and the Ansar, and he ate with them and drank wine, before it was prohibited. He said, "The Muhajirun are better than the Ansar." Then a man took the jawbone of a camel and struck him, cutting his nose. He went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him, and this verse was revealed. This was narrated by Mus'ab ibn Sa'd from his father. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "A man from the Ansar prepared a meal and invited Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. When the wine took effect on them, they boasted and insulted one another. The Ansari stood up with the jawbone of a camel and struck Sa'd on the head, and blood was on his face. Sa'd went to complain to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the prohibition of wine was revealed in His words: ﴿Indeed, intoxicants and gambling...﴾ up to His words: ﴿...that you may prosper﴾."

The second: Umar ibn al-Khattab said, "O Allah, make clear to us a satisfactory explanation regarding wine." So the verse in al-Baqarah was revealed. He said, "O Allah, make clear to us a satisfactory explanation regarding wine," so the verse in an-Nisa' was revealed: ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [an-Nisa': 43]. He said, "O Allah, make clear to us a satisfactory explanation regarding wine," and then this verse was revealed. This was narrated by Abu Maysara from Umar.

The third: some Muslims drank it, and some of them fought with others and spoke words that Allah does not approve. Then this verse was revealed. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: two tribes from the Ansar drank, and when they became intoxicated, some of them played with others. When they became sober, each man saw the traces on his face, head, and beard, and would say, "My brother so-and-so did this to me! By Allah, if he had been kind to me, he would not have done this to me." Until enmities entered their hearts, though they had been brothers with no enmity in their hearts. Then this verse was revealed. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas.

We have already discussed khamr and maysir in al-Baqarah. At the beginning of this surah, we mentioned two opinions regarding an-nusub (the stone idols), which are the two that the exegetes mention concerning al-ansab. We also mentioned there al-azlam (the divining arrows). As for ar-rijs (filth/abomination), az-Zajjaj said: it is a term for everything that is considered repugnant from an action. It is said: "rajusa ar-rajulu yarjusu" and "rajisa yarjasu," when a man does an ugly deed. Ar-rajs, with a fatha on the ra', means the intensity of a sound. So ar-rijs is the action whose mention is ugly and which rises in ugliness. It is said: "ra'dun rajjas," meaning a thunder whose sound is intense.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿from the work of Satan﴾. Ibn Abbas said: from Satan's adornment. If it is asked: how is it attributed to him when it is not his act? The answer: attributing it to him is figurative (majaz, metaphorical usage), and it is attributed to him because he is the one who calls to it and makes it appealing. Do you not see that if a man incited another man to strike a third man, it would be correct to say to him: "This is from your work."

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿so avoid it﴾. Az-Zajjaj said: leave it. Its etymology in the language is: be a side apart from it. If it is asked: how did He mention several things in this verse, then say: "avoid it"? The answer: the pronoun returns to ar-rijs, and ar-rijs applies to khamr, maysir, al-ansab, and al-azlam. The return of the pronoun to it is in the same position as its return to the collective noun to which it refers and which it indicates. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 91–92:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to occur among you through wine and gambling﴾. As for "wine," the occurrence of enmity and hatred in it is in the manner we mentioned in the occasion of revelation of the verse, through fighting and disputing. As for gambling, Qatadah said: A man would gamble away his family and his wealth, and then he would be left grieving and plundered, and he would look at his wealth in another's hand, and this would bring about enmity and hatred for him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ In this there are two views.

The first: It is a question in form, but its meaning is a command (amr). Its implied sense is: "Desist!" Al-Farra' (al-Farra', the grammarian) said: A Bedouin repeated to me, "Are you silent? Are you silent?" and he meant: "Be silent! Be silent!"

The second: It is a question in its true sense, not with the meaning of a command. Our shaykh, Ali ibn Ubayd Allah, mentioned that a group used to drink wine after this verse, saying: "He has not forbidden it; He only said: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾" Then some of us said: "We have desisted," and some of us said: "We have not desisted." So when the verse was revealed: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden indecent acts, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, and sin﴾ [al-A'raf: 33], it was forbidden, because "sin" (al-ithm) is a name for wine. This view is worthless, and the first is more sound.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ in what they command you, and beware of opposing them. ﴿But if you turn away﴾, i.e., you turn away, ﴿then know that the duty of Our Messenger﴾ Muhammad (ﷺ) ﴿is only the clear notification﴾. This is a warning to them, as if He said: "Know that you have deserved punishment by your turning away."
