Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 93:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon those who have believed and done righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾. The occasion of its revelation: some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) died while drinking wine, at a time when it was permitted. When it was prohibited, some people said: "What about our companions who died while drinking it?" So this verse was revealed. This was related by al-Bara' ibn 'Azib. "Al-junah" (blame) means sin. As for "what they have eaten," there are three opinions.

(p-420) The first: what they drank of wine before its prohibition. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and the majority. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said, "I did not taste (atʿam) bread and condiment, nor water, nor sleep." The poet said:

"If you wish, I will forbid women other than you, and if you wish, I will not taste cool water (nuqakh) nor sleep (barad)."

Al-nuqakh is the water that refreshes the heart with its coolness, and al-barad is sleep.

The second: what they drank of wine and ate of gambling (maysir).

The third: what they ate of permissible things. And regarding His saying: ﴿when they fear Allah﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: they feared Allah after the prohibition, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: they feared sins and polytheism.

The third: they feared opposing Allah in His command. And regarding His saying: ﴿and believed﴾, there are two opinions.

One: they believed in Allah and His Messenger. The second: they believed in its prohibition. ﴿And did righteous deeds﴾: Muqatil said: they maintained the obligatory duties.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then they feared Allah﴾. Regarding this repeated "fear," there are four opinions.

The first: that what is meant is fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The second: that it is fear regarding wine and gambling after their prohibition. The third: that it is the persistence in piety. The fourth: that the first fear addresses those who drank it before the prohibition, and the second addresses those who drank it after the prohibition.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and believed﴾. Regarding this repeated "belief" there are two opinions.

One: they affirmed everything that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. The second: they believed in what would come of the abrogating and the abrogated.

(p-421) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then they feared Allah and did good﴾. Regarding this third "fear" there are four opinions.

The first: they avoided returning to wine after its prohibition, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: they feared wronging people. The third: they guarded against doubtful matters. The fourth: they feared all prohibited things.

As for "ihsan" (doing good), there are two opinions. One: they did good in deed by abstaining from drinking it after the prohibition, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: they did good in deed after its prohibition, said by Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 94:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of the game (ṣayd)﴾. The exegetes (mufassirūn) said: "When it was the year of al-Ḥudaybiyah, and the Prophet (ﷺ) stayed at al-Tan'im, wild animals and birds would come upon them in their encampments while they were in the state of ihram (iḥrām, the sacred state of pilgrimage). So this verse was revealed, and they were forbidden from it as a trial." Al-Zajjaj said: The lam in "layabluwannakum" is the lam of oath, and its meaning is: "We will surely test your obedience from your disobedience."

As for "min" (some of), there are two opinions. The first: it is for partition (tab'īḍ). Then in this there are two views. One: it means land game only, not sea game. The second: it means game as long as they are in ihram, as if that were a part of the game. The second opinion: it is for specifying the kind (bayān al-jins), like His saying: ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 30].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Which your hands and your lances can reach﴾. Mujahid said: That which the hand can reach is the chicks, the eggs, and the small game; and that which the lances can reach is the large game.

(p-422) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That Allah may know﴾. Muqatil said: That Allah may see who fears Him in the unseen while not having seen Him, so that he does not take the game while he is in ihram. ﴿Then whoever transgresses﴾, i.e., takes the game deliberately after the prohibition for the muhrim from killing game, ﴿for him is a painful punishment﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: His belly and back will be stretched (by beating) with lashes, and his garments will be stripped off.

The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 5, verse 95:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram (iḥrām, the sacred state entered for pilgrimage).﴾ By this verse God, Mighty and Majestic, makes clear in what manner the trial occurs, at what time, and what is due from the one who kills it after the prohibition.

Regarding His saying ﴿while you are in the state of ihram﴾ there are three opinions.

The first: "while you are in ihram for hajj or 'umrah (the lesser pilgrimage)." This is what most of the scholars said. The second: "while you are in the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram)." It is said: aḥrama, when one enters the Ḥaram, and anjada, when one goes to Najd. The third: combining the two statements.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever among you kills it intentionally﴾ has two views.

One: that he intends to kill it while remembering that he is in ihram. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata'.

The second: that he intends to kill it while forgetting his ihram. This was said by Mujahid. As for killing it by mistake, there are two views.

One: that it is the same as intentional killing. This was said by 'Umar, 'Uthman and the majority. al-Zuhri said: "The Qur'an was revealed concerning intention, and the Sunnah established the rule for error," meaning: it placed the one who erred in the same category as the one who intended, regarding the obligation of the compensation (jaza'). It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The hyena is game, and a ram is due for it if the one in ihram kills it." This is general, covering both the intentional and the mistaken killer. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: what was mentioned within the verse of threat (wa'īd) specifies the mention of intention, and that applies only to the intentional killer.

The second: that there is nothing due. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Tawus, 'Ata', Salim, al-Qasim and Dawud. From Ahmad there are two narrations, the more sound of which is that it is obligatory.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then a compensation like what he killed from the livestock (al-na'am)﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read: ﴿fa-jaza'un mithlu﴾ with the noun in the construct and "mithl" in the genitive. 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: "fa-jaza'un" with tanwin (nunation) and "mithlu" in the nominative. Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads it as a construct, then His saying ﴿from the livestock﴾ serves as a description of the compensation. And He said "like what he killed," since what is due upon him is the compensation for the one killed, not the compensation for its like, because they say: "I honour your like," meaning: "I honour you." So the meaning is: the compensation for what he killed.

Whoever reads "mithl" in the nominative, the meaning is: upon him is a compensation from the livestock equal to the one killed, and the implied sense is: upon him is a compensation.

Ibn Qutaybah said: al-na'am is camels, though it may also include cattle and sheep, and camels are the predominant sense. al-Zajjaj said: in the language, al-na'am is camels, cattle and sheep. If camels stand alone, they are called na'am; if cattle and sheep stand alone, they are not called na'am.

(p-424) * Section

Qadi Abu Ya'la said: The game for which compensation is due upon killing it is that which is lawful to eat, such as the gazelle, the wild ass, the ostrich and the like, or that which is born of an animal whose flesh is eaten, such as the sim', which is born of the hyena and the wolf. As for every other beast of prey, there is no compensation for the one who kills it, whether he initiated its killing or it attacked him and he killed it in self-defence, because a beast of prey has no equivalent in form or value, so it does not fall under the verse. Also, the Prophet ﷺ permitted the one in ihram to kill the snake, the scorpion, the mischievous rodent (fuwaysiqa), the crow, the kite, the rabid dog and the predatory beast. He said: the obligation for killing game, where it has an equivalent among the livestock, is its equivalent, and where it has no equivalent, its value. This is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa said: what is obligatory for it is its value, and he interpreted "mithl" as "value." But the apparent meaning of the verse refutes what he said. Also, the Companions interpreted the verse as referring to equivalence in form. Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-mithl" is the counterpart, so for a gazelle there is a sheep, and for an ostrich there is a camel.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿judged by two men of justice among you﴾ means: concerning the compensation. He mentioned two because game differs in its own nature, so judgment on its equivalent requires two just men.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿among you﴾ means: from among the people of your religion (millah).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿as an offering (hadyan) reaching the Ka'bah﴾ al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and the meaning is: they judge it while it is intended to be offered. The wording "bāligha al-Ka'bah" is in the definite form, but its meaning is indefinite: "bālighan al-Ka'bah," except that the tanwin was omitted for lightness. Ibn 'Abbas said: when he comes to Makkah, he slaughters it and gives it in charity.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿or an expiation (kaffarah)﴾ Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: "aw kaffaratun" with tanwin, and "ṭa'āmun" in the nominative. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read: "aw kaffaratu" in the nominative without tanwin, then ﴿ṭa'āmu masākīn﴾ as a construct. Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads it in the nominative without the construct makes "ṭa'ām" an appositive (ʿaṭf bayān) to "kaffarah," because the food is the expiation itself. He did not make "kaffarah" a construct of "ṭa'ām," because the expiation is for killing the game, not for the food. Whoever makes "kaffarah" a construct of "ṭa'ām" does so because, when He gave the expiator the choice between the offering, the food and the fasting, the construct was permissible for that reason, so it is as if He said: the expiation of food, not the expiation of an offering or of fasting. The meaning is: or upon him is the substitute for the compensation and the expiation, which is feeding the poor (ṭa'ām masākīn). Is the value of the food to be measured by the value of the counterpart or the value of the game? There are two views.

One: the value of the counterpart. This was said by 'Ata', al-Shafi'i and Ahmad.

The second: the value of the game. This was said by Qatadah, Abu Hanifa and Malik.

(p-426) Concerning the amount of food for each poor person, there are two views.

One: two mudds (mudd, a dry measure of about a handful and a quarter) of wheat. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hanifa.

The second: one mudd of wheat. This was said by al-Shafi'i. From Ahmad there are two narrations, parallel to the two views.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾ Abu Razin, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, al-Jahdari and Talhah read: ﴿aw 'adlu dhālika﴾ with a kasrah on the 'ayn. We have explained this meaning in (al-Baqarah). Our companions said: he fasts one day for each mudd of wheat, or half a sa' (sa', a dry measure of about four mudds) of dates or barley. Abu Hanifa said: he fasts one day for half a sa' in total. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: he fasts one day for each mudd of the whole.

Section

Is this compensation in order (al-tartib) or by choice (al-takhyir)? There are two views.

One: that it is by choice among the offering of the counterpart, the fasting, and the feeding.

The second: that it is in order. If he does not find the offering, he buys food; if he is poor, he fasts. This was said by Ibn Sirin. Both views are reported from Ibn 'Abbas. The first was said by the majority of jurists.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿that he may taste the evil of his deed﴾ means: the consequence of his sin. al-Zajjaj said: "al-wabāl" is the heaviness of a thing in what is disliked, and from it comes the saying: "ṭa'āmun wabīl" and "mā'un wabīl," when they are heavy. God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So We seized him with a heavy seizing﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 16], meaning: heavy and severe.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿God has pardoned what is past﴾ has two views.

One: what was past in the time of ignorance (jahiliyyah), of their killing game while they were in ihram. This was said by 'Ata'.

(p-427) The second: what was past of killing game the first time. This was related by Ibn Jarir, and the first is more sound. According to the first view, His saying ﴿and whoever returns﴾ means returning in Islam; according to the second, it means returning a second time after a first. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "'āda" is in the place of "ya'ūdu," and he recited:

"If they hear a suspicion, they fly with it in joy; and if I am mentioned with evil in their presence, they lend an ear."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then God will take retribution from him﴾ "al-intiqām" is exaggeration in punishment. This threat of retribution does not prevent imposing a second compensation if he returns. This is the view of the majority, and Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad held it. It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i and Dawud that there is no compensation upon him for the second offence; he is only promised retribution.

**The Words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea﴾.** Aḥmad said: Everything in the sea may be eaten except the frog and the crocodile, because the crocodile eats people, meaning that it preys on them. Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Thawrī said: Nothing from it is permitted except fish. Ibn Abī Layla and Mālik said: Everything in it is permitted, including the frog and other creatures. As for its food (ṭaʿām), there are three opinions.

The first: it is what the sea casts up dead. This was said by Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Ayyūb and Qatāda.

The second: it is its salted (malīḥ) portion. This was said by Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Suddī, and it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and ʿIkrima in the same way as the two opinions. The reports from al-Nakhaʿī differ: it is reported from him as in the two opinions, and it is also reported from him that he combined them, saying: its food is the salted portion and what it casts up.

The third: it is what grows by its water from the crops of the land. It is only called "the food of the sea" because it grows by its water. This is related by al-Zajjāj. As for the word (matāʿ, "provision"), there are two opinions.

One: it is benefit (manfaʿa). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan and Qatāda.

The second: it is lawfulness (ḥill). This was said by al-Nakhaʿī. Muqātil said: ﴿a provision for you﴾ means for those who are resident, and ﴿for the travellers﴾ means for those who are on journeys.

**The Words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿But forbidden to you is the game of the land as long as you are in the state of iḥrām﴾.** As for hunting, it is forbidden to the one in the state of iḥrām (muḥrim). If game is hunted on his account, eating it is forbidden to him, contrary to Abū Ḥanīfa. If he eats it, he is liable for compensation (ḍamān), contrary to one of al-Shāfiʿī's two opinions. If the muḥrim slaughters a game animal, it is carrion (maytah), contrary to one of al-Shāfiʿī's two opinions also. If a non-muḥrim slaughters game within the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram), it is also carrion, contrary to the majority of the Ḥanafiyya.

The Word of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah made the Ka'bah﴾. "Ja'ala" means "ṣayyara" (made, rendered). There are two views on why the House is called "Ka'bah."

The first: because it is square (murabba'ah). This was said by 'Ikrimah and Mujahid.

The second: because of its height and its protrusion (nutū'). It is said: "ka'abat al-mar'ah ka'ābah," and she is "kā'ib," when her breasts have protruded.

The meaning of calling the House "ḥarām" is that it is forbidden to hunt near it, to cut its grass (khalā), or to cut its trees, and its sanctity is greatly magnified. The intended meaning of the "prohibition of the House" is the entire Sacred Precinct (Ḥaram), as He said: ﴿an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾, meaning the Ḥaram. "Al-qiyām" (the means of support) has the same meaning as "al-qiwām." Ibn 'Amir read "qiyaman" without an alif. Abu 'Ali said: its basis is one of two matters: either he made it a verbal noun (maṣdar), like "al-shiba'" (satiety), or he dropped the alif while intending it, as the extended form (mamdūd) is shortened.

There are six views on the meaning of the statement:

First: a support for religion and markers for the Hajj. Narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: a support for the affairs of whoever turns toward it. Narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Qatadah said: a man, if he committed every offence and then sought refuge in it, would not be touched or approached. And a man, if he met the killer of his father in the sacred month, would not confront him or approach him. And when a man intended the House, he would hang a necklace of hair, which would protect him and keep him safe from people; and when he returned, he would hang a necklace of idhkhir (a fragrant grass) or of the bark of the samur tree, which would keep him safe from people until he reached his family. These are barriers that Allah placed among the people in the Jahiliyyah.

Third: a support for the continuance of religion, so that there will always be religion on earth as long as it is visited for pilgrimage and faced in prayer. Said by al-Hasan.

Fourth: a support of worldly affairs and religious affairs. Said by Abu 'Ubaydah.

Fifth: a support for the people, meaning in what they were commanded to undertake as an obligation within it. Mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

Sixth: a support for their livelihoods and earnings through the trade that comes to them by means of it. Mentioned by some of the exegetes.

As for "al-shahr al-ḥarām" (the sacred month), what is meant is the sacred months (al-ashhur al-ḥurum), in which people were safe from one another, and that was a support for them. Likewise, when a man offered an animal as a sacrifice (hady) or garlanded his camel, he was safe however he conducted himself. Allah, Exalted is He, made these things a safeguard for people through what He placed in their hearts of magnifying them.

The Word of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿That is so that you may know﴾. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned four views regarding what is referred to by "that."

First: Allah, Exalted is He, informed in this surah of many unseen matters from the reports of the prophets and others, and revealed matters concerning the condition of the Jews and the hypocrites. So He said: "That is so that you may know," meaning: that unseen knowledge which I have informed you of from Allah indicates to you that He knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth, and nothing is hidden from Him.

Second: the Arabs used to shed blood without right and seize property without justification, and one of them would kill someone other than the killer. But when they entered the sacred city or the sacred month came, they refrained from killing. The meaning is: Allah made the Ka'bah a place of safety, and the sacred month a time of safety, for if He had not made for the Jahiliyyah a time in which fear would cease, they would have perished. That indicates that He knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth.

Third: Allah, Exalted is He, turned the hearts of creation toward Makkah in the known months, so when they arrived there, its people lived alongside them; and were it not for that, they would have died of hunger, because He knows what good that brings them, and so that they may draw evidence from it that He knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth.

Fourth: Allah, Exalted is He, made Makkah a place of safety, and likewise the sacred month. When a wild gazelle entered the Ḥaram, it became familiar with people, did not flee from the dog, and the dog did not pursue it. But when they both left the boundaries of the Ḥaram, the dog pursued it and it fled from it in fear. And the bird becomes familiar with people within the Ḥaram, and keeps flying until it approaches the House; when it comes near it, it turns away from it and does not fly over it, out of reverence for it. And when an ailment afflicts it, it throws itself upon the roof of the House seeking healing through it. These are wonders in that place and in that month, which have shown that Allah, Exalted is He, knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth.
