Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 99:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Upon the Messenger is only the conveying (of the message)﴾. In this verse there is a severe warning. Muqatil claimed that it and the verse that follows it were revealed concerning the matter of Shurayh ibn Dabi'ah and his companions, who were pilgrims from al-Yamamah, when the Muslims intended to raid them; the mention of that has already passed at the beginning of the surah. Is this verse muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) or not? On this there are two opinions.

One of them: it is muhkam, and it indicates that what is obligatory upon the Messenger is the conveying (tabligh), and that guidance is not upon him. The second: it was before the command to fight, and then it was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword.

Allah's words: ﴿Not equal are the evil and the good﴾. Jabir ibn Abdullah narrated that "a man said: O Messenger of Allah, wine used to be my trade, so will that wealth benefit me if I spend it in obedience to Allah? The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Indeed Allah accepts only the good,' and then this verse was revealed confirming the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

Regarding "the evil and the good" there are four opinions.

The first: lawful and unlawful. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan. The second: the believer and the disbeliever. This was said by al-Suddi. The third: the obedient and the disobedient. The fourth: the bad (inferior) and the good (excellent). Al-Mawardi mentioned these two.

The meaning of "al-i'jab" (admiration) here is: delight in something that one wonders at.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 101:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are six reports.

The first: "The people asked the Prophet ﷺ persistently, until they pressed him with questions. He stood up angry, delivering a sermon, and said: 'Ask me; by God, you will not ask me about anything while I am standing in this place except that I will make it clear to you.' A man of Quraysh stood up, called ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥudhafa, who, when he quarrelled, was called by other than his father's name, and said: 'O Prophet of God, who is my father?' He said: 'Your father is Ḥudhafa.' Another man stood up and said: 'Where is my father?' He said: 'In the Fire.' ʿUmar stood up and said: 'We are content with God as Lord, with Islam as religion, with Muhammad as Prophet, and with the Qur'an as leader. We are people recently converted from the Jahiliyya, and God knows best who our fathers are.' Then his anger subsided, and this verse was revealed." Narrated by Abu Ṣāliḥ from Abu Hurayra, and Qatada from Anas.

The second: "The Messenger of God ﷺ addressed the people and said: 'God has prescribed for you the Hajj.' ʿUkkasha ibn Miḥṣan stood up and said: 'Every year, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'If I had said yes, it would have become obligatory; and if it had become obligatory and you then abandoned it, you would have gone astray. Leave me alone as long as I leave you alone, for those who perished before you perished only through their excessive questioning and their disputing with their prophets.' Then this verse was revealed." Narrated by Muhammad ibn Ziyad from Abu Hurayra. It is also said that the questioner was al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis.

The third: "Some people used to ask the Messenger of God ﷺ mockingly. A man would say: 'Who is my father?' and a man whose camel had strayed would say: 'Where is my camel?' Then this verse was revealed." Narrated by Abu al-Jawriyya from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fourth: "Some people asked the Messenger ﷺ about the baḥīra, the sāʾiba, the waṣīla and the ḥām, and this verse was revealed." Narrated by Mujahid from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Jubayr said likewise.

The fifth: Some people used to ask for signs and miracles, and this verse was revealed. This meaning is reported from ʿIkrima.

The sixth: It was revealed concerning their wishing for obligations, their saying: "We wish that God, exalted is He, had permitted us to fight the polytheists," and their asking about the deeds most beloved to God. This was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Al-Zajjaj said: "ashyāʾa" (things) is in the genitive position, but it is given a fatḥa because it is not declinable (ghayr munṣarif). "Tubda lakum" means "become apparent to you." God, exalted is He, informs that asking about this kind of thing should not occur, because the answer about it would distress them. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "in tubda lakum" means: if the Qur'an is revealed about them with severity, it will distress you.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you ask about them when the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be made apparent to you﴾. That is: when the Qur'an is being revealed concerning them with an obligation or a prohibition, or a ruling, and there is no evidence in the apparent text of what has been revealed that explains what you need; then if you ask about them at that time, they will be made apparent to you. Regarding his saying: ﴿God has pardoned you in them﴾, there are two opinions.

One: it refers to the things.

The second: it refers to the questions. According to the first opinion, there is an inversion (taqdīm and taʾkhīr) in the verse, and the meaning is: "Do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you; God has pardoned them." The meaning of "God has pardoned them" is: He refrained from mentioning them, so He did not make a ruling obligatory concerning them. According to the second opinion, the verse is in its ordinary arrangement, and the meaning of "God has pardoned them" is: He did not take you to account for them.

(p-436) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Certainly a people before you asked such questions﴾. Regarding these people there are four opinions.

The first: they are those who asked Jesus for the descent of the table (al-ma'idah), related by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan.

The second: they are the people of Salih when they asked for the she-camel, according to the view of al-Suddi. These two opinions are understood as referring to their asking for signs (al-ayat).

The third: the people are those who asked about the cow and its slaughter. Had they slaughtered any cow, it would have sufficed, but they made it strict, so Allah made it strict upon them. This is related by Ibn Zayd. This accords with the case of one who asked about the Hajj, for had Allah wished to make it strict upon them by adding to the obligation, He would have done so.

The fourth: they are those who said to a prophet of theirs: "Send us a king, and we will fight in the way of Allah." This is also related from Ibn Zayd, and it fits with the view of those who said that they asked about jihad and the obligations out of mere wishing for them. Muqatil said: The Children of Israel used to ask their prophets about things, and when the prophets informed them of them, they abandoned their statement and did not believe them, so they became disbelievers in those very things.

God Almighty's saying: ﴿Allah did not appoint any bahira (a she-camel whose ear was slit as a sign that she was set free from use)﴾, meaning: He did not make that obligatory, nor did He command it.

Regarding the *bahira*, there are four opinions.

The first: it is the she-camel which, when she had given birth to five offspring, they looked at the fifth. If it was a male, they slaughtered it and both men and women ate it. If it was a female, they slit her ear and she became forbidden to women, who could not benefit from her or taste her milk, while her benefits were for men alone. When she died, men and women shared in her. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Qutayba chose it.

The second: it is the she-camel that bore five females with no male among them. They would target the fifth and slit her ear. This was said by 'Ata'.

The third: it is the daughter of the *sa'iba*. This was said by Ibn Ishaq and al-Farra'. Ibn Ishaq said: When a she-camel bore ten females in succession with no male among them, she was released (*suyyibat*). If after that she gave birth to a female, her ear was slit, she was named *bahira*, and she was left to go with her mother.

The fourth: it is the she-camel which, when she had given birth to five offspring and the last of them was a male, they slit her ear, that is, they split it, and refrained from riding her and from slaughtering her. She was not driven away from water, nor prevented from pasture, and whoever met her did not ride her. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

As for the *sa'iba*: it is a form of the active participle with the meaning of the passive, and it means the one released (*al-musayyaba*), like His saying: ﴿in a pleasant life﴾, meaning one that is pleasing. Regarding the *sa'iba* there are five opinions.

The first: it is the animal released from the livestock for the gods; they did not ride it, did not milk it, did not shear its wool, and did not load anything on it. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: a man would release from his property whatever he wished and bring it to the keepers of the gods, who would feed the wayfarer from its milk and meat, except for women. They would not give women any of it unless it died, and then men and women shared in it. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. (p-438) Al-Sha'bi said: They used to present camels and sheep to their gods and leave them with the gods, so none would drink from them except a man. If any of them died, men and women ate it.

The third: it is the she-camel which, when she had given birth to ten offspring, all of them females, was released. She was not ridden, her wool was not shorn, and none drank her milk except a guest or her young, until she died. When she died, men and women ate her. This was mentioned by al-Farra'.

The fourth: it is the camel released by a vow that a man made, that if Allah Exalted delivered him from an illness, or brought him safely to his home, he would do this. This was said by Ibn Qutayba. Al-Zajjaj said: When a man vowed something of this kind, he would say: "My she-camel is *sa'iba*," and she was like the *bahira* in that no benefit was taken from her and she was not prevented from water or pasture.

The fifth: it is the camel on which a pilgrimage was performed and which was then released, not used, in gratitude for the success of that pilgrimage. This was related by al-Mawardi from al-Shafi'i.

As for the *wasila* (a ewe whose offspring were treated as dedicated to the gods), there are five opinions.

The first: it is the ewe which, when she had given birth to seven offspring, they looked at the seventh. If it was a female, women could not benefit from her in any way unless she died, and then men and women ate her. If it was a male, they slaughtered it and all of them ate it. If there was a male and a female, they said: "She has joined her brother," so she was left with her brother and not slaughtered, and her benefits were for men without women. When she died, men and women shared in her. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Qutayba took a similar view, saying: If the seventh was a male, it was slaughtered and men and women ate of it; if it was a female, she was left among the livestock; and if there was a male and a female, they said: "She has joined her brother," so she was not slaughtered because of that, and her meat was forbidden to women, and the milk of the female was forbidden to women unless some of her died, and then men and women ate it.

The second: it is the firstborn ewe which was the first to give birth to a female among the camels, then gave birth to another female after her. They would keep her for their idols and call her *wasila*, meaning that one of the two had joined the other with no male between them. This was narrated by al-Zuhri from Ibn al-Musayyab.

The third: it is the ewe which bore ten consecutive females over five births. They called her *wasila*, and whatever she bore after that was for males and not for females. This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

The fourth: it is the ewe which bore seven births, two kids at a time. If in her seventh she bore a female kid and a male kid, it was said: "She has joined her brother," and she took the place of the *sa'iba*. This was said by al-Farra'.

The fifth: the ewe, if she bore a female, was theirs, and if she bore a male, they dedicated it to their gods; if she bore a male and a female, they said: "She has joined her brother," and they did not slaughter the male for their gods. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

As for the *ham* (a stallion camel): there are six opinions.

The first: it is the stud camel which sired ten births from his loins. They say: "He has protected his back," so they released him for their idols, and he was not ridden. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, and Abu 'Ubayda and al-Zajjaj chose it.

The second: it is the stud camel whose offspring bore offspring of his own, and they said: "This one has protected his back," so they did not ride him, did not shear his wool, and did not prevent him from water or pasture. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba chose it.

The third: it is the stud camel from whose offspring ten females appeared, from his daughters and his daughters' daughters. This was said by 'Ata'.

(p-440) The fourth: it is the one who had seven consecutive female offspring. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: it is the one whose loins produced ten, all of which covered camels. This was said by Abu Rawq.

The sixth: it is the stud camel that served the camels of a man for ten years, after which he was left free, and it was said: "He has protected his back." This was mentioned by al-Mawardi from al-Shafi'i.

Al-Zajjaj said: What we have mentioned concerning the *bahira*, the *sa'iba*, the *wasila* and the *ham* is the most established of what we have related from the people of lexicography. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has informed us in this verse that He did not forbid any of these things, and that those who disbelieved fabricated lies against Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Muqatil said: Their fabrication was their saying that Allah had forbidden it and commanded us with it.

Regarding His saying ﴿and most of them do not understand﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: "and most of them," meaning the followers, "do not understand that this is a lie against Allah," from the leaders who made these things forbidden. This was said by al-Sha'bi.

The second: they do not understand that this prohibition came from the Shaytan. This was said by Qatada.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them﴾ meaning: when it is said to these polytheists who forbade for themselves these livestock animals: "Come to what Allah has sent down in the Qur'an" of permitting what you have forbidden upon yourselves. They say: ﴿Sufficient for us is﴾ that is, it suffices us ﴿what we found our fathers upon﴾ of the religion and the way. ﴿Even though their fathers knew nothing﴾ of the religion ﴿and were not guided﴾ to it? Would they follow them in their error?

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 105:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, take care of yourselves. The one who is astray cannot harm you if you are [rightly] guided.﴾ Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two opinions.

The first: "The Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to Hajar, and over them was al-Mundhir ibn Sawi, calling them to Islam; if they refused, then they were to pay the jizya (poll tax). When the letter reached him, he presented it to those who were with him among the Arabs, the Jews, the Christians and the Magians, and they acknowledged the jizya but disliked Islam. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to them: 'As for the Arabs, do not accept from them anything except Islam or the sword; as for the People of the Book and the Magians, accept the jizya from them.' When he read the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) letter to them, the Arabs embraced Islam, and the People of the Book and the Magians gave the jizya. The hypocrites of Makkah said: 'How strange of Muhammad! He claims that Allah sent him to fight people entirely until they submit, yet he has accepted the jizya from the Magians of Hajar and the People of the Book, so why did he not compel them to Islam? He has rejected it from our Arab brothers.' This grieved the Muslims, so this verse was revealed." It was related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

Muqatil said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would not accept the jizya except from the People of the Book. When the Arabs embraced Islam, willingly and unwillingly, he accepted it from the Magians of Hajar. The hypocrites criticised this, so this verse was revealed."

The second: A man, when he embraced Islam, would be told: "You have foolishly deviated from your fathers and led them astray, and you should have helped them." So this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the verse is: Allah has only obligated you concerning the affair of your own selves, and He does not hold you accountable for the sins of others. This verse does not necessitate abandoning enjoining good, because the believer, if he abandons it while being able to do it, is then astray and not rightly guided.

Uthman ibn Affan said: "Its interpretation has not yet come." Ibn Mas'ud said: "Its interpretation is at the end of time: say what is accepted from you; when you are overcome, then take care of yourselves."

Regarding His saying: ﴿The one who is astray cannot harm you if you are [rightly] guided﴾ there are two opinions. The first: The one who goes astray by abandoning enjoining good cannot harm you if you yourselves are rightly guided, enjoining good and forbidding evil. This was said by Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman and Ibn al-Musayyib.

The second: The one among the People of the Book who goes astray cannot harm you if they pay the jizya. This was said by Mujahid.

Regarding His saying: ﴿Then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ it is an alert to the recompense.

Section

According to what we have mentioned from al-Zajjaj regarding the meaning of the verse, it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated). However, some exegetes have held that it is mansukh (abrogated), and they have two opinions regarding its abrogating verse.

The first: that it is the verse of the sword.

The second: that its last part abrogated its first part. It is narrated from Abu Ubayd that he said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an that combines the abrogating and the abrogated other than this one. The place of the abrogated part in it extends to His saying ﴿The one who is astray cannot harm you﴾, and the abrogating part is His saying: ﴿if you are [rightly] guided﴾. The guidance here is enjoining good and forbidding evil."

(p-444) His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, the testimony among you﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Bada' used to travel to Makkah. A man from Quraysh, from the Banu Sahm, accompanied them, and he died in a land where there was none of the Muslims. He bequeathed his estate to the two of them. When they arrived, they handed it over to his family, but they concealed a cup of silver that he had with him, which was adorned with gold. They said, 'We did not see it.' So they were brought before the Prophet (ﷺ), who made them swear by God that they had not concealed anything, and he released them. Then the cup was found in the possession of some people from Makkah, who said, 'We bought it from Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Bada'.' The guardians of the Sahmi man stood up and took the cup. Two men from among them swore by God: 'This cup belongs to our companion, and our testimony is more deserving than theirs, and we have not transgressed.' So this verse was revealed, and the one after it."

Muqatil said: "The name of the deceased was Bazil ibn Abi Maryah, a freed slave of al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi. Tamim and 'Adi were Christians. Tamim then embraced Islam, and 'Adi died a Christian."

As for the tafsir (exegesis) of the verse: al-Farra' said: "The meaning of the verse is: let two witnesses testify for you when death approaches one of you." Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning is: the testimony of this situation is the testimony of two men. So 'testimony' (shahadah) is omitted, and 'two' (ithnan) takes its place." Ibn al-Anbari said: "The meaning of the verse is: let two witness for you during your travel, when death approaches you and you wish to make a bequest."

Regarding this testimony there are three opinions:

First: It is the testimony concerning the bequest that was established before the judges. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Musa, Shurayh, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, and the majority of scholars (al-jumhur).

Second: It is the oath of the two executors (wasiy) by God, when the heirs doubt them. This is the view of Mujahid.

Third: It is the testimony of the bequest, meaning its witnessing, like His saying: ﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. God made the executor here two for emphasis. Those who held this view used as evidence His saying: ﴿they swear by God﴾, and they said: "A witness is not obligated to take an oath." As for "the approach of death," it means the approach of its causes and preliminaries. His saying ﴿at the time of the bequest﴾ means: at the time of the bequest.

Regarding His saying ﴿from among you﴾ there are two views:

First: From among the people of your religion and community. This was stated by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Shurayh, Ibn Sirin, and al-Sha'bi, and it is the view of our companions (the Hanbali school).

Second: From among your clan and tribe, who are also Muslims. This was stated by al-Hasan, Ikrimah, al-Zuhri, and al-Suddi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or two others from other than you﴾. Its implied meaning is: or the testimony of two others from other than you. Regarding His saying ﴿from other than you﴾ there are two views:

First: From other than your religion and community. This was stated by the proponents of the first view.

Second: From other than your clan and tribe, who are also Muslims. This was stated by the proponents of the second view.

Regarding the particle "aw" (or) there are two views:

First: It does not indicate choice (takhyir). The meaning is: "or two others from other than you if you do not find them among you." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr.

Second: It indicates choice (takhyir). This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Section

Whoever holds that the verse refers to the testimony of two Muslims, whether from the tribe or from outside the tribe, has no doubt about the decisive (muhkam) nature of this verse. As for the one who holds that the meaning of ﴿or two others from other than you﴾ is the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab) when they testify concerning a bequest during travel, they have two views on it:

First: It is muhkam (not abrogated), and the ruling based on it remains in effect. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Sirin, Qatadah, al-Sha'bi, al-Thawri, Ahmad, and others.

Second: It is abrogated (mansukh) by His saying: ﴿and call to witness two just men from among you﴾. This is the view of Zayd ibn Aslam, and Abu Hanifah, Malik, and al-Shafi'i lean toward it. They said: "The people of disbelief are not just (ʿudul)." The first view is more sound, because this is a situation of necessity (darurah), just as the testimony of women without a man with them is permitted in some situations, such as menstruation, postpartum bleeding, and the cry of a newborn (istihlal).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿if you travel in the land﴾. This condition is connected to the testimony. The meaning is: let two witness for you if you travel in the land, that is, if you journey. ﴿and the calamity of death befalls you﴾: there is an omitted element in it. Its implied meaning is: and you have entrusted the bequest to them and handed over your property to them. ﴿You detain them after the prayer﴾: this is addressed to the heirs if they doubt. Ibn 'Abbas said: "This is part of the sense of His saying: ﴿or two others from other than you﴾, that is, from among the disbelievers. As for when the two are Muslims, there is no oath upon them." Regarding this "prayer" there are two views:

(p-448) First: It is the 'Asr prayer. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and Shurayh, Ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim, Qatadah, and al-Sha'bi also said so.

Second: It is after their prayer according to their religion. This was related by al-Suddi from Ibn 'Abbas, and he held this view.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The people in the Hijaz used to swear after the 'Asr prayer, because it is the time when people gather." Ibn Qutaybah said: "Because it is a time that the people of the religions venerate."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿they swear by God﴾, that is, they take an oath ﴿if you doubt﴾, that is, if you have doubts, O guardians of the deceased. The meaning of the verse is: when the one to whom the bequest was entrusted comes with the estate of the deceased, and the heir accuses them, they are made to swear after the 'Asr prayer that they did not steal and did not betray. The condition in ﴿if you doubt﴾ is connected to "you detain them," as if He had said: "If you doubt, detain them and make them swear, and they will swear by God: ﴿we will not exchange it﴾, that is, with our oaths. It was also said: with the distortion of our testimony. The pronoun "it" refers to the meaning. ﴿any price﴾, that is, any goods of this world. ﴿even if he were a near relative﴾, that is, even if the one for whom we testify were a relative of ours. He specified the near relative because of the inclination of a person toward his relative. The meaning is: we will not show favor to anyone in our testimony, nor incline toward a close relative in false speech. ﴿and we will not conceal the testimony of God﴾. It is attributed to Him only because He commanded its establishment and forbade its concealment.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited: ﴿wa-la naktumu shahadata﴾ with tanwin, then "Allahi" with cutting the hamzah (qat' al-hamzah) and shortening it (qasr), with a kasrah on the ha', and the nun quiescent in connected speech. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Ikrimah recited "shahadatan" with tanwin in connected speech, with the ha' in fatha. Abu Imran al-Jawni recited "shahadatan" with tanwin and quiescence in connected speech, and "Allaha" with cutting the hamzah and shortening it, with the ha' in fatha. Al-Sha'bi and Ibn al-Sumayfa' recited "shahadatan" with tanwin and quiescence in connected speech, "Allahi" with cutting the hamzah and lengthening it (madd), with a kasrah on the ha'. Abu al-'Aliyah and 'Amr ibn Dinar recited the same, except that they put the ha' in fatha.

The scholars differed as to the reason why the oath was made obligatory upon these two witnesses, and there are three opinions:

First: Because they were not from among the people of Islam. This meaning was reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.

Second: Because of a bequest written in the hand of the deceased, and his heirs lacked some of what was in it. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: Because the heirs used to say: "The property of our deceased was greater," so they accused the two witnesses of embezzlement. This was stated by al-Hasan and Mujahid.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 107:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Then if it becomes known that the two have become guilty of sin﴾. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: When the first verse was revealed, "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) summoned 'Adi and Tamim and had them swear by oath at the pulpit (minbar) that they had not betrayed anything of what had been entrusted to them. They swore, and he let them go. Then the vessel that they had concealed appeared, so the heirs of the deceased brought the two of them before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed: ﴿Then if it becomes known that the two have become guilty of sin﴾." The meaning of "becomes known" (ʿuthira) is "is discovered." That is, if the family of the deceased, or whoever is in charge of his affairs, discovers that the two witnesses, who are "two others from outside your own people," ﴿have become guilty of sin﴾ by deviating from uprightness in their testimony, ﴿then two others shall take their place﴾, that is, in place of these two traitors, ﴿from among those against whom the two claimants have a right﴾.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read "istuhigga" with a damma on the ta' (passive), and "al-awlayani" in the dual. Regarding the phrase ﴿from among those against whom [it is due]﴾ there are two opinions. The first is that they are the dhimmis (non-Muslim protected subjects). The second is that they are the two guardians (waliyyan). According to the first opinion, there are four views on the meaning of ﴿istahagga ʿalayhim﴾:

The first: the bequest (al-iyṣa') is due against them. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is "from the people concerning whom the bequest is due, which the two heirs of the deceased are entitled to." Likewise al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "from those against whom the bequest or the instruction has become due."

The second: it is injustice (al-zulm). The meaning is: "from those against whom the injustice of the two heirs is due," so "injustice" is omitted and the two heirs are put in its place. Ibn al-Qasim also mentioned this.

The third: it is leaving what they had undertaken of testimony, because of the evidence of their betrayal.

The fourth: it is sin (al-ithm). The meaning is: sin has become due from them, and "ʿalā" stands in place of "min" (from), as in His saying: ﴿who, when they take from people, take in full﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 2], that is, "from people." Al-Farra' said: "ʿalā" has the sense of "fi" (in), as in His saying: ﴿over the kingdom of Solomon﴾ [al-Baqara 102], that is, "in his kingdom." Abu ʿAli al-Farisi mentioned the two opinions. According to these views, the object of "istahagga" is omitted and implied.

According to the second opinion regarding ﴿istahagga ʿalayhim﴾, there are two views:

The first: "the two heirs have a claim from them," and this is the choice of Ibn Qutayba.

The second: "sin has been inflicted upon them" (janā ʿalayhimu l-ithm), mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

As for "al-awlayani," al-Akhfash said: "al-awlayani" are two, the singular of which is "al-awla," and the plural is "al-awlawn." Then the exegetes have two opinions concerning them.

The first: they are the heirs of the deceased, as the majority said. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-awlayani," according to the opinion of most of the Basrans, are in the nominative as a substitute (badal, a grammatical substitute) for the pronoun in "yaqumani," and the meaning is: "Let the two heirs stand in for the deceased in place of these two traitors." Abu ʿAli said: "al-awlayani" must either be in the nominative as the subject of a sentence, or the predicate of an omitted subject, as if he had said: "two others shall stand in their place, they being the two heirs," or it is a substitute for the pronoun in "yaqumani." The implied meaning is: "the two heirs shall stand."

The second opinion: "al-awlayani" are the two dhimmis, and the meaning is: they are the ones entitled through the betrayal. According to this, the meaning is: "they shall stand, except from those against whom [it is due]." A poet said:

*Would that we had a drink of Zamzam's water, chilled, having spent the night at Tahyan.*

That is, as a substitute for Zamzam's water. Qurra' related from Ibn Kathir, Hafs and ʿAsim: "istahagga" with a fatha on the ta' and the ha', "al-awlayani" in the dual. The meaning is: the two heirs have a claim against them concerning the bequest which the deceased made, and the object is omitted. Hamza and Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read: "istuhigga" with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha', and "al-awwalina" with a kasra on the lam and a fatha on the nun, in the plural, and the implied meaning is: "from the first ones (al-awwalin) against whom the sin was due," that is, sin was inflicted upon them, because they had been first in mention. Do you not see that ﴿two just men from among you﴾ was mentioned before His saying: ﴿or two others from outside your own people﴾? Al-Halabi related from ʿAbd al-Warith "al-awwalayni," with a fatha and shadda on the waw, a fatha on the lam, a sukun on the ya', and a kasra on the nun, which is the dual of "awwal." Al-Hasan al-Basri read: "istahagga" with a fatha on the ta' and the ha', and "al-awwalun," the dual of "awwal," as a substitute for His saying: ﴿then two others﴾.

Ibn Qutayba said: the most suitable of the opinions for the verse is that God, exalted is He, intended to teach us how testimony to the bequest is given at the time of approaching death. So He said: ﴿two just men from among you﴾, that is, two just men from among the Muslims [whom you call as witnesses to the bequest], and He knew that among people there is one who travels and is accompanied on his journey by People of the Book and not by Muslims, and who alights at a village inhabited by none but them, and death comes upon him, and he finds no Muslim to witness for him. So He said: ﴿or two others from outside your own people﴾, that is, from outside the people of your religion, [﴿when you journey through the land﴾, that is, when you travel, ﴿and the calamity of death befalls you﴾, and the sentence is complete. So the two just men from among the Muslims are for both the settled and the traveler in general, if it is possible to call them as witnesses while traveling, and the two dhimmis are for the traveler only, when no others are found]. Then He said: ﴿You shall detain them after the prayer, and they swear by God, if you doubt﴾. He intended: detain them after the afternoon prayer, if you doubt their testimony and fear that they have betrayed or altered [anything]. Then if they swear, their testimony stands. ﴿Then if it becomes known﴾ [after this oath], that is, it appears ﴿that the two have become guilty of sin﴾, that is, they have broken the oath with a lie [in a statement], or with betrayal [in a deposit], ﴿then two others﴾, that is, two men stand in place of them in the oath, from among the relatives of the deceased, ﴿against whom the two claimants have a right﴾, and they are the two heirs. It is said: "This one is the nearer (al-awla) to so-and-so," then "with so-and-so" is omitted from the speech, and it is said: "This is the nearer, and these two are the nearer," and "ʿalayhim" means "minhum" (from them). They swear by God: "We have discovered the betrayal and lying of the two dhimmis, and we did not transgress against them, and our testimony is more correct, because of their unbelief and our belief." So they recover from the two dhimmis what they betrayed, and the ruling made by their testimony is annulled. Others said: "our testimony," that is, "our oath is more deserving," and the oath was called a testimony because it is like testimony to what is sworn to, that it is so.

The exegetes said: When this verse was revealed, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs and al-Muttalib ibn Abi Wada'a al-Sahmi stood up and swore by God, and the vessel was handed over to them and to the heirs of the deceased.
﴿And fear Allah﴾: [that you swear falsely], or betray a trust, and listen to the admonition.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the Messengers﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The accusative of "day" (yawm) is governed by His words ﴿and fear Allah﴾, meaning: "and fear the Day of their being gathered by Him." The meaning of His questioning the Messengers is a rebuke to those to whom they were sent. As for the Messengers' words, ﴿We have no knowledge﴾, there are six opinions concerning it.

The first: they will be so overwhelmed that their intellects are dazed when Hell roars, so they say, ﴿We have no knowledge﴾. Then their intellects will be returned to them, and they will set off with their proof. This was related by Abu al-Duha from Ibn Abbas, and al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Suddi also said so.

The second: the meaning is, ﴿We have no knowledge﴾ except for knowledge that You know better than we do. This was related by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas.

The third: what is meant by His words ﴿What response were you given?﴾ is: what did your peoples do after you, and what innovations did they introduce? So they say, ﴿We have no knowledge﴾. This was said by Ibn Jurayj, but it is far-fetched.

The fourth: the meaning is, ﴿We have no knowledge﴾ alongside Your knowledge, because You know the unseen. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The fifth: the meaning is, ﴿We have no knowledge﴾ like Your knowledge, since You know what the people displayed and what they concealed, while we know what they displayed and do not know what they concealed. So Your knowledge of them is more penetrating than ours. This is the view chosen by Ibn al-Anbari.

The sixth: ﴿We have no knowledge﴾ of all their deeds, since we knew some of them during our lifetimes but do not know what happened after our deaths, and reward is only deserved by that with which one's life ends. This was related by Ibn al-Anbari. The exegetes said: when the Prophets refer the knowledge to Allah, the nations will be struck dumb, and they will know that what reached them in the world is not hidden from Him, and that all of them cannot escape His grip.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Knower of the unseen things﴾. Al-Khattabi said: al-ʿAllam (the All-Knowing) has the same meaning as al-ʿAlim (the Knower), and the pattern faʿʿal is a pattern of intensification. As for "al-ghuyub" (the unseen things), it is the plural of ghayb, which is whatever is hidden from you.

(p-454)

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 110:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When Allah said, "O Jesus"⁠﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: its meaning is: "And when He says."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Remember My favour upon you and upon your mother﴾. In His reminding him of the blessings there are two benefits.

The first: making the nations hear of the honour with which He distinguished him.

The second: confirming His proof against those who deny it. Among His blessings upon Maryam is that He chose her and purified her, and brought her provision without any cause. Al-Hasan said: the meaning of "remembering the blessing" is "giving thanks." As for "niʿmah" (blessing), its wording is singular while its meaning is plural. If it is asked: why did He say here ﴿then you blow into it⁠﴾ and in Al ʿImran "fihi" (into it, masculine)? The answer: it is permissible that the mention of the bird is according to the meaning of the collective, and it is made feminine according to the meaning of the group. It is also permissible that "fihi" refers to the bird and "fiha" refers to the form (hayʾah); this was mentioned by Abu ʿAli al-Farisi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is nothing but evident magic⁠﴾. Ibn Kathir and ʿAsim read here, and in Hud and As-Saff, "illa sihrun mubin" (without the alif). And in Yunus he read ﴿innahu la-sahirun mubin⁠﴾ with an alif. Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿAmir read all four with "sihrun mubin" without an alif. Whoever reads "sihr" (magic) refers to what he brought, and whoever reads "sahir" (magician) refers to the person.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 111:

There are two opinions regarding the "revelation" (al-wahy) to the disciples (al-Hawariyyun).

The first: it means "inspiration" (al-ilham). This was said by al-Farra'. As-Suddi said: "He cast it into their hearts."

The second: it means "command" (al-amr), so its meaning is: "I commanded the disciples," and "ila" (to) is extra (silah). This was said by Abu 'Ubayda.

Regarding His saying ﴿and bear witness﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: they meant Allah, exalted is He. The second: 'Isa, peace be upon him.

His saying ﴿that we are Muslims﴾ means: sincere in worship and in monotheism (tawhid). The explanation of what was omitted here has already been given earlier.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 112:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Can your Lord send down to us a table spread with food from heaven?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: That is, "Is He able?" Al-Kisa'i read: "Can you (tastatee`u) ask your Lord" with the taa' and with the Lord in the accusative (naṣb). Al-Farra' said: its meaning is, "Are you able to ask your Lord" [p-456].

Ibn al-Anbari said: No one should suppose that the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) doubted God's power. This is like when a person says to his companion, "Are you able (hal tastati'u) to stand with me?" while he knows that he is able, but he means, "Would it be easy for you?" Abu 'Ali said: the meaning is, "Would He do that if you asked Him?" Some claimed that they said this before their faith and knowledge had become firm, so Jesus answered them with his saying: ﴿Fear God, if you are believers﴾, lest you attribute to Him incapacity. The first view is more sound.

As for "al-ma'idah" (the table), the lexicographers said: al-ma'idah is whatever has food on it from the spread (al-akhwina); if there is no food on it, it is not a ma'idah. And al-ka's (the cup) is any vessel that contains drink; if there is no drink in it, it is not a ka's. Al-Zajjaj related this. Al-Farra' said: I heard some Arabs say of the tray on which a gift is presented: it is al-muhda, with a short vowel (maqsur), as long as the gift is on it; but when it is empty it reverts to its name, whether it is a tray (tabaq), a spread (khiwan), or something else. Al-Zajjaj reported from Abu 'Ubaydah that its form is fa'ilah, but in meaning it is maf'ulah, like ﴿in a pleasing life﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21]. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it derives from giving (al-'ata'), and al-mumtad is the one from whom giving is sought, the form mu'tamal (al-muftaʿal), from whom giving is requested. The poet said:

"To the Commander of the Faithful, the one sought for bounty"

(p-457) And Mada Zayd 'Amran means: he gave 'Amr. Al-Zajjaj said: the origin, in my view, of "ma'idah" is that it is fa'ilah from mada yamidu, meaning it moves, as though it sways with what is upon it. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-ma'idah is food, from madani yamiduni, as though it sways the eaters, that is, gives them, or it is fa'ilah in the sense of maf'ul bih, that is, the eaters are swayed by it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Fear God, if you are believers﴾ — concerning this there are three views.

One: fear Him by not asking Him for trial, for if it descends and you disbelieve, you will be punished. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: [fear Him] by asking Him for what the nations before you did not ask, related by Abu 'Ubayd.

The third: [fear Him] by doubting His power.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 113:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "We want to eat from it"﴾. This is an excuse from them, by which they explained the reason for their request when they were forbidden from it. Regarding their desire to eat from it, there are three opinions.

The first: they wanted this out of need and severe hunger. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: so that they might increase in faith (iman). This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

The third: for seeking blessing (tabarruk) through it. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Regarding His saying, ﴿and our hearts may be at rest﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: our hearts may be at rest that Allah has sent you to us as a prophet.

The second: that Allah has chosen us as your helpers.

The third: that Allah has answered you. Ibn 'Abbas said: 'Isa said to them, "Would you like to fast for Allah thirty days, and then ask Him for nothing without He giving you what you ask?" So they fasted, and then they asked for the table. So the meaning of ﴿and we would know that you have told us the truth﴾ is: that if we fast thirty days, we will not ask Allah for anything without Him giving it to us. Regarding this knowledge there are two opinions. (p-458) One of them: it is a knowledge that arises for them which had not existed before; this is the view of those who said their request came before their knowledge had become firm.

The second: it is an increase of knowledge upon knowledge and certainty upon certainty; this is the view of those who said their request came after their knowing. al-A'mash recited "wa-ta'lama" with a ta' (i.e., "and the hearts may know"), and the meaning is: and the hearts may know that you have told us the truth. Regarding His saying, ﴿among the witnesses﴾, there are four opinions.

The first: among the two witnesses to Allah regarding His power, and to you regarding prophethood. The second: before the Children of Israel when we return to them, for they were with 'Isa in the wilderness at this request. The third: among the witnesses before those who come from our people with what we have witnessed of the signs indicating that you are a prophet.

The fourth: among the witnesses for you before Allah, that you conveyed what you were sent with.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿It will be a festival for us, for the first of us and the last of us﴾. Ibn Muhayṣin, Ibn al-Samayfaʿ and al-Jahdari read ﴿لأوَّلِنا وآخِرِنا﴾ (li-awwalinā wa-ākhirinā) with the hamza raised and the waw lightened, and the meaning is: the day on which it was sent down will be a festival for us, which we and those after us will honour. This is the view of Qatada and al-Suddi. Ka'b said: it was sent down to them on a Sunday, so they took it as a festival. Ibn Qutayba said: ʿĪdan (festival) means a gathering (majmaʿan). Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad said: al-ʿīd (festival) is every day that gathers people, as if they return to it (ʿādū ilayhi). Ibn al-Anbari said: it was called ʿīd because of the return (al-ʿawd) from grief (al-taraḥ) to joy (al-faraḥ).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and a sign from You﴾, that is, a sign from You that points to Your oneness and to the truth of the prophethood of Your Prophet. Ibn al-Samayfaʿ, Ibn Muhayṣin and al-Ḍaḥḥak read ﴿وأنَّهُ مِنك﴾ (wa-annahu minka) with the hamza opened and the nun doubled, (p-459) Regarding His words ﴿وارْزُقْنا﴾ (warzuqnā, "and provide for us") there are two views. One: provide us with that from Your presence. The second: provide us with gratitude for what You have bestowed upon us by answering us.

**The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 5, Verse 115**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah said, "Indeed, I will send it down to you."﴾ Nafi', 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir read "munazzilu-ha" (مُنَزِّلُها) with a shadda (emphatic doubling) on the zay, and the rest read it without a shadda. This is a promise to answer the request of 'Isa (Jesus). The scholars differed on whether it was actually sent down, on two views.

The first view: it was sent down. This is the view of the majority. Wahb ibn Munabbih related from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, from Salman al-Farisi, who said: When 'Isa saw that they were earnest in seeking it, he wore a garment of hair, then performed ablution and ritual bathing, and set his feet in his prayer niche (mihrab, the recess in a wall indicating the direction of prayer) until they were level, joining heel to heel and aligning finger with finger. He placed his right hand upon his left above his chest, lowered his head in humility, and then let his eyes flow with weeping, so that his tears kept running down his cheek and dripping from the edges of his beard, until the earth was wet with his tears in front of his face. Then he raised his head to the sky and said, "O Allah, our Lord, send down upon us a table (ma'idah) from the sky." While 'Isa was thus, a table descended upon us from the sky, a red cloth spread between two clouds, one cloud beneath it and one cloud above it, while 'Isa was weeping and humbly pleading, saying, "My God, make it a blessing and not a punishment," until it settled before him, with the disciples (al-hawariyyun) around him. He and his companions came forward and sat around it, and there, over it, was a covered cloth. 'Isa said, "Whichever of you is most secure in himself and least afflicted before his Lord, let him take this cloth and uncover for us this sign." They said, "O Spirit of Allah, you are most entitled to that, so uncover it." He renewed his ablution, prayed two rak'ahs, and asked his Lord to permit him to uncover it. Then he sat before it, took hold of the cloth, and there, upon it, was a roasted fish with no bones in it. Around it were all kinds of herbs except leeks, at its head was vinegar, at its tail was salt, and around it were five loaves: on one loaf were dates, on another olives, and on another five pomegranates. Shim'un, the head of the disciples, said, "O Spirit of Allah, is this from the food of this world, or from the food of Paradise?" 'Isa said, "Glory be to Allah! Will you not desist? How I fear for you!" Shim'un said, "No, by the God of the Children of Israel, I did not intend any harm by this." 'Isa said, "What you see upon it is neither food of this world nor food of Paradise. It is a thing that Allah originated, and He said to it, 'Be,' and it was, faster than the blink of an eye." The disciples said, "O Spirit of Allah, we only want you to show us a sign in this sign." He said, "Glory be to Allah! Are you not content with this sign?" Then he turned to the fish and said, "Return, by Allah's permission, alive and fresh." It returned, thrashing upon the table. Then he said, "Return as you were," and it returned roasted. He said, "O Spirit of Allah, you should be the first to eat from it." He said, "I seek refuge in Allah! Rather, let whoever asked for it eat from it." When they saw his refusal, they feared that its descent was a punishment. When 'Isa saw that, he invited the poor, the chronically ill, and the orphans to it, and said, "Eat from the provision of your Lord and the supplication of your Prophet, so that its wholesomeness is for you and its punishment is for others." Then there ate from it one thousand and seven hundred people, who departed from it satisfied, while it remained as it was when it descended. Every sick person who ate from it was cured, and every poor person who ate from it became wealthy. Then it descended upon them again, and they crowded around it, so 'Isa divided them into turns. It used to descend upon them for forty days: it descended one day and was absent one day. It used to descend at the height of the forenoon, and they would eat from it until, when they had finished, it rose to the sky while they watched its shadow on the earth.

Qatadah said: It used to descend upon them morning and evening, wherever they were. Others said: It descended twice on Sunday. It was also said: it descended in the morning and evening of Sunday, and for this reason they made it a festival.

Regarding what was upon the table, there are eight views:

The first: it was bread and meat. This is related from 'Ammar ibn Yasir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said, "The table descended from the sky as bread and meat."

The second: it was a roasted fish, five loaves, dates, olives, and pomegranates, which we have mentioned from Salman.

The third: it was fruit from the fruits of Paradise. This was said by 'Ammar ibn Yasir. Qatadah said: fruit from the fruits of Paradise and food from its food.

The fourth: bread and fish. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami also said it.

The fifth: a piece of thareed (bread soaked in broth). This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The sixth: that it brought down upon it everything except meat. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The seventh: a fish containing the taste of every kind of food. This was said by 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi.

The eighth: bread of rice and herbs. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second view: it was not sent down. Qatadah related from al-Hasan that the table was not sent down, because when Allah, Exalted is He, said, ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves after that, I will surely punish him with a punishment I have not inflicted upon anyone among the worlds﴾, they said, "We have no need for it." Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid, who said: A table was sent down with various kinds of food upon it, and he presented it to them and informed them that it would be a punishment if they disbelieved, so they refused it, and it was not sent down. Layth related from Mujahid, who said: This is a parable that Allah, Exalted is He, struck for His creation, to forbid them from asking the prophets for signs, and nothing was sent down to them. The first view is more sound.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves after that﴾, meaning: after the sending down of the table.

Regarding the punishment mentioned, there are two views:

The first: it is transformation (maskh) into animals. The second: it is a kind of punishment with which no one else has been punished.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that it be hastened for them in this world, and it is permissible that it be in the Hereafter.

Regarding "the worlds" (al-'alamin), there are two views: the first, that it is general; the second, that it means the worlds of their own times.

The exegetes mentioned that a group of the people of the table were transformed. Regarding the cause of their transformation, there are three views:

The first: they were commanded not to betray or hoard, but they betrayed and hoarded, so they were transformed into apes and swine. This was narrated by 'Ammar ibn Yasir from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The second: 'Isa restricted the table to the poor, so the wealthy spoke foul words, cast doubt upon the people about it, and became skeptical. When those who doubted it reached the evening and took their beds, Allah transformed them into swine. This was said by Salman al-Farisi.

The third: those who witnessed the table and returned to their people informed them, but those who had not witnessed it mocked them and said, "He has only bewitched your eyes and captivated your hearts." Whoever Allah wills good for remains firm in his insight, and whoever He wills trial for returns to his disbelief. So 'Isa cursed them, and they became swine by morning. They remained for three days, and then they perished. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-463) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when God says, "O Jesus, son of Mary"﴾. There are two views on when this statement will be made.

One is that He will say it to him on the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Jurayj.

The second is that He said it to him when He raised him up to Himself. This was said by al-Suddi. The first is more sound.

Regarding *idh* (when), there are three views.

The first is that it is redundant (*za'ida*), and the meaning is "and God said." This was said by Abu 'Ubayda.

The second is that it retains its original sense, and the meaning is "and when God says it to him." This was said by Ibn Qutayba.

The third is that it means *idha* (whenever/when), as in His saying: ﴿If only you could see when they are terrified﴾ [Saba: 51], meaning "when." Abu al-Najm said:

"Then may God reward you on my behalf, when He rewarded
the Gardens of Eden in the lofty heavens."

The wording of the verse is that of a question, but its meaning is rebuke directed at those who claimed this about Jesus. Abu 'Ubayda said: He said "two gods" because, when they associated the masculine with the feminine, the masculine was given precedence and they were made masculine in form. If it is objected that the Christians did not take Mary as a god, how then does God say this about them? The answer is that when they said, "She did not bear a human being, but she bore a god," it followed for them that, in respect of partnership (*al-ba'diyya*), she is in the position of one who bore him, and so they became in the position of one who said it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Glory be to You"﴾, that is, a declaration of Your freedom from every imperfection. ﴿"It is not for me to say what I have no right to"﴾, that is, I am not entitled to worship, so as to call people to it. 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib related from Maysara, who said: When God, may He be exalted, said to Jesus, ﴿"Did you say to people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides God?'"﴾, every joint of his body trembled until he fell down, for fear that he might have said it. He did not say, "I did not say it," but he said: (If ﴿I have said it, You would have known it﴾).

If it is asked: what is the wisdom in God questioning him about this when He knows he did not say it? The answer is that it establishes the proof against his people and refutes their claim that he had commanded them to it. It is also an affirmation by Jesus of his own incapacity in His saying, ﴿"nor do I know what is in Yourself"﴾, and of his servanthood in His saying, ﴿"Worship God, my Lord and your Lord"﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"You know what is within me, and I do not know what is within You"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: You know what I conceal, and I do not know what is in Your knowledge. The interpretation is: You know what I know, and I do not know what You know.

Allah's words: ﴿That worship Allah﴾. Muqatil said: "Affirm His oneness."

Allah's words: ﴿And I was a witness over them﴾, meaning: over what they did while I was living among them. His words: ﴿When You caused me to die﴾ have two interpretations. One: by raising me up to the sky. The other: by death at the end of the term (of life). "Al-Raqib" (the Watcher) has been explained in Surat al-Nisa', and "al-Shahid" (the Witness) in Al 'Imran.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verse 118:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Almighty, the Most Wise.﴾ Al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliyah said: "If You punish them, it is because they persisted in their disbelief; and if You forgive them, it is because of a repentance that came from them."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Jesus knew that among them were those who believed and those who persisted in disbelief, so he said, speaking of them as a whole: ﴿If You punish them﴾, meaning: if You punish those among them who disbelieved, then indeed they are Your servants, and You are just with them, because You had made the truth clear to them and they disbelieved. And if You forgive them, meaning: if You forgive those among them who gave up (their disbelief) and believed, then that is a bounty from You, because it would have been within Your right not to forgive them after the enormity of their slander. And in Your forgiving them You are Almighty, nothing that You desire is withheld from You, and You are Wise in that."

Ibn al-Anbari said: "The meaning of the speech is: it is not fitting for anyone to object to You. So if You punish them, there is no objection against You; and if You forgive them—though You will not forgive them if they die upon disbelief—there is no objection against You."

Others said: "Pardon does not diminish Your might, nor does it take You outside Your judgment."

Abu Dharr narrated that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood in prayer for a night repeating one verse: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants, and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Almighty, the Most Wise.﴾"

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 5, verses 119–120:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah said, "This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness."﴾ The majority (al-Jumhur) read al-yawm (the day) in the nominative (raf'), while Nafi' read it in the accusative (nasb) as an adverb of time (zarf). Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: Allah said this to Jesus, "on a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness." It is also permissible that the meaning be: Allah said, "This which We have mentioned occurs on a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness." By "the day" is meant the Day of Resurrection. He singled out the benefit of truthfulness for it because it is the Day of Recompense. And concerning this truthfulness there are two opinions.

The first: it is their truthfulness in this world, which benefits them in the Hereafter.

The second: it is their truthfulness in the Hereafter, which benefits them there. And in this verse there is an affirmation of Jesus in what he said.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him﴾, i.e., because of their obedience, and they are pleased with Him because of His reward. And in His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them﴾ there is a reminder of the servanthood of Jesus, and an exhortation to hang one's hopes on Allah alone.
